abstract: Multi-layer perceptrons are often slow to learn nonlinear functions with complex local structure due to the global nature of their function approximations. It is shown that standard multi-layer perceptrons are actually a special case of a more general network formulation that incorporates B-splines into the node computations. This allows novel spline network architectures to be developed that can combine the generalization capabilities and scaling properties of global multi-layer feedforward networks with the computational efficiency and learning speed of local computational paradigms. Simulation results are presented for the well known spiral problem of Weiland and of Lang and Witbrock to show the effectiveness of the Spline Net approach. 1.

paragraphs: The paper addresses slow learning when multilayer perceptrons approximate nonlinear functions with complicated local structure. The authors attribute this difficulty to the global nature of their function approximations. Their proposed response is to incorporate B-splines into node computations, giving the network a broader set of ways to represent a function.

The resulting formulation includes ordinary multilayer perceptrons as a special case. This relationship allows the authors to develop spline network architectures within a framework that also contains familiar feedforward networks. The aim is to combine the generalization and scaling properties of global networks with the computational efficiency and learning speed associated with local computation.

The paper presents simulations on the spiral problem to demonstrate the effectiveness of the Spline Net approach. The significance is the architectural connection between global and local approximation: these become features that can be combined through the node formulation. The reported demonstration supports using spline-based computations to address learning problems whose structure varies in complex ways across the input space.
summary.tldr: Spline networks generalize multilayer perceptrons to combine global approximation properties with efficient local computation.

title: Multi-Layer Perceptrons with B-Spline Receptive Field Functions

paragraphs: The paper presents electronic circuits built around the Neuron MOS transistor, also called neuMOS or vMOS. This device is designed to reproduce neuron-like behavior at the level of a single transistor. The authors use it as a building block for circuits that carry out functions associated with intelligent processing.

One example is searching a memory array for the data most similar to a query directly in hardware. Another is what the authors call Soft Hardware: circuitry whose logic function can change in real time through external control signals, without physically modifying the hardware. These examples emphasize both data-dependent selection and controllable circuit functionality.

The paper also describes a neural network with self-learning capability implemented on the chip. Together, the examples connect the proposed transistor to memory search, reconfigurable logic, and learning. The authors observe architectural similarities between the resulting circuits and biological systems. The main contribution is the implementation of these capabilities using a neuron-like device as a physical circuit primitive.
summary.tldr: Neuron MOS transistors support hardware similarity search, externally reconfigurable logic, and neural circuits with on-chip learning.

title: Implementing Intelligence on Silicon Using Neuron-Like Functional MOS Transistors

The resultant actor/critic algorithm is novel in two ways: it updates the critic only when the most probable action is executed from any given state, and it rewards the actor using cri(cid:173) teria that depend on the relative probability of the action that was executed.

paragraphs: The paper constructs an actor/critic learning algorithm that is equivalent to Q-learning and proves its convergence. In an actor/critic arrangement, the actor represents how actions are selected and the critic represents their evaluation through a value function. The contribution connects this division of responsibilities to a learning method expressed through state-action values.

The equivalence comes from encoding Q-values jointly within the actor's policy and the critic's value function. The two components therefore carry information that Q-learning represents in another form. This is a deliberate mathematical construction, so the connection is stronger than an observation that two independently designed methods sometimes learn similar behavior.

The resulting updates have two distinctive features. The critic changes only when the most probable action in the current state is taken. The actor receives reinforcement according to criteria involving the relative probability of the action actually chosen. These rules are central to the construction. The paper's significance is the demonstrated equivalence and convergence of this particular actor/critic algorithm.
summary.tldr: The paper proves convergence for an actor/critic algorithm constructed to encode and reproduce Q-learning.

title: An Actor/Critic Algorithm that is Equivalent to Q-Learning

abstract: In this paper we introduce new algorithms for optimizing noisy plants in which each experiment is very expensive. The algorithms build a global non-linear model of the expected output at the same time as using Bayesian linear regression analysis of locally weighted polynomial models. The local model answers queries about confi(cid:173) dence, noise, gradient and Hessians, and use them to make auto(cid:173) mated decisions similar to those made by a practitioner of Response Surface Methodology. The global and local models are combined naturally as a locally weighted regression. We examine the ques(cid:173) tion of whether the global model can really help optimization, and we extend it to the case of time-varying functions. We compare the new algorithms with a highly tuned higher-order stochastic op(cid:173) timization algorithm on randomly-generated functions and a sim(cid:173) ulated manufacturing task. We note significant improvements in total regret , time to converge, and final solution quality.

paragraphs: The paper addresses optimization when measurements are noisy and every experiment is expensive. In this setting, an optimizer must make productive use of the observations it has already collected. The proposed algorithms build a global nonlinear model of expected output while also performing Bayesian analysis of locally weighted polynomial models.

The local models provide estimates of uncertainty, noise, gradients, and curvature. These quantities guide automated decisions resembling those a practitioner would make in response surface methodology. Global and local information are brought together through locally weighted regression, linking the broader response model with detailed information around a candidate operating region.

The authors investigate whether the global model helps optimization and extend the approach to functions that change over time. Comparisons use randomly generated functions and a simulated manufacturing task against a carefully tuned higher-order stochastic optimizer. They report improvements in total regret, convergence time, and final solution quality. The findings support using accumulated observations for both modeling the response and directing subsequent expensive experiments.
summary.tldr: Combining global response models with local Bayesian estimates improves optimization when experiments are noisy and costly.

title: Memory-based Stochastic Optimization

abstract: This paper develops arguments for a family of temporal log-linear models to represent spatio-temporal correlations among the spiking events in a group of neurons. The models can represent not just pairwise correlations but also correlations of higher order. Methods are discussed for inferring the existence or absence of correlations and estimating their strength. A frequentist and a Bayesian approach to correlation detection are compared. The frequentist method is based on G 2 statistic with estimates obtained via the Max-Ent principle. In the Bayesian approach a Markov Chain Monte Carlo Model Composition (MC3) algorithm is applied to search over connectivity structures and Laplace's method is used to approximate their posterior probability. Performance of the methods was tested on synthetic data. The methods were applied to experimental data obtained by the fourth author by means of measurements carried out on behaving Rhesus monkeys at the Hadassah Medical School of the Hebrew University. As conjectured, neural connectivity structures need not be neither hierarchical nor decomposable. Learning Quasi-synchronization Patterns among Spiking Neurons 77

paragraphs: Neurons can exhibit coordinated spike timing involving more than two cells at once. This paper develops temporal log-linear models for describing such patterns across neurons and time. The models include higher-order correlations, allowing the analysis to ask whether a group relationship exists beyond the pairwise relationships among its members.

The authors compare two approaches to detecting correlations and estimating their strength. The frequentist approach uses a G-squared statistic with maximum-entropy estimates. The Bayesian approach searches possible connectivity structures through Markov Chain Monte Carlo Model Composition and uses Laplace's method to approximate their posterior probabilities. Both approaches address which relationships the data support.

The methods were tested on synthetic data and applied to recordings from behaving rhesus monkeys. The reported conclusion is that neural connectivity structures need not be hierarchical or decomposable. This matters for model design: restricting the allowable organization to those convenient forms could exclude structures relevant to the observed coordination. The framework makes richer patterns available for statistical investigation.
summary.tldr: Temporal log-linear models detect pairwise and higher-order spike correlations without requiring hierarchical or decomposable connectivity structures.

title: Learning Exact Patterns of Quasi-synchronization among Spiking Neurons from Data on Multi-unit Recordings

abstract: We discuss a solution to the problem of separating waveforms pro(cid:173) duced by multiple cells in an extracellular neural recording. We take an explicitly probabilistic approach, using latent-variable mod(cid:173) els of varying sophistication to describe the distribution of wave(cid:173) forms produced by a single cell. The models range from a single Gaussian distribution of waveforms for each cell to a mixture of hidden Markov models. We stress the overall statistical structure of the approach, allowing the details of the generative model chosen to depend on the specific neural preparation.

paragraphs: An extracellular recording can contain waveforms generated by several nearby neurons. Separating those contributions requires describing how waveforms from the same cell vary and distinguishing that variation from differences between cells. This paper frames the task explicitly as probabilistic inference, using models of how individual cells generate their recorded waveforms.

The proposed models contain latent variables: aspects of the generating process that are not directly observed in the recording. Their complexity ranges from a single Gaussian distribution for each cell to a mixture of hidden Markov models. These alternatives offer different levels of detail for describing the distribution of waveforms associated with a cell.

The authors emphasize the common statistical framework rather than prescribing one generative model for every experiment. The model's details can be chosen to match the specific neural preparation. This matters because waveform separation then rests on an explicit account of within-cell variability. It provides a structured way to relate assumptions about recorded signals to the inference of their cellular origins.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic latent-variable models separate neighboring neurons' waveforms while allowing the signal model to suit the recording preparation.

title: On the Separation of Signals from Neighboring Cells in Tetrode Recordings

abstract: We present a simple approach for computing reasonable policies for factored Markov decision processes (MDPs), when the opti(cid:173) mal value function can be approximated by a compact linear form. Our method is based on solving a single linear program that ap(cid:173) proximates the best linear fit to the optimal value function. By applying an efficient constraint generation procedure we obtain an iterative solution method that tackles concise linear programs. This direct linear programming approach experimentally yields a signif(cid:173) icant reduction in computation time over approximate value- and policy-iteration methods (sometimes reducing several hours to a few seconds). However, the quality of the solutions produced by linear programming is weaker-usually about twice the approxi(cid:173) mation error for the same approximating class. Nevertheless, the speed advantage allows one to use larger approximation classes to achieve similar error in reasonable time.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a direct way to compute reasonable policies for factored Markov decision processes. Its starting assumption is that a compact linear representation can approximate the optimal value function, which describes the value of states for decision making. The method seeks a useful approximation within that representation.

The approach formulates a single linear program that approximates the best linear fit to the optimal value function. An efficient constraint-generation procedure turns its solution into an iterative process involving concise linear programs. This provides a route to value approximation that differs from repeatedly applying approximate value iteration or policy iteration.

Experiments show a substantial speed advantage, sometimes reducing computation from hours to seconds. That gain comes with weaker solutions within the same approximation class: the reported approximation error is usually about twice as large. The authors argue that the saved computation allows larger approximation classes to be used, making similar error achievable in reasonable time. The result is therefore a practical tradeoff between speed and representational richness.
summary.tldr: Direct linear programming speeds up value approximation for factored MDPs, trading larger same-class error for room to use richer approximations.

title: Direct value-approximation for factored MDPs

abstract: There is growing evidence from psychophysical and neurophysiological studies that the brain utilizes Bayesian principles for inference and de- cision making. An important open question is how Bayesian inference for arbitrary graphical models can be implemented in networks of spik- ing neurons. In this paper, we show that recurrent networks of noisy integrate-and-fire neurons can perform approximate Bayesian inference for dynamic and hierarchical graphical models. The membrane potential dynamics of neurons is used to implement belief propagation in the log domain. The spiking probability of a neuron is shown to approximate the posterior probability of the preferred state encoded by the neuron, given past inputs. We illustrate the model using two examples: (1) a motion de- tection network in which the spiking probability of a direction-selective neuron becomes proportional to the posterior probability of motion in a preferred direction, and (2) a two-level hierarchical network that pro- duces attentional effects similar to those observed in visual cortical areas V2 and V4. The hierarchical model offers a new Bayesian interpretation of attentional modulation in V2 and V4.

paragraphs: Evidence that perception follows Bayesian principles raises a mechanistic question: how could networks of spiking neurons perform the required inference? This paper constructs recurrent networks of noisy integrate-and-fire neurons that carry out approximate Bayesian inference for dynamic and hierarchical graphical models.

The proposed connection uses changes in neuronal membrane potential to implement belief propagation in logarithmic form. A neuron's probability of firing approximates the posterior probability of its preferred state, given earlier inputs. Neural activity therefore has a probabilistic interpretation: firing likelihood represents the model's updated belief about a particular state.

Two examples illustrate the construction. In a motion network, a direction-selective neuron's firing probability becomes proportional to the posterior probability of motion in its preferred direction. A two-level hierarchical network produces attentional effects resembling observations in visual areas V2 and V4. These examples support a possible neural implementation of approximate inference and offer a Bayesian interpretation of attentional modulation, without establishing that biological circuits necessarily use this mechanism.
summary.tldr: Recurrent networks of noisy spiking neurons implement approximate Bayesian inference and reproduce examples of motion coding and attention-related effects.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian Inference in Networks of Spiking Neurons

abstract: This paper presents an application of Boosting for classifying labeled graphs, general structures for modeling a number of real-world data, such as chemical compounds, natural language texts, and bio sequences. The proposal consists of i) decision stumps that use subgraph as features, and ii) a Boosting algorithm in which subgraph-based decision stumps are used as weak learners. We also discuss the relation between our algorithm and SVMs with convolution kernels. Two experiments using natural language data and chemical compounds show that our method achieves comparable or even better performance than SVMs with convolution kernels as well as improves the testing efficiency.
originalAbstract: This paper presents an application of Boosting for classifying labeled graphs, general structures for modeling a number of real-world data, such as chemical compounds, natural language texts, and bio sequences. The proposal consists of i) decision stumps that use subgraph as features, and ii) a Boosting algorithm in which subgraph-based decision stumps are used as weak learners. We also discuss the relation between our algorithm and SVMs with convolution kernels. Two experiments using natural language data and chemical compounds show that our method achieves comparable or even better performance than SVMs with convolution kernels as well as improves the testing efficiency.

paragraphs: The paper develops a classifier for labeled graphs, structures that can represent objects such as chemical compounds, language data, and biological sequences. In this setting, useful information lies in the graph's component structures. The authors use subgraphs as features, allowing the classifier to base its decisions on patterns within the larger object.

The method combines simple subgraph-based decision rules through boosting. Each individual rule is a decision stump, serving as a weak learner in the overall algorithm. This provides a way to build a graph classifier from many simple structural judgments. The paper also discusses how this approach relates to support vector machines using convolution kernels.

Two experiments, involving natural-language data and chemical compounds, compare the method with those support vector machines. The reported predictive performance is comparable or better, while testing efficiency improves. These findings support the approach on the evaluated tasks: subgraph-based boosting can provide useful classification performance together with more efficient prediction.
summary.tldr: Boosting simple subgraph-based classifiers matches or improves on convolution-kernel SVM performance while improving testing efficiency in two experiments.

title: An Application of Boosting to Graph Classification

abstract: An auditory "scene", composed of overlapping acoustic sources, can be viewed as a complex object whose constituent parts are the individual sources. Pitch is known to be an important cue for auditory scene analy- sis. In this paper, with the goal of building agents that operate in human environments, we describe a real-time system to identify the presence of one or more voices and compute their pitch. The signal processing in the front end is based on instantaneous frequency estimation, a method for tracking the partials of voiced speech, while the pattern-matching in the back end is based on nonnegative matrix factorization, an unsupervised algorithm for learning the parts of complex objects. While supporting a framework to analyze complicated auditory scenes, our system maintains real-time operability and state-of-the-art performance in clean speech.

paragraphs: The paper treats an auditory scene as a collection of overlapping sound sources whose individual contributions need to be identified. Pitch is an important cue for this task. With agents operating in human environments as its motivation, the work presents a real-time system for detecting the presence of one or more voices and estimating their pitches.

The system joins two processing stages. The front end uses instantaneous-frequency estimation to track partials in voiced speech. The back end performs pattern matching with nonnegative matrix factorization, an unsupervised method for learning parts of complex objects. Together, these stages connect a representation of speech's frequency components with a method for identifying constituent patterns.

The authors report that the system maintains real-time operation and state-of-the-art performance on clean speech while supporting a framework for more complicated auditory scenes. Those claims have different scopes: clean speech is the stated setting for the performance comparison, whereas multiple overlapping sources motivate the broader framework. The contribution is their integration into a working pitch-analysis system.
summary.tldr: The system combines instantaneous-frequency tracking and nonnegative matrix factorization for real-time voice detection and pitch estimation.

title: Real-Time Pitch Determination of One or More Voices by Nonnegative Matrix Factorization

abstract: We consider the situation in semi-supervised learning, where the “label sampling” mechanism stochastically depends on the true response (as well as potentially on the features). We suggest a method of moments for estimating this stochastic dependence using the unlabeled data. This is potentially useful for two distinct purposes: a. As an input to a supervised learning procedure which can be used to “de-bias” its results using labeled data only and b. As a potentially interesting learning task in itself. We present several examples to illustrate the practical usefulness of our method.
originalAbstract: We consider the situation in semi-supervised learning, where the “label sampling” mechanism stochastically depends on the true response (as well as potentially on the features). We suggest a method of moments for estimating this stochastic dependence using the unlabeled data. This is potentially useful for two distinct purposes: a. As an input to a supervised learning procedure which can be used to “de-bias” its results using labeled data only and b. As a potentially interesting learning task in itself. We present several examples to illustrate the practical usefulness of our method.

paragraphs: In semi-supervised learning, some examples have observed labels and others do not. This paper considers a setting where the chance of receiving a label depends on the true response, and possibly also on the example's features. Consequently, the labeled examples can reflect the process that selected them as well as the underlying population.

The authors propose using unlabeled data to estimate this selection process. Their approach uses a method of moments: it estimates the stochastic dependence through statistical quantities rather than treating label availability as unrelated to the response. The object being learned is therefore the mechanism governing which labels become visible, a separate target from predicting those labels.

The estimated mechanism has two potential uses. It could inform a supervised procedure that corrects selection bias while subsequently using labeled data only. Alternatively, understanding how labels are sampled may itself be valuable. The paper illustrates practical usefulness through several examples; the proposed correction remains a potential application rather than an unconditional promise of unbiased predictions.
summary.tldr: The paper uses unlabeled data to estimate response-dependent label sampling, potentially enabling correction of selection bias.

title: A Method for Inferring Label Sampling Mechanisms in Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: We devise and experiment with a dynamical kernel-based system for tracking hand movements from neural activity. The state of the system corresponds to the hand location, velocity, and acceleration, while the system’s input are the instantaneous spike rates. The system’s state dynamics is defined as a combination of a linear mapping from the previous estimated state and a kernel-based mapping tailored for modeling neural activities. In contrast to generative models, the activity-to-state mapping is learned using discriminative methods by minimizing a noise-robust loss function. We use this approach to predict hand trajectories on the basis of neural activity in motor cortex of behaving monkeys and find that the proposed approach is more accurate than both a static approach based on support vector regression and the Kalman filter.

paragraphs: The paper develops a system that reconstructs hand movement from neural activity while explicitly tracking how movement evolves over time. Its internal state contains hand position, velocity, and acceleration, and its incoming measurements are instantaneous neural spike rates. The task is therefore to recover a changing trajectory from a stream of neural observations.

Each state estimate combines two contributions: a linear transformation of the previous estimated state and a kernel-based mapping designed to model neural activity. This allows earlier movement estimates and current neural signals to inform the next prediction together. The activity-to-state mapping is trained directly with a loss function designed to be robust to noise.

The authors test the approach using motor-cortex activity from behaving monkeys. In those experiments, it predicts hand trajectories more accurately than both static support vector regression and a Kalman filter. These findings support the usefulness of combining temporal state information with a learned kernel mapping for the evaluated neural decoding task.
summary.tldr: A temporal kernel model combines previous movement estimates with neural spike rates to improve hand-trajectory prediction in monkey recordings.

title: A Temporal Kernel-Based Model for Tracking Hand Movements from Neural Activities

abstract: We propose a new approach for dealing with the estimation of the location of change-points in one-dimensional piecewise constant signals observed in white noise. Our approach consists in reframing this task in a variable selection context. We use a penalized least-squares criterion with a l1-type penalty for this purpose. We prove that, in an appropriate asymptotic framework, this method provides consistent estimators of the change-points. Then, we explain how to implement this method in practice by combining the LAR algorithm and a reduced version of the dynamic programming algorithm and we apply it to synthetic and real data.
originalAbstract: We propose a new approach for dealing with the estimation of the location of change-points in one-dimensional piecewise constant signals observed in white noise. Our approach consists in reframing this task in a variable selection context. We use a penalized least-squares criterion with a l1-type penalty for this purpose. We prove that, in an appropriate asymptotic framework, this method provides consistent estimators of the change-points. Then, we explain how to implement this method in practice by combining the LAR algorithm and a reduced version of the dynamic programming algorithm and we apply it to synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to locate abrupt changes in a one-dimensional signal that stays constant between changes and is observed in white noise. The challenge is to distinguish genuine shifts in the underlying level from fluctuations introduced by noise. Its approach translates the search for change locations into a variable-selection problem.

The method uses a least-squares fitting criterion together with an l1-type penalty. In this formulation, selecting variables corresponds to identifying changes in the signal. The penalty makes selection part of the fitting objective, connecting change-point estimation to sparse regression methods rather than treating every possible change location as an independent decision.

The authors prove consistency of the estimated change points within an appropriate asymptotic framework. This is a qualified large-sample result, rather than a claim of exact recovery for every noisy signal. For practical implementation, they combine the LAR algorithm with a reduced dynamic-programming procedure and apply the method to synthetic and real data. The contribution links a statistical guarantee to a concrete computational approach.
summary.tldr: Recasting change-point detection as sparse variable selection yields an l1-penalized method with consistency guarantees in an appropriate asymptotic setting.

title: Catching Change-points with Lasso

abstract: Randomized neural networks are immortalized in this AI Koan: In the days when Sussman was a novice, Minsky once came to him as he sat hacking at the PDP-6. What are you doing?'' asked Minsky. I am training a randomly wired neural net to play tic-tac-toe,'' Sussman replied. Why is the net wired randomly?'' asked Minsky. Sussman replied, I do not want it to have any preconceptions of how to play.'' Minsky then shut his eyes. Why do you close your eyes?'' Sussman asked his teacher. So that the room will be empty,'' replied Minsky. At that moment, Sussman was enlightened. We analyze shallow random networks with the help of concentration of measure inequalities. Specifically, we consider architectures that compute a weighted sum of their inputs after passing them through a bank of arbitrary randomized nonlinearities. We identify conditions under which these networks exhibit good classification performance, and bound their test error in terms of the size of the dataset and the number of random nonlinearities.

What are you doing?'' asked Minsky. I am training a randomly wired neural net to play tic-tac-toe,'' Sussman replied. Why is the net wired randomly?'' asked Minsky. Sussman replied, I do not want it to have any preconceptions of how to play.'' Minsky then shut his eyes. Why do you close your eyes?'' Sussman asked his teacher. So that the room will be empty,'' replied Minsky. At that moment, Sussman was enlightened. We analyze shallow random networks with the help of concentration of measure inequalities. Specifically, we consider architectures that compute a weighted sum of their inputs after passing them through a bank of arbitrary randomized nonlinearities. We identify conditions under which these networks exhibit good classification performance, and bound their test error in terms of the size of the dataset and the number of random nonlinearities.

paragraphs: This paper studies shallow networks that process inputs through a bank of randomized nonlinear transformations and combine the resulting values in a weighted sum. The question is whether this kind of random construction can support good classification. Randomness defines the intermediate transformations, while the final weighted combination supplies the network's prediction.

The authors analyze these architectures using concentration-of-measure inequalities, mathematical tools for controlling the behavior of random quantities. They identify conditions under which the networks classify well. This makes the role of randomization precise: the results depend on stated conditions, rather than asserting that any arbitrary random network will necessarily be a useful classifier.

The analysis bounds test error in terms of both the amount of training data and the number of randomized nonlinearities. Those quantities describe two distinct resources: examples available for learning and transformations available for representing the input. Relating both to prediction error gives a theoretical basis for evaluating randomized representations and clarifies how the size of the random feature bank enters the learning guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper gives conditional classification guarantees for weighted random nonlinear features, bounding test error by data and feature counts.

title: Weighted Sums of Random Kitchen Sinks: Replacing minimization with randomization in learning

abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm, based upon the dependent Dirichlet process mixture model (DDPMM), for clustering batch-sequential data containing an unknown number of evolving clusters. The algorithm is derived via a low-variance asymptotic analysis of the Gibbs sampling algorithm for the DDPMM, and provides a hard clustering with convergence guarantees similar to those of the k-means algorithm. Empirical results from a synthetic test with moving Gaussian clusters and a test with real ADS-B aircraft trajectory data demonstrate that the algorithm requires orders of magnitude less computational time than contemporary probabilistic and hard clustering algorithms, while providing higher accuracy on the examined datasets.

paragraphs: Clustering sequential batches of data becomes difficult when groups evolve and their number is unknown. The paper develops an algorithm for this setting from the dependent Dirichlet process mixture model. Its aim is to retain a model of changing clusters while making the actual clustering computation substantially faster.

The authors derive the procedure by examining the low-variance limit of a Gibbs sampling algorithm for that model. The resulting method produces hard assignments, placing observations into individual clusters. It also has convergence guarantees resembling those of k-means, connecting a probabilistic model of evolving groups to a simpler clustering procedure.

Evaluation uses moving Gaussian clusters in synthetic data and real aircraft trajectories recorded through ADS-B. On those datasets, the method takes orders of magnitude less computation time than the contemporary probabilistic and hard clustering methods considered, while also achieving higher accuracy. These findings support the value of the asymptotic derivation for the tested dynamic clustering problems. The reported speed and accuracy advantages are empirical results on those datasets, rather than universal performance guarantees.
summary.tldr: A low-variance derivation turns a dependent mixture model into an efficient hard-clustering algorithm for unknown numbers of evolving groups.

title: Dynamic Clustering via Asymptotics of the Dependent Dirichlet Process Mixture

abstract: A common assumption in machine vision is that the training and test samples are drawn from the same distribution. However, there are many problems when this assumption is grossly violated, as in bio-medical applications where different acquisitions can generate drastic variations in the appearance of the data due to changing experimental conditions. This problem is accentuated with 3D data, for which annotation is very time-consuming, limiting the amount of data that can be labeled in new acquisitions for training. In this paper we present a multi-task learning algorithm for domain adaptation based on boosting. Unlike previous approaches that learn task-specific decision boundaries, our method learns a single decision boundary in a shared feature space, common to all tasks. We use the boosting-trick to learn a non-linear mapping of the observations in each task, with no need for specific a-priori knowledge of its global analytical form. This yields a more parameter-free domain adaptation approach that successfully leverages learning on new tasks where labeled data is scarce. We evaluate our approach on two challenging bio-medical datasets and achieve a significant improvement over the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: This paper addresses domain adaptation when training images and new images have substantially different appearances. Biomedical acquisitions motivate the problem: changes in experimental conditions can alter the data, while annotating new three-dimensional images is time-consuming. The goal is to use learning across tasks when a new acquisition has few labeled examples.

The proposed multi-task algorithm uses boosting to learn nonlinear mappings for the observations in each task. These mappings place the tasks in a shared feature space with a single decision boundary. Instead of specifying the global analytical form of each mapping in advance, the boosting construction learns the transformation as part of the adaptation procedure.

The authors describe the resulting approach as more parameter-free and evaluate it on two challenging biomedical datasets. They report a significant improvement over the state of the art in those experiments. The main contribution is a way to share the classification rule while allowing task-specific changes in representation, supporting transfer to new tasks with limited labeled data.
summary.tldr: Boosting learns nonlinear task-specific mappings into a shared classification space, improving domain adaptation on two biomedical datasets.

title: Non-Linear Domain Adaptation with Boosting

abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA), a well-established technique for data analysis and processing, provides a convenient form of dimensionality reduction that is effective for cleaning small Gaussian noises presented in the data. However, the applicability of standard principal component analysis in real scenarios is limited by its sensitivity to large errors. In this paper, we tackle the challenge problem of recovering data corrupted with errors of high magnitude by developing a novel robust transfer principal component analysis method. Our method is based on the assumption that useful information for the recovery of a corrupted data matrix can be gained from an uncorrupted related data matrix. Speciﬁcally, we formulate the data recovery problem as a joint robust principal component analysis problem on the two data matrices, with shared common principal components across matrices and individual principal components speciﬁc to each data matrix. The formulated optimization problem is a minimization problem over a convex objective function but with non-convex rank constraints. We develop an efﬁcient proximal projected gradient descent algorithm to solve the proposed optimization problem with convergence guarantees. Our empirical results over image denoising tasks show the proposed method can effectively recover images with random large errors, and signiﬁcantly outperform both standard PCA and robust PCA.

paragraphs: Standard principal component analysis can clean small Gaussian noise but is sensitive to large errors. This paper tackles recovery from high-magnitude corruption by borrowing information from a related, uncorrupted data matrix. The availability of useful information in that related matrix is an explicit assumption of the approach.

The authors jointly model the corrupted and clean matrices with robust principal component analysis. Some principal components are shared across the matrices, while others remain specific to each. This structure allows recovery to use common information without requiring both datasets to have identical components. The resulting optimization problem has a convex objective together with nonconvex rank constraints.

An efficient proximal projected gradient descent algorithm is developed with convergence guarantees. In image-denoising experiments, the method effectively recovers images containing random large errors and significantly outperforms both standard PCA and robust PCA. These findings support transfer from related clean data in the evaluated setting. The convergence statement accompanies the proposed solver; the abstract does not identify it as a guarantee of globally optimal recovery.
summary.tldr: Jointly modeling corrupted data and related clean data improves recovery from large image errors through shared and dataset-specific principal components.

title: Robust Transfer Principal Component Analysis with Rank Constraints

abstract: We use the notion of local Rademacher complexity to design new algorithms for learning kernels. Our algorithms thereby benefit from the sharper learning bounds based on that notion which, under certain general conditions, guarantee a faster convergence rate. We devise two new learning kernel algorithms: one based on a convex optimization problem for which we give an efficient solution using existing learning kernel techniques, and another one that can be formulated as a DC-programming problem for which we describe a solution in detail. We also report the results of experiments with both algorithms in both binary and multi-class classification tasks.

We devise two new learning kernel algorithms: one based on a convex optimization problem for which we give an efficient solution using existing learning kernel techniques, and another one that can be formulated as a DC-programming problem for which we describe a solution in detail. We also report the results of experiments with both algorithms in both binary and multi-class classification tasks.

paragraphs: Kernel learning chooses a similarity representation suited to a learning task. This paper designs kernel-learning algorithms using local Rademacher complexity, a quantity that supports sharper learning bounds. Under certain general conditions, those bounds guarantee faster convergence, giving the authors a theoretical reason to use this complexity measure in algorithm design.

The paper develops two approaches. One leads to a convex optimization problem and can be solved efficiently using existing kernel-learning techniques. The other is expressed as a difference-of-convex, or DC, programming problem, for which the authors describe a solution procedure in detail. These formulations provide different routes from the same complexity-based motivation to practical optimization.

Both algorithms are evaluated on binary and multiclass classification tasks. The abstract reports these experiments without specifying a comparative performance outcome. The main stated contribution is therefore the construction of two kernel-learning methods grounded in sharper bounds, together with procedures for solving their optimization problems. The faster convergence guarantee retains its dependence on the conditions required by the theory.
summary.tldr: Two kernel-learning algorithms use local Rademacher complexity to benefit from sharper bounds that guarantee faster convergence under stated conditions.

title: Learning Kernels Using Local Rademacher Complexity

abstract: An associative memory is a structure learned from a dataset $\mathcal{M}$ of vectors (signals) in a way such that, given a noisy version of one of the vectors as input, the nearest valid vector from $\mathcal{M}$ (nearest neighbor) is provided as output, preferably via a fast iterative algorithm. Traditionally, binary (or $q$-ary) Hopfield neural networks are used to model the above structure. In this paper, for the first time, we propose a model of associative memory based on sparse recovery of signals. Our basic premise is simple. For a dataset, we learn a set of linear constraints that every vector in the dataset must satisfy. Provided these linear constraints possess some special properties, it is possible to cast the task of finding nearest neighbor as a sparse recovery problem. Assuming generic random models for the dataset, we show that it is possible to store super-polynomial or exponential number of $n$-length vectors in a neural network of size $O(n)$. Furthermore, given a noisy version of one of the stored vectors corrupted in near-linear number of coordinates, the vector can be correctly recalled using a neurally feasible algorithm.

paragraphs: An associative memory retrieves a valid stored vector when given a corrupted version. This paper proposes a sparse-recovery formulation of that task. Instead of starting from the traditional Hopfield-network approach, it learns linear constraints that all vectors in the dataset must satisfy.

When those constraints have suitable properties, finding the nearest valid vector can be expressed as a sparse recovery problem. The constraint structure is therefore central: it connects the learned representation of the dataset with the procedure for correcting corruption. The model uses that connection to develop a recall algorithm that the authors describe as neurally feasible.

They also establish correct recall when a stored vector is corrupted in a near-linear number of coordinates. These capacity and correction results are tied to the stated dataset assumptions and constraint properties, demonstrating what the sparse-recovery construction can achieve in that setting.
summary.tldr: Under suitable constraint properties and random dataset models, sparse recovery enables compact associative memories with large storage capacity and substantial error correction.

title: Associative Memory via a Sparse Recovery Model

abstract: Variational inference is an umbrella term for algorithms which cast Bayesian inference as optimization. Classically, variational inference uses the Kullback-Leibler divergence to define the optimization. Though this divergence has been widely used, the resultant posterior approximation can suffer from undesirable statistical properties. To address this, we reexamine variational inference from its roots as an optimization problem. We use operators, or functions of functions, to design variational objectives. As one example, we design a variational objective with a Langevin-Stein operator. We develop a black box algorithm, operator variational inference (OPVI), for optimizing any operator objective. Importantly, operators enable us to make explicit the statistical and computational tradeoffs for variational inference. We can characterize different properties of variational objectives, such as objectives that admit data subsampling---allowing inference to scale to massive data---as well as objectives that admit variational programs---a rich class of posterior approximations that does not require a tractable density. We illustrate the benefits of OPVI on a mixture model and a generative model of images.

paragraphs: Variational inference turns Bayesian inference into an optimization problem. A common choice is to optimize a Kullback-Leibler divergence, but the resulting posterior approximation can have undesirable statistical properties. This paper revisits the choice of objective, asking how alternative objectives can make the statistical and computational tradeoffs of approximation more explicit.

The authors construct objectives using operators, which are functions acting on other functions. A Langevin-Stein operator supplies one example. They also develop operator variational inference, or OPVI, as a black-box algorithm for optimizing operator objectives. The framework separates designing an objective with useful properties from providing a general procedure for optimizing it.

Different operator objectives can support different capabilities. Some permit data subsampling, helping inference scale to large datasets; others admit variational programs, expressive posterior approximations that need not have a tractable density. The paper characterizes such properties and illustrates OPVI on a mixture model and an image generative model. Its contribution is a broader design framework for inference objectives and their associated tradeoffs.
summary.tldr: Operator variational inference builds and optimizes alternative posterior-approximation objectives with explicit statistical and computational tradeoffs.

title: Operator Variational Inference

abstract: In this paper, we study the {\em pooled data} problem of identifying the labels associated with a large collection of items, based on a sequence of pooled tests revealing the counts of each label within the pool. In the noiseless setting, we identify an exact asymptotic threshold on the required number of tests with optimal decoding, and prove a {\em phase transition} between complete success and complete failure. In addition, we present a novel {\em noisy} variation of the problem, and provide an information-theoretic framework for characterizing the required number of tests for general random noise models. Our results reveal that noise can make the problem considerably more difficult, with strict increases in the scaling laws even at low noise levels. Finally, we demonstrate similar behavior in an {\em approximate recovery} setting, where a given number of errors is allowed in the decoded labels.

paragraphs: In the pooled data problem, each test examines a group of items and reports how many items carry each label. The task is to reconstruct the individual labels from these aggregate counts. This paper asks how many pooled tests are fundamentally required, distinguishing the information contained in the observations from the mechanics of a particular decoding algorithm.

For noiseless observations and optimal decoding, the authors identify an exact asymptotic threshold in the number of tests. They prove a phase transition separating complete recovery from complete failure. This describes a sharp change in what is recoverable as the available number of tests crosses the threshold in the asymptotic setting.

The paper also introduces a noisy version and develops an information-theoretic framework for general random noise models. Its results show that even low noise can strictly worsen the scaling of the required test count. Similar behavior appears when some labeling mistakes are permitted, showing that allowing approximate recovery does not eliminate the demonstrated sensitivity to noise.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies a sharp noiseless recovery threshold for pooled labels and shows that even low noise can worsen required test-count scaling.

title: Phase Transitions in the Pooled Data Problem

abstract: We formulate a supervised learning problem, referred to as continuous ranking, where a continuous real-valued label Y is assigned to an observable r.v. X taking its values in a feature space X and the goal is to order all possible observations x in X by means of a scoring function s : X → R so that s(X) and Y tend to increase or decrease together with highest probability. This problem generalizes bi/multi-partite ranking to a certain extent and the task of finding optimal scoring functions s(x) can be naturally cast as optimization of a dedicated functional cri- terion, called the IROC curve here, or as maximization of the Kendall τ related to the pair (s(X), Y ). From the theoretical side, we describe the optimal elements of this problem and provide statistical guarantees for empirical Kendall τ maximiza- tion under appropriate conditions for the class of scoring function candidates. We also propose a recursive statistical learning algorithm tailored to empirical IROC curve optimization and producing a piecewise constant scoring function that is fully described by an oriented binary tree. Preliminary numerical experiments highlight the difference in nature between regression and continuous ranking and provide strong empirical evidence of the performance of empirical optimizers of the criteria proposed.

paragraphs: When labels are continuous numbers, a learning task can focus on ordering observations so their scores track those labels. This paper formalizes that objective as continuous ranking. The desired scoring function makes scores and labels move together with high probability, emphasizing the quality of the induced ordering.

The authors express the learning objective through an IROC curve or Kendall’s tau, which measures agreement between the score ordering and label ordering. They characterize optimal solutions and give statistical guarantees for maximizing empirical Kendall’s tau under appropriate conditions on the candidate scoring functions. This establishes a theoretical basis for learning directly from a ranking criterion.

They also propose a recursive algorithm for empirical IROC optimization. It produces a piecewise-constant score described by an oriented binary tree. Preliminary numerical experiments highlight the distinction between continuous ranking and regression and provide strong empirical evidence for the proposed optimization criteria. The work thus supplies a problem formulation, conditional guarantees, and a concrete tree-based learning method.
summary.tldr: Continuous ranking learns score orderings for real-valued labels using dedicated criteria and a recursive tree-based algorithm.

title: Ranking Data with Continuous Labels through Oriented Recursive Partitions

abstract: In this paper, we propose a Runtime Neural Pruning (RNP) framework which prunes the deep neural network dynamically at the runtime. Unlike existing neural pruning methods which produce a fixed pruned model for deployment, our method preserves the full ability of the original network and conducts pruning according to the input image and current feature maps adaptively. The pruning is performed in a bottom-up, layer-by-layer manner, which we model as a Markov decision process and use reinforcement learning for training. The agent judges the importance of each convolutional kernel and conducts channel-wise pruning conditioned on different samples, where the network is pruned more when the image is easier for the task. Since the ability of network is fully preserved, the balance point is easily adjustable according to the available resources. Our method can be applied to off-the-shelf network structures and reach a better tradeoff between speed and accuracy, especially with a large pruning rate.

paragraphs: Runtime Neural Pruning adapts a network's computation to the image it is processing. The framework retains the original network and decides at runtime which channels to prune, using the input and current feature maps. This makes the amount of computation responsive to the particular sample, with more pruning for easier images.

The decisions proceed from the bottom of the network upward, one layer at a time. The authors formulate this sequence as a Markov decision process and train an agent through reinforcement learning. The agent assesses convolutional-kernel importance and chooses channel-wise pruning conditioned on each sample, allowing successive decisions to reflect the features currently available.

Because the full network remains available, the operating balance between computation and prediction quality can be adjusted to available resources. The method applies to existing network structures, and the authors report a better speed–accuracy tradeoff, especially at large pruning rates. The contribution is an adaptive use of network capacity that allocates less computation to inputs judged easier for the task.
summary.tldr: Runtime Neural Pruning uses reinforcement learning to choose input-dependent channel pruning, improving the reported speed–accuracy tradeoff.

title: Runtime Neural Pruning

abstract: Recently, linear formulations and convex optimization methods have been proposed to predict diffusion-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (dMRI) data given estimates of brain connections generated using tractography algorithms. The size of the linear models comprising such methods grows with both dMRI data and connectome resolution, and can become very large when applied to modern data. In this paper, we introduce a method to encode dMRI signals and large connectomes, i.e., those that range from hundreds of thousands to millions of fascicles (bundles of neuronal axons), by using a sparse tensor decomposition. We show that this tensor decomposition accurately approximates the Linear Fascicle Evaluation (LiFE) model, one of the recently developed linear models. We provide a theoretical analysis of the accuracy of the sparse decomposed model, LiFESD, and demonstrate that it can reduce the size of the model significantly. Also, we develop algorithms to implement the optimisation solver using the tensor representation in an efficient way.

paragraphs: Linear models can predict diffusion-weighted MRI measurements from estimates of brain connections produced by tractography. Their size grows with both the imaging data and the resolution of the estimated connectome. For modern datasets, this creates a substantial computational burden, particularly when the connection representation contains hundreds of thousands or millions of fascicles.

The paper introduces a sparse tensor decomposition that encodes the imaging signals and large connectomes together. It uses this representation to approximate the Linear Fascicle Evaluation model, known as LiFE. The resulting sparse decomposed model, LiFESD, is designed to retain an accurate approximation while significantly reducing model size.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis of approximation accuracy and demonstrate the reduction in storage required by the model. They also develop optimization algorithms that operate efficiently with the tensor representation. The contribution therefore addresses both the size of the representation and the computations performed on it, making the compact encoding useful within the solver rather than merely as a way to store the original model.
summary.tldr: LiFESD uses sparse tensors to compactly approximate a model linking tractography-derived brain connections to diffusion MRI signals.

title: Unified representation of tractography and diffusion-weighted MRI data using sparse multidimensional arrays

abstract: In this work, we try to understand the differences between exact and approximate inference algorithms in structured prediction. We compare the estimation and approximation error of both underestimate and overestimate models. The result shows that, from the perspective of learning errors, performances of approximate inference could be as good as exact inference. The error analyses also suggest a new margin for existing learning algorithms. Empirical evaluations on text classification, sequential labelling and dependency parsing witness the success of approximate inference and the benefit of the proposed margin.
originalAbstract: In this work, we try to understand the differences between exact and approximate inference algorithms in structured prediction. We compare the estimation and approximation error of both underestimate and overestimate models. The result shows that, from the perspective of learning errors, performances of approximate inference could be as good as exact inference. The error analyses also suggest a new margin for existing learning algorithms. Empirical evaluations on text classification, sequential labelling and dependency parsing witness the success of approximate inference and the benefit of the proposed margin.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves choosing outputs with internal structure, such as a sequence of labels or a dependency parse. The inference procedure determines which output a learned model selects. This paper asks how replacing exact inference with an approximation affects learning error, rather than judging the approximation only by how closely it reproduces an exact inference result.

The analysis compares estimation and approximation errors for both underestimate and overestimate models. Considering these sources of error together matters because accuracy within the inference procedure is only one part of the learning problem. The stated result is that approximate inference could perform as well as exact inference from the perspective of learning errors; it does not establish that every approximation will do so.

The error analysis also motivates a new margin for existing learning algorithms, connecting the theoretical comparison to a concrete training change. Evaluations on text classification, sequential labeling, and dependency parsing support the usefulness of approximate inference and show benefits from the proposed margin.
summary.tldr: An analysis of structured prediction shows that approximate inference can match exact inference in learning error and motivates an improved training margin.

title: A Learning Error Analysis for Structured Prediction with Approximate Inference

abstract: We consider the problem of online convex optimization in two different settings: arbitrary and i.i.d. sequence of convex loss functions. In both settings, we provide efficient algorithms whose cumulative excess risks are controlled with fast-rate sparse bounds. First, the excess risks bounds depend on the sparsity of the objective rather than on the dimension of the parameters space. Second, their rates are faster than the slow-rate $1/\sqrt{T}$ under additional convexity assumptions on the loss functions. In the adversarial setting, we develop an algorithm BOA+ whose cumulative excess risks is controlled by several bounds with different trade-offs between sparsity and rate for strongly convex loss functions. In the i.i.d. setting under the Łojasiewicz's assumption, we establish new risk bounds that are sparse with a rate adaptive to the convexity of the risk (ranging from a rate $1/\sqrt{T}$ for general convex risk to $1/T$ for strongly convex risk). These results generalize previous works on sparse online learning under weak assumptions on the risk.

First, the excess risks bounds depend on the sparsity of the objective rather than on the dimension of the parameters space. Second, their rates are faster than the slow-rate $1/\sqrt{T}$ under additional convexity assumptions on the loss functions. In the adversarial setting, we develop an algorithm BOA+ whose cumulative excess risks is controlled by several bounds with different trade-offs between sparsity and rate for strongly convex loss functions. In the i.i.d. setting under the Łojasiewicz's assumption, we establish new risk bounds that are sparse with a rate adaptive to the convexity of the risk (ranging from a rate $1/\sqrt{T}$ for general convex risk to $1/T$ for strongly convex risk). These results generalize previous works on sparse online learning under weak assumptions on the risk.

paragraphs: This paper studies online convex optimization when losses arrive either in an arbitrary sequence or as independent, identically distributed observations. The goal is to obtain efficient algorithms whose excess-risk guarantees reflect sparsity instead of the full number of parameters. This distinction matters when the objective's relevant structure is sparse despite a large parameter space.

For arbitrary loss sequences, the authors develop BOA+. With strongly convex losses, it has several bounds offering different trade-offs between sparsity and convergence rate. Additional convexity assumptions enable rates faster than the usual inverse-square-root dependence on the number of rounds. The faster guarantees are therefore tied to properties of the losses.

For independent, identically distributed losses, the analysis uses a Łojasiewicz assumption. The resulting sparse bounds adapt to the risk's convexity, ranging from a 1/sqrt(T) rate for general convex risk to 1/T for strongly convex risk. The contribution broadens sparse online learning guarantees while showing how stronger curvature can translate into faster learning.
summary.tldr: Efficient online algorithms obtain sparsity-sensitive risk bounds, with faster rates under additional convexity assumptions.

title: Efficient online algorithms for fast-rate regret bounds under sparsity

abstract: Measuring similarities between unlabeled time series trajectories is an important problem in many domains such as medicine, economics, and vision. It is often unclear what is the appropriate metric to use because of the complex nature of noise in the trajectories (e.g. different sampling rates or outliers). Experts typically hand-craft or manually select a specific metric, such as Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), to apply on their data. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end framework, autowarp, that optimizes and learns a good metric given unlabeled trajectories. We define a flexible and differentiable family of warping metrics, which encompasses common metrics such as DTW, Edit Distance, Euclidean, etc. Autowarp then leverages the representation power of sequence autoencoders to optimize for a member of this warping family. The output is an metric which is easy to interpret and can be robustly learned from relatively few trajectories. In systematic experiments across different domains, we show that autowarp often outperforms hand-crafted trajectory similarity metrics.

Sequence autoencoders provide learned representations that help optimize a member of this family. Experiments across multiple domains show that autowarp often outperforms handcrafted similarity measures. The word often is consequential: the evidence supports an adaptable alternative to manual metric choice, without claiming that one learned distance wins in every setting or for every type of time series.
summary.tldr: Autowarp uses sequence autoencoders to learn an interpretable warping metric from unlabeled trajectories, often outperforming handcrafted distances.

title: Learning a Warping Distance from Unlabeled Time Series Using Sequence Autoencoders

abstract: Feed-forward convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are currently state-of-the-art for object classification tasks such as ImageNet. Further, they are quantitatively accurate models of temporally-averaged responses of neurons in the primate brain's visual system. However, biological visual systems have two ubiquitous architectural features not shared with typical CNNs: local recurrence within cortical areas, and long-range feedback from downstream areas to upstream areas. Here we explored the role of recurrence in improving classification performance. We found that standard forms of recurrence (vanilla RNNs and LSTMs) do not perform well within deep CNNs on the ImageNet task. In contrast, novel cells that incorporated two structural features, bypassing and gating, were able to boost task accuracy substantially. We extended these design principles in an automated search over thousands of model architectures, which identified novel local recurrent cells and long-range feedback connections useful for object recognition. Moreover, these task-optimized ConvRNNs matched the dynamics of neural activity in the primate visual system better than feedforward networks, suggesting a role for the brain's recurrent connections in performing difficult visual behaviors.

paragraphs: Feedforward convolutional networks can classify objects and model time-averaged responses in the primate visual system. Biological vision also contains local recurrent connections and feedback from later areas to earlier ones. This paper investigates whether incorporating those architectural features improves recognition and better accounts for neural activity over time.

Simply inserting standard recurrence is insufficient in the reported experiments: vanilla recurrent networks and LSTMs perform poorly within deep CNNs on ImageNet. New recurrent cells with bypassing and gating substantially improve accuracy. The authors then search thousands of architectures using these design principles, identifying useful local recurrent cells and long-range feedback connections.

The resulting task-optimized convolutional recurrent networks match the dynamics of primate visual activity better than feedforward networks. This links success on object recognition to a closer match with changing neural responses, beyond time-averaged activity alone. The findings suggest that recurrent connections contribute to difficult visual behavior; they do not establish that the discovered architectures are exact descriptions of the brain.
summary.tldr: Carefully designed recurrence improves object recognition and matches primate visual-response dynamics better than feedforward networks in the reported study.

title: Task-Driven Convolutional Recurrent Models of the Visual System

abstract: Since Multiplicative Weights (MW) updates are the discrete analogue of the continuous Replicator Dynamics (RD), some researchers had expected their qualitative behaviours would be similar. We show that this is false in the context of graphical constant-sum games, which include two-person zero-sum games as special cases. In such games which have a fully-mixed Nash Equilibrium (NE), it was known that RD satisfy the permanence and Poincare recurrence properties, but we show that MW updates with any constant step-size eps > 0 converge to the boundary of the state space, and thus do not satisfy the two properties. Using this result, we show that MW updates have a regret lower bound of Omega( 1 / (eps T) ), while it was known that the regret of RD is upper bounded by O( 1 / T ). Interestingly, the regret perspective can be useful for better understanding of the behaviours of MW updates. In a two-person zero-sum game, if it has a unique NE which is fully mixed, then we show, via regret, that for any sufficiently small eps, there exist at least two probability densities and a constant Z > 0, such that for any arbitrarily small z > 0, each of the two densities fluctuates above Z and below z infinitely often.

paragraphs: Multiplicative weights is a discrete counterpart of continuous replicator dynamics, which might suggest similar long-term behavior. The paper disproves that expectation for graphical constant-sum games, a class including two-player zero-sum games. The main setting assumes a fully mixed Nash equilibrium, where every available action receives positive probability.

For these games, continuous replicator dynamics were known to satisfy permanence and Poincare recurrence. The authors show that multiplicative weights with any fixed positive step size approaches the boundary of the strategy space instead, so those properties fail. They also derive a regret lower bound of order 1/(epsilon T), compared with the known continuous-dynamics upper bound of order 1/T.

A further result concerns two-player zero-sum games with a unique, fully mixed equilibrium. For sufficiently small fixed step sizes, at least two probability densities repeatedly exceed a positive threshold and fall below arbitrarily small positive values, infinitely often. Thus, approaching the boundary can coexist with persistent fluctuations. The results establish a qualitative difference between discrete and continuous updates, even when the discrete step size is small.
summary.tldr: With a fixed positive step size, multiplicative weights approaches the boundary in the studied games, unlike continuous replicator dynamics.

title: Multiplicative Weights Updates with Constant Step-Size in Graphical Constant-Sum Games

abstract: Graphs are ubiquitous data structures for representing interactions between entities. With an emphasis on applications in chemistry, we explore the task of learning to generate graphs that conform to a distribution observed in training data. We propose a variational autoencoder model in which both encoder and decoder are graph-structured. Our decoder assumes a sequential ordering of graph extension steps and we discuss and analyze design choices that mitigate the potential downsides of this linearization. Experiments compare our approach with a wide range of baselines on the molecule generation task and show that our method is successful at matching the statistics of the original dataset on semantically important metrics. Furthermore, we show that by using appropriate shaping of the latent space, our model allows us to design molecules that are (locally) optimal in desired properties.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to generate graphs whose distribution resembles graphs observed during training, with molecule generation as its main application. It proposes a variational autoencoder in which both the encoder and decoder have graph structure. This makes the representation of relationships between entities part of the model on both sides of the encoding and generation process.

The decoder constructs a graph through an ordered sequence of extension steps. Introducing a sequence gives the generator a concrete construction process, but it also imposes an ordering on a graph. The authors discuss and analyze design choices intended to reduce potential disadvantages of that linearization. The ordering is therefore an explicit modeling decision whose consequences receive attention.

Experiments compare the method with a broad set of molecule-generation baselines and show that it matches important statistics of the original dataset. The authors also shape the latent space to support searching for molecules with desired properties. They demonstrate locally optimal designs, which supports property-directed generation without claiming that the search finds the globally best molecule.
summary.tldr: A graph-structured variational autoencoder generates molecules matching dataset statistics and supports locally optimal property-directed design.

title: Constrained Graph Variational Autoencoders for Molecule Design

abstract: We consider the task of recovering two real or complex $m$-vectors from phaseless Fourier measurements of their circular convolution. Our method is a novel convex relaxation that is based on a lifted matrix recovery formulation that allows a nontrivial convex relaxation of the bilinear measurements from convolution. We prove that if the two signals belong to known random subspaces of dimensions $k$ and $n$, then they can be recovered up to the inherent scaling ambiguity with $m >> (k+n) \log^2 m$ phaseless measurements. Our method provides the first theoretical recovery guarantee for this problem by a computationally efficient algorithm and does not require a solution estimate to be computed for initialization. Our proof is based Rademacher complexity estimates. Additionally, we provide an ADMM implementation of the method and provide numerical experiments that verify the theory.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovery of two unknown signals from Fourier measurements of their circular convolution when phase information is missing. Both signals may be real or complex. The challenge combines disentangling the two inputs with recovering information absent from the measurements, so the observations do not directly expose either original signal.

The proposed method reformulates the task as matrix recovery and then constructs a convex relaxation of the measurements' bilinear structure. This produces a computationally efficient approach with a theoretical recovery guarantee. It also avoids requiring an initial estimate of the solution, making the guarantee independent of first finding a suitable starting reconstruction.

The guarantee assumes that the signals lie in known random subspaces of dimensions k and n, and requires m to be sufficiently larger than (k+n) log² m. Recovery is only up to the problem's inherent scaling ambiguity. The proof uses Rademacher complexity estimates, and the authors provide an ADMM implementation with numerical experiments supporting the theory. These conditions specify the setting in which the recovery claim applies.
summary.tldr: A convex matrix-recovery method provably reconstructs two convolved signals from phaseless measurements under known random-subspace assumptions.

title: Blind Deconvolutional Phase Retrieval via Convex Programming

abstract: Fairness is essential for human society, contributing to stability and productivity. Similarly, fairness is also the key for many multi-agent systems. Taking fairness into multi-agent learning could help multi-agent systems become both efficient and stable. However, learning efficiency and fairness simultaneously is a complex, multi-objective, joint-policy optimization. To tackle these difficulties, we propose FEN, a novel hierarchical reinforcement learning model. We first decompose fairness for each agent and propose fair-efficient reward that each agent learns its own policy to optimize. To avoid multi-objective conflict, we design a hierarchy consisting of a controller and several sub-policies, where the controller maximizes the fair-efficient reward by switching among the sub-policies that provides diverse behaviors to interact with the environment. FEN can be trained in a fully decentralized way, making it easy to be deployed in real-world applications. Empirically, we show that FEN easily learns both fairness and efficiency and significantly outperforms baselines in a variety of multi-agent scenarios.
