paragraphs: Learning fair behavior in a multi-agent system is difficult because agents must balance fairness with efficiency while their policies interact. FEN addresses this as a joint learning problem. The method first decomposes fairness at the level of individual agents and gives each agent a reward that combines fairness and efficiency.

Each agent uses a hierarchical policy rather than a single undifferentiated behavior. A controller chooses among several sub-policies, which provide different ways to interact with the environment. The controller learns to maximize the combined fair-efficient reward by switching between these behaviors. This division is designed to reduce conflict between the objectives while preserving behavioral variety.

FEN can be trained in a fully decentralized manner, which the authors identify as helpful for real-world deployment. Their experiments report that it learns both fairness and efficiency and significantly outperforms the evaluated baselines across varied multi-agent scenarios. The findings support hierarchical control as a practical way to coordinate competing learning objectives in those settings, rather than establishing a universal guarantee of fair outcomes.
summary.tldr: FEN uses decentralized hierarchical reinforcement learning to balance fairness and efficiency by switching among diverse agent behaviors.

title: Learning Fairness in Multi-Agent Systems

abstract: Humans and other animals are frequently near-optimal in their ability to integrate noisy and ambiguous sensory data to form robust percepts---which are informed both by sensory evidence and by prior expectations about the structure of the environment. It is suggested that the brain does so using the statistical structure provided by an internal model of how latent, causal factors produce the observed patterns. In dynamic environments, such integration often takes the form of \emph{postdiction}, wherein later sensory evidence affects inferences about earlier percepts. As the brain must operate in current time, without the luxury of acausal propagation of information, how does such postdictive inference come about? Here, we propose a general framework for neural probabilistic inference in dynamic models based on the distributed distributional code (DDC) representation of uncertainty, naturally extending the underlying encoding to incorporate implicit probabilistic beliefs about both present and past. We show that, as in other uses of the DDC, an inferential model can be learnt efficiently using samples from an internal model of the world. Applied to stimuli used in the context of psychophysics experiments, the framework provides an online and plausible mechanism for inference, including postdictive effects.

paragraphs: Perception combines uncertain sensory evidence with expectations about how the world works. In a changing environment, later observations can also alter the interpretation of an earlier event, a phenomenon called postdiction. The paper asks how a neural system could perform this revision while continuing to process information in the present.

The proposed framework uses a distributed distributional code, or DDC, to represent uncertainty. It extends that representation to carry implicit probabilistic beliefs about both current and past states. This allows new sensory evidence to inform beliefs about earlier events within an ongoing inference process, without requiring information to physically travel backward in time.

The authors show that the inference model can be learned efficiently from samples generated by an internal model of the world. Applied to stimuli associated with psychophysics experiments, the framework produces postdictive effects through an online inference mechanism. Its contribution is a neurally plausible account of how maintaining uncertainty about the past can support perceptual revision as further evidence arrives.
summary.tldr: A neural uncertainty representation supports online perception that revises beliefs about past events when new sensory evidence arrives.

title: A neurally plausible model for online recognition and postdiction in a dynamical environment

abstract: In principle, meta-reinforcement learning algorithms leverage experience across many tasks to learn fast and effective reinforcement learning (RL) strategies. However, current meta-RL approaches rely on manually-defined distributions of training tasks, and hand-crafting these task distributions can be challenging and time-consuming. Can ``useful'' pre-training tasks be discovered in an unsupervised manner? We develop an unsupervised algorithm for inducing an adaptive meta-training task distribution, i.e. an automatic curriculum, by modeling unsupervised interaction in a visual environment. The task distribution is scaffolded by a parametric density model of the meta-learner's trajectory distribution. We formulate unsupervised meta-RL as information maximization between a latent task variable and the meta-learner’s data distribution, and describe a practical instantiation which alternates between integration of recent experience into the task distribution and meta-learning of the updated tasks. Repeating this procedure leads to iterative reorganization such that the curriculum adapts as the meta-learner's data distribution shifts. Moreover, we show how discriminative clustering frameworks for visual representations can support trajectory-level task acquisition and exploration in domains with pixel observations, avoiding the pitfalls of alternatives. In experiments on vision-based navigation and manipulation domains, we show that the algorithm allows for unsupervised meta-learning that both transfers to downstream tasks specified by hand-crafted reward functions and serves as pre-training for more efficient meta-learning of test task distributions.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning uses experience across tasks to learn how to learn quickly. Its training tasks are often manually designed, which can require substantial effort. This paper develops an unsupervised method that discovers and updates a training-task distribution through interaction with a visual environment.

A parametric density model of the learner’s trajectories supports the evolving curriculum. The objective maximizes information between a latent task variable and the learner’s data distribution. In practice, the method alternates between incorporating recent experience into the task distribution and meta-learning on the revised tasks. Repeating these steps reorganizes the curriculum as the learner’s experience changes. Discriminative clustering of visual representations supports task acquisition and exploration at the trajectory level.

Experiments use navigation and manipulation environments with visual observations. The learned behavior transfers to downstream tasks defined by manually designed reward functions, and the unsupervised training also improves the efficiency of subsequent meta-learning on test-task distributions. These results support automatic curriculum discovery as useful preparation for later tasks, even when their rewards are specified separately.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised curriculum adapts tasks to a visual meta-RL learner’s experience and supports downstream transfer and more efficient later meta-learning.

title: Unsupervised Curricula for Visual Meta-Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study three fundamental statistical-learning problems: distribution estimation, property estimation, and property testing. We establish the profile maximum likelihood (PML) estimator as the first unified sample-optimal approach to a wide range of learning tasks. In particular, for every alphabet size $k$ and desired accuracy $\varepsilon$: \textbf{Distribution estimation} Under $\ell_1$ distance, PML yields optimal $\Theta(k/(\varepsilon^2\log k))$ sample complexity for sorted-distribution estimation, and a PML-based estimator empirically outperforms the Good-Turing estimator on the actual distribution; \textbf{Additive property estimation} For a broad class of additive properties, the PML plug-in estimator uses just four times the sample size required by the best estimator to achieve roughly twice its error, with exponentially higher confidence; \textbf{$\alpha$-R\'enyi entropy estimation} For an integer $\alpha>1$, the PML plug-in estimator has optimal $k^{1-1/\alpha}$ sample complexity; for non-integer $\alpha>3/4$, the PML plug-in estimator has sample complexity lower than the state of the art; \textbf{Identity testing} In testing whether an unknown distribution is equal to or at least $\varepsilon$ far from a given distribution in $\ell_1$ distance, a PML-based tester achieves the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors of $k$. With minor modifications, most of these results also hold for a near-linear-time computable variant of PML.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether profile maximum likelihood, or PML, can serve as one statistical approach across distribution estimation, property estimation, and hypothesis testing. Its main contribution is a collection of sample-efficiency guarantees, showing that the same approach achieves optimal or near-optimal requirements across a wide range of tasks.

For sorted-distribution estimation under l1 distance, PML achieves optimal sample complexity of order k/(ε² log k). For a broad class of additive properties, its plug-in estimator uses four times the best estimator’s sample size to obtain roughly twice the error with exponentially higher confidence. Rényi entropy results distinguish integer orders above one, where sample complexity is optimal, from non-integer orders above three quarters, where the stated bounds improve on prior results.

For identity testing, a PML-based method is optimal up to logarithmic factors in alphabet size. An estimator based on PML also empirically outperforms Good-Turing for actual-distribution estimation. Most theoretical results extend, with minor changes, to a near-linear-time variant. These distinctions matter: exact optimality, approximate optimality, and empirical improvement apply to different claims.
summary.tldr: Profile maximum likelihood provides a unified approach with optimal or near-optimal sample requirements across many estimation and testing tasks.

title: The Broad Optimality of Profile Maximum Likelihood

abstract: Recurrent neural networks are the foundation of many sequence-to-sequence models in machine learning, such as machine translation and speech synthesis. With applied quantum computing in its infancy, there already exist quantum machine learning models such as variational quantum eigensolvers which have been used e.g. in the context of energy minimization tasks. Yet, to date, no viable recurrent quantum network has been proposed. In this work we construct the first quantum recurrent neural network (QRNN) with demonstrable performance on non-trivial tasks such as sequence learning and integer digit classification. The QRNN cell is built from parametrized quantum neurons, which, in conjunction with amplitude amplification, creates a nonlinear activation of polynomials of its inputs and hidden state, and allows the extraction of a probability distribution over predicted classes at each step. To study the model's performance, we provide an implementation in pytorch, which allows the relatively efficient optimization of parametrized quantum circuits with tens of thousands of parameters, and which demonstrates that model does not appear to suffer from the vanishing gradient problem that plagues many exting quantum classifiers and classical RNNs. We establish a QRNN training setup by benchmarking optimization hyperparameters, and analyse suitable network topologies for simple memorisation and sequence prediction tasks from Elman's seminal paper (1990). We then proceed to evaluate the QRNN on MNIST classification, by feeding the QRNN each image pixel-by-pixel; with a network utilizing only 12 qubits we reach a test set accuracy over 98\% when discriminating between the digits `0' and `1'.

Its recurrent cell uses parameterized quantum neurons together with amplitude amplification. These components create nonlinear activations involving polynomials of the current input and hidden state, and allow a distribution over predicted classes to be extracted at each step.

To study training, the authors provide a PyTorch implementation that supports relatively efficient optimization of quantum circuits with tens of thousands of parameters. They benchmark optimization settings and examine network structures for memorization and sequence prediction. In these investigations, the model does not appear to suffer from the vanishing-gradient problem affecting many quantum classifiers and classical recurrent networks.

The authors also evaluate classification by feeding MNIST images to the model one pixel at a time. A network using 12 qubits achieves more than 98% test accuracy when distinguishing digits zero and one. This result concerns that two-digit task. Together, the experiments demonstrate a recurrent quantum construction capable of nontrivial sequence learning and classification, alongside a setup for studying its optimization.
summary.tldr: A quantum recurrent network demonstrates sequence learning and exceeds 98% accuracy on pixel-by-pixel MNIST zero-versus-one classification using 12 qubits.

title: Recurrent Quantum Neural Networks

abstract: We propose Geo-PIFu, a method to recover a 3D mesh from a monocular color image of a clothed person. Our method is based on a deep implicit function-based representation to learn latent voxel features using a structure-aware 3D U-Net, to constrain the model in two ways: first, to resolve feature ambiguities in query point encoding, second, to serve as a coarse human shape proxy to regularize the high-resolution mesh and encourage global shape regularity. We show that, by both encoding query points and constraining global shape using latent voxel features, the reconstruction we obtain for clothed human meshes exhibits less shape distortion and improved surface details compared to competing methods. We evaluate Geo-PIFu on a recent human mesh public dataset that is 10x larger than the private commercial dataset used in PIFu and previous derivative work. On average, we exceed the state of the art by 42.7% reduction in Chamfer and Point-to-Surface Distances, and 19.4% reduction in normal estimation errors.

Its goal is to improve both the overall consistency of the reconstructed human shape and the fine surface details that make clothing geometry recognizable.

A structure-aware three-dimensional U-Net learns the voxel features, which serve two purposes. First, they help resolve ambiguity when encoding points queried by the implicit representation. Second, they provide a coarse approximation of human shape that constrains the higher-resolution mesh. The same geometric information therefore guides local point interpretation and encourages regularity across the complete reconstruction.

Average improvements include a 42.7% reduction in Chamfer and point-to-surface distances and a 19.4% reduction in normal estimation errors. These results support combining coarse geometric guidance with detailed implicit reconstruction.
summary.tldr: Geo-PIFu uses learned three-dimensional shape guidance to improve clothed-human mesh reconstruction from a single image.

title: Geo-PIFu: Geometry and Pixel Aligned Implicit Functions for Single-view Human Reconstruction

abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) aims to learn from multiple training tasks the ability to adapt efficiently to unseen test tasks. Despite the success, existing meta-RL algorithms are known to be sensitive to the task distribution shift. When the test task distribution is different from the training task distribution, the performance may degrade significantly. To address this issue, this paper proposes \textit{Model-based Adversarial Meta-Reinforcement Learning} (AdMRL), where we aim to minimize the worst-case sub-optimality gap \--- the difference between the optimal return and the return that the algorithm achieves after adaptation \--- across all tasks in a family of tasks, with a model-based approach. We propose a minimax objective and optimize it by alternating between learning the dynamics model on a fixed task and finding the \textit{adversarial} task for the current model \--- the task for which the policy induced by the model is maximally suboptimal. Assuming the family of tasks is parameterized, we derive a formula for the gradient of the suboptimality with respect to the task parameters via the implicit function theorem, and show how the gradient estimator can be efficiently implemented by the conjugate gradient method and a novel use of the REINFORCE estimator. We evaluate our approach on several continuous control benchmarks and demonstrate its efficacy in the worst-case performance over all tasks, the generalization power to out-of-distribution tasks, and in training and test time sample efficiency, over existing state-of-the-art meta-RL algorithms.

AdMRL addresses this problem by targeting the worst adaptation shortfall within a family of tasks: the gap between optimal return and the return achieved after adaptation.

It learns a dynamics model on a fixed task, then searches for an adversarial task on which the policy induced by the current model is most suboptimal. Continuous control experiments support improvements in worst-case performance, generalization to out-of-distribution tasks, and training and testing sample efficiency over existing methods. These are empirical findings; minimizing worst-case suboptimality is the training objective, not an unconditional guarantee of optimal adaptation.
summary.tldr: AdMRL trains against tasks where adaptation is most suboptimal, improving robustness and sample efficiency in continuous control experiments.

title: Model-based Adversarial Meta-Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The task of maximizing a monotone submodular function under a cardinality constraint is at the core of many machine learning and data mining applications, including data summarization, sparse regression and coverage problems. We study this classic problem in the fully dynamic setting, where elements can be both inserted and removed. Our main result is a randomized algorithm that maintains an efficient data structure with a poly-logarithmic amortized update time and yields a $(1/2-epsilon)$-approximate solution. We complement our theoretical analysis with an empirical study of the performance of our algorithm.
originalAbstract: The task of maximizing a monotone submodular function under a cardinality constraint is at the core of many machine learning and data mining applications, including data summarization, sparse regression and coverage problems. Our main result is a randomized algorithm that maintains an efficient data structure with a poly-logarithmic amortized update time and yields a $(1/2-epsilon)$-approximate solution. We complement our theoretical analysis with an empirical study of the performance of our algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper studies selecting a limited number of elements to maximize a monotone submodular objective. Such objectives express diminishing returns: adding an element contributes less as the selected collection grows. The problem appears in applications including summarization, sparse regression, and coverage, where a small selection should retain substantial value.

The authors consider a fully dynamic setting, meaning that available elements can be inserted and removed. Their randomized algorithm maintains a data structure as those changes occur. It provides a (1/2−ε)-approximate solution while requiring only polylogarithmic amortized update time, combining a solution-quality guarantee with efficient maintenance.

The approximation guarantee measures the maintained solution against the optimal objective value. The amortized time guarantee concerns update costs averaged across a sequence of changes, rather than a separate bound of that form for every individual update. An empirical study complements the theoretical analysis. The main contribution is a way to maintain a provably useful constrained selection while the underlying collection changes in both directions.
summary.tldr: A randomized dynamic algorithm maintains a (1/2−ε)-approximate submodular selection with polylogarithmic amortized update time.

title: Fully Dynamic Algorithm for Constrained Submodular Optimization

abstract: Reservoir Computing is a class of simple yet efficient Recurrent Neural Networks where internal weights are fixed at random and only a linear output layer is trained. In the large size limit, such random neural networks have a deep connection with kernel methods. Our contributions are threefold: a) We rigorously establish the recurrent kernel limit of Reservoir Computing and prove its convergence. b) We test our models on chaotic time series prediction, a classic but challenging benchmark in Reservoir Computing, and show how the Recurrent Kernel is competitive and computationally efficient when the number of data points remains moderate. c) When the number of samples is too large, we leverage the success of structured Random Features for kernel approximation by introducing Structured Reservoir Computing. The two proposed methods, Recurrent Kernel and Structured Reservoir Computing, turn out to be much faster and more memory-efficient than conventional Reservoir Computing.

paragraphs: Reservoir computing uses a recurrent network with fixed random internal weights and trains only a linear output layer. This makes training simple, but the size of the random network still affects computation and memory. The paper develops two alternatives by connecting large reservoirs to kernel methods and structured random features.

First, the authors rigorously establish a recurrent-kernel limit and prove convergence to it. On chaotic time-series prediction, the resulting Recurrent Kernel method is competitive and computationally efficient when the number of data points is moderate. This connects a limiting mathematical description of the random network to a usable prediction method.

For larger sample counts, the authors introduce Structured Reservoir Computing, drawing on structured random features used in kernel approximation. The two approaches therefore address different data-size regimes within the same broader connection. Both are reported to be much faster and more memory-efficient than conventional reservoir computing. The moderate-data qualification is central to the stated efficiency of the direct recurrent-kernel approach.
summary.tldr: A proven recurrent-kernel limit and a structured-reservoir alternative improve the speed and memory efficiency of reservoir computing.

title: Reservoir Computing meets Recurrent Kernels and Structured Transforms

abstract: To be well-behaved, systems that process preference data must satisfy certain conditions identified by economic decision theory and by social choice theory. In ML, preferences and rankings are commonly learned by fitting a probabilistic model to noisy preference data. The behavior of this learning process from the view of economic theory has previously been studied for the case where the data consists of rankings. In practice, it is more common to have only pairwise comparison data, and the formal properties of the associated learning problem are more challenging to analyze. We show that a large class of random utility models (including the Thurstone–Mosteller Model), when estimated using the MLE, satisfy a Pareto efficiency condition. These models also satisfy a strong monotonicity property, which implies that the learning process is responsive to input data. On the other hand, we show that these models fail certain other consistency conditions from social choice theory, and in particular do not always follow the majority opinion. Our results inform existing and future applications of random utility models for societal decision making.

paragraphs: Preference-learning systems often receive comparisons between two alternatives rather than complete rankings. Fitting a probabilistic model to those comparisons produces an aggregate judgment, but that judgment can be assessed against principles from economics and social choice. This paper studies which such principles the learning process satisfies.

The analysis covers a large class of random utility models estimated by maximum likelihood, including the Thurstone–Mosteller model. The authors prove that these models satisfy a Pareto efficiency condition. They also establish a strong monotonicity property, meaning that the learning procedure responds to changes in its input comparisons in the formally specified way.

These positive properties do not extend to every desirable consistency requirement. The same models violate some conditions from social choice theory and do not always follow the majority opinion. The findings distinguish several meanings of well-behaved preference aggregation: satisfying efficiency and responsiveness does not ensure majority agreement. This matters when learned preferences inform societal decisions, because the choice of statistical model also determines which decision principles its outputs can satisfy.
summary.tldr: Maximum-likelihood random utility models satisfy efficiency and responsiveness properties for pairwise preferences but can disagree with the majority.

title: Axioms for Learning from Pairwise Comparisons

abstract: Object detection has achieved promising success, but requires large-scale fully-annotated data, which is time-consuming and labor-extensive. Therefore, we consider object detection with mixed supervision, which learns novel object categories using weak annotations with the help of full annotations of existing base object categories. Previous works using mixed supervision mainly learn the class-agnostic objectness from fully-annotated categories, which can be transferred to upgrade the weak annotations to pseudo full annotations for novel categories. In this paper, we further transfer mask prior and semantic similarity to bridge the gap between novel categories and base categories. Specifically, the ability of using mask prior to help detect objects is learned from base categories and transferred to novel categories. Moreover, the semantic similarity between objects learned from base categories is transferred to denoise the pseudo full annotations for novel categories. Experimental results on three benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method over existing methods. Codes are available at https://github.com/bcmi/TraMaS-Weak-Shot-Object-Detection.

paragraphs: Object detection usually depends on expensive, detailed annotations. Mixed supervision reduces that burden by using fully annotated base categories to help learn new categories that have only weak annotations. Earlier approaches mainly transfer a general ability to recognize objects, using it to turn weak labels into more detailed pseudo annotations.

This paper transfers two additional kinds of knowledge. First, it learns from base categories how a mask prior can help locate objects, then applies that capability to new categories. Second, it transfers learned semantic similarities between objects to remove noise from the new categories' pseudo annotations. These mechanisms address both detection and the quality of the generated supervision.

The approach matters because transferred knowledge can do more than indicate that something is an object: it can also guide detection and assess the annotations used for further learning. Experiments on three benchmark datasets show that the proposed method is effective relative to existing methods. The results support using mask-related and semantic knowledge to bridge fully annotated and weakly annotated categories.
summary.tldr: Transferring mask priors and semantic similarities improves detection and cleans pseudo annotations for object categories with weak supervision.

title: Mixed Supervised Object Detection by Transferring Mask Prior and Semantic Similarity

abstract: Gaussian processes with derivative information are useful in many settings where derivative information is available, including numerous Bayesian optimization and regression tasks that arise in the natural sciences. Incorporating derivative observations, however, comes with a dominating $O(N^3D^3)$ computational cost when training on $N$ points in $D$ input dimensions. This is intractable for even moderately sized problems. While recent work has addressed this intractability in the low-$D$ setting, the high-$N$, high-$D$ setting is still unexplored and of great value, particularly as machine learning problems increasingly become high dimensional. In this paper, we introduce methods to achieve fully scalable Gaussian process regression with derivatives using variational inference. Analogous to the use of inducing values to sparsify the labels of a training set, we introduce the concept of inducing directional derivatives to sparsify the partial derivative information of the training set. This enables us to construct a variational posterior that incorporates derivative information but whose size depends neither on the full dataset size $N$ nor the full dimensionality $D$. We demonstrate the full scalability of our approach on a variety of tasks, ranging from a high dimensional Stellarator fusion regression task to training graph convolutional neural networks on PubMed using Bayesian optimization. Surprisingly, we additionally find that our approach can improve regression performance even in settings where only label data is available.

paragraphs: Derivative observations can improve Gaussian process regression by supplying information about how a function changes. Incorporating them directly is expensive: the stated training cost grows as O(N³D³), with N observations and D input dimensions. The paper targets settings where both the dataset and dimensionality are large.

The authors introduce inducing directional derivatives to compress derivative information, analogous to using inducing values to summarize function observations. This construction supports a variational posterior whose size depends on neither the full number of data points nor the full input dimensionality. It provides a compact uncertainty representation while still incorporating information about the function’s derivatives.

Experiments demonstrate scalability across tasks including high-dimensional stellarator fusion regression and Bayesian optimization for training graph convolutional networks on PubMed. The authors also find that the approach can improve regression when only labels are available. That empirical observation extends its potential usefulness beyond datasets with observed derivatives. The main computational contribution is the compressed posterior construction; independence of its size from N and D should not be read as every computation being independent of them.
summary.tldr: Inducing directional derivatives enable compact variational Gaussian process regression with derivative information in large, high-dimensional problems.

title: Scaling Gaussian Processes with Derivative Information Using Variational Inference

abstract: Adversarial risk quantifies the performance of classifiers on adversarially perturbed data. Numerous definitions of adversarial risk---not all mathematically rigorous and differing subtly in the details---have appeared in the literature. In this paper, we revisit these definitions, make them rigorous, and critically examine their similarities and differences. Our technical tools derive from optimal transport, robust statistics, functional analysis, and game theory. Our contributions include the following: generalizing Strassen’s theorem to the unbalanced optimal transport setting with applications to adversarial classification with unequal priors; showing an equivalence between adversarial robustness and robust hypothesis testing with $\infty$-Wasserstein uncertainty sets; proving the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium in the two-player game between the adversary and the algorithm; and characterizing adversarial risk by the minimum Bayes error between distributions belonging to the $\infty$-Wasserstein uncertainty sets. Our results generalize and deepen recently discovered connections between optimal transport and adversarial robustness and reveal new connections to Choquet capacities and game theory.

paragraphs: Adversarial risk measures classifier performance when inputs can be perturbed by an adversary. Several definitions exist, with subtle differences and varying mathematical rigor. This paper puts those definitions on a rigorous footing and examines how they relate, using tools from optimal transport, robust statistics, functional analysis, and game theory.

One result connects adversarial robustness to robust hypothesis testing with infinity-Wasserstein uncertainty sets. Another characterizes adversarial risk through the minimum Bayes error between distributions in those sets. These links translate questions about adversarial classification into questions about distinguishing uncertain distributions. The authors also extend Strassen's theorem to unbalanced optimal transport, with applications to classification when class priors are unequal.

The paper further proves the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium in the game between the adversary and the learning algorithm. Alongside connections to Choquet capacities, these results deepen the mathematical account of robustness. The contribution is a set of rigorous relationships that clarifies how different formulations fit together and connects adversarial classification to other established mathematical problems.
summary.tldr: The paper rigorously relates definitions of adversarial risk to optimal transport, robust hypothesis testing, and game-theoretic equilibrium.

title: The Many Faces of Adversarial Risk

abstract: We approach self-supervised learning of image representations from a statistical dependence perspective, proposing Self-Supervised Learning with the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (SSL-HSIC). SSL-HSIC maximizes dependence between representations of transformations of an image and the image identity, while minimizing the kernelized variance of those representations. This framework yields a new understanding of InfoNCE, a variational lower bound on the mutual information (MI) between different transformations. While the MI itself is known to have pathologies which can result in learning meaningless representations, its bound is much better behaved: we show that it implicitly approximates SSL-HSIC (with a slightly different regularizer).Our approach also gives us insight into BYOL, a negative-free SSL method, since SSL-HSIC similarly learns local neighborhoods of samples. SSL-HSIC allows us to directly optimize statistical dependence in time linear in the batch size, without restrictive data assumptions or indirect mutual information estimators. Trained with or without a target network, SSL-HSIC matches the current state-of-the-art for standard linear evaluation on ImageNet, semi-supervised learning and transfer to other classification and vision tasks such as semantic segmentation, depth estimation and object recognition. Code is available at https://github.com/deepmind/ssl_hsic.

paragraphs: SSL-HSIC learns image representations by directly measuring statistical dependence. It encourages representations of transformed images to retain information about image identity while controlling their kernelized variance. This provides a self-supervised objective grounded in dependence rather than an indirect estimate of mutual information.

The framework also explains aspects of existing methods. The authors show that InfoNCE approximately implements SSL-HSIC with a somewhat different regularizer, helping explain why that bound can behave better than mutual information itself. They also connect SSL-HSIC to BYOL through the local neighborhoods of samples that the methods learn.

The proposed objective can be optimized in time linear in batch size without restrictive data assumptions or indirect mutual-information estimators. With or without a target network, it matches leading results on the evaluated ImageNet linear classification, semi-supervised, and transfer tasks, including segmentation and depth estimation. The contribution therefore combines a competitive learning method with a statistical perspective that links several approaches to self-supervised representation learning.
summary.tldr: SSL-HSIC directly optimizes statistical dependence, connects InfoNCE and BYOL conceptually, and matches leading results on evaluated representation-learning tasks.

title: Self-Supervised Learning with Kernel Dependence Maximization

abstract: The advent of generative radiance fields has significantly promoted the development of 3D-aware image synthesis. The cumulative rendering process in radiance fields makes training these generative models much easier since gradients are distributed over the entire volume, but leads to diffused object surfaces. In the meantime, compared to radiance fields occupancy representations could inherently ensure deterministic surfaces. However, if we directly apply occupancy representations to generative models, during training they will only receive sparse gradients located on object surfaces and eventually suffer from the convergence problem. In this paper, we propose Generative Occupancy Fields (GOF), a novel model based on generative radiance fields that can learn compact object surfaces without impeding its training convergence. The key insight of GOF is a dedicated transition from the cumulative rendering in radiance fields to rendering with only the surface points as the learned surface gets more and more accurate. In this way, GOF combines the merits of two representations in a unified framework. In practice, the training-time transition of start from radiance fields and march to occupancy representations is achieved in GOF by gradually shrinking the sampling region in its rendering process from the entire volume to a minimal neighboring region around the surface. Through comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets, we demonstrate that GOF can synthesize high-quality images with 3D consistency and simultaneously learn compact and smooth object surfaces. Our code is available at https://github.com/SheldonTsui/GOF_NeurIPS2021.

paragraphs: Generative radiance fields distribute training gradients throughout a volume, which helps optimization but can leave object surfaces diffuse. Occupancy representations offer definite surfaces, yet using them directly concentrates gradients on those surfaces and can make training fail to converge. This paper addresses the tension between learning reliably and recovering well-defined geometry.

Generative Occupancy Fields begin with the broader rendering behavior of radiance fields and progressively move toward surface-based rendering. As the learned surface becomes more accurate, the method shrinks the region sampled during rendering, moving from the full volume to a small neighborhood around the surface. This staged transition connects the training advantages of one representation with the geometric advantages of the other.

Experiments across multiple datasets show high-quality synthesized images with 3D consistency alongside compact, smooth surfaces. The findings indicate that surface formation and successful generative training can be pursued together through a gradual rendering transition. The contribution is therefore about both the resulting images and the object geometry learned while producing them.
summary.tldr: Generative Occupancy Fields gradually concentrate rendering near learned surfaces to produce 3D-consistent images and compact geometry without impeding convergence.

title: Generative Occupancy Fields for 3D Surface-Aware Image Synthesis

abstract: We consider the challenging problem of predicting intrinsic object properties from a single image by exploiting differentiable renderers. Many previous learning-based approaches for inverse graphics adopt rasterization-based renderers and assume naive lighting and material models, which often fail to account for non-Lambertian, specular reflections commonly observed in the wild. In this work, we propose DIBR++, a hybrid differentiable renderer which supports these photorealistic effects by combining rasterization and ray-tracing, taking the advantage of their respective strengths---speed and realism. Our renderer incorporates environmental lighting and spatially-varying material models to efficiently approximate light transport, either through direct estimation or via spherical basis functions. Compared to more advanced physics-based differentiable renderers leveraging path tracing, DIBR++ is highly performant due to its compact and expressive shading model, which enables easy integration with learning frameworks for geometry, reflectance and lighting prediction from a single image without requiring any ground-truth. We experimentally demonstrate that our approach achieves superior material and lighting disentanglement on synthetic and real data compared to existing rasterization-based approaches and showcase several artistic applications including material editing and relighting.
originalAbstract: We consider the challenging problem of predicting intrinsic object properties from a single image by exploiting differentiable renderers. Many previous learning-based approaches for inverse graphics adopt rasterization-based renderers and assume naive lighting and material models, which often fail to account for non-Lambertian, specular reflections commonly observed in the wild. In this work, we propose DIBR++, a hybrid differentiable renderer which supports these photorealistic effects by combining rasterization and ray-tracing, taking the advantage of their respective strengths---speed and realism. Our renderer incorporates environmental lighting and spatially-varying material models to efficiently approximate light transport, either through direct estimation or via spherical basis functions. Compared to more advanced physics-based differentiable renderers leveraging path tracing, DIBR++ is highly performant due to its compact and expressive shading model, which enables easy integration with learning frameworks for geometry, reflectance and lighting prediction from a single image without requiring any ground-truth. We experimentally demonstrate that our approach achieves superior material and lighting disentanglement on synthetic and real data compared to existing rasterization-based approaches and showcase several artistic applications including material editing and relighting.

paragraphs: Recovering an object's properties from one image requires separating the effects of geometry, material, and illumination. Simple rendering models struggle with specular reflections, where appearance depends strongly on viewing and lighting conditions. DIB-R++ addresses this inverse graphics problem with a differentiable renderer that combines rasterization's speed with ray tracing's ability to represent realistic effects.

The renderer includes environmental lighting and materials that vary across an object's surface. It approximates light transport using direct estimation or spherical basis functions. A compact shading model makes the approach computationally efficient relative to the more advanced path-tracing renderers discussed in the paper, while supporting integration into learning systems.

These systems can predict geometry, reflectance, and lighting from a single image without requiring ground-truth supervision. On synthetic and real data, the authors report better separation of material and lighting than existing rasterization-based approaches. Material editing and relighting examples illustrate why that separation matters: the recovered factors support changing one aspect of appearance while reasoning about the others separately.
summary.tldr: DIB-R++ combines rasterization and ray tracing to learn more separable material and lighting properties from single images.

title: DIB-R++: Learning to Predict Lighting and Material with a Hybrid Differentiable Renderer

abstract: In this paper we consider the training stability of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and propose a family of RNNs, namely SBO-RNN, that can be formulated using stochastic bilevel optimization (SBO). With the help of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), we manage to convert the SBO problem into an RNN where the feedforward and backpropagation solve the lower and upper-level optimization for learning hidden states and their hyperparameters, respectively. We prove that under mild conditions there is no vanishing or exploding gradient in training SBO-RNN. Empirically we demonstrate our approach with superior performance on several benchmark datasets, with fewer parameters, less training data, and much faster convergence. Code is available at https://zhang-vislab.github.io.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks can be difficult to train when gradients become too small or too large. This paper introduces SBO-RNN, a family of recurrent networks built from stochastic bilevel optimization. The formulation gives the network’s hidden states and their hyperparameters distinct roles in a nested learning problem.

Using stochastic gradient descent, the authors convert that optimization problem into an RNN. The forward computation solves the lower-level problem of learning hidden states, while backpropagation addresses the upper-level problem of learning their hyperparameters. This connects the architecture’s ordinary training operations to an explicit two-level optimization structure.

Under conditions described as mild in the abstract, the authors prove that SBO-RNN training has neither vanishing nor exploding gradients. The guarantee is conditional on those assumptions. Empirical evaluations on several benchmark datasets report superior performance together with fewer parameters, less training data, and much faster convergence. The paper thus combines a theoretical stability result with evidence that the reformulation can improve practical learning efficiency.
summary.tldr: SBO-RNN derives recurrent networks from bilevel optimization, with conditional gradient-stability guarantees and reported gains in performance and training efficiency.

title: SBO-RNN: Reformulating Recurrent Neural Networks via Stochastic Bilevel Optimization

abstract: Robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs) are a useful building block of robust reinforcement learning algorithms but can be hard to solve. This paper proposes a fast, exact algorithm for computing the Bellman operator for S-rectangular robust Markov decision processes with $L_\infty$-constrained rectangular ambiguity sets. The algorithm combines a novel homotopy continuation method with a bisection method to solve S-rectangular ambiguity in quasi-linear time in the number of states and actions. The algorithm improves on the cubic time required by leading general linear programming methods. Our experimental results confirm the practical viability of our method and show that it outperforms a leading commercial optimization package by several orders of magnitude.

This can make them difficult to solve even though they are useful components of robust reinforcement learning algorithms. The paper targets the cost of computing their Bellman operator.

The proposed algorithm applies to S-rectangular robust MDPs with L-infinity-constrained rectangular ambiguity sets. These structural conditions define the uncertainty model for which the result holds. The method combines a new homotopy continuation procedure with bisection to compute the operator exactly, exploiting that structure instead of relying on a general linear programming solver.

The resulting computation takes quasi-linear time in the numbers of states and actions, improving on the cubic time associated with leading general linear programming methods. Experiments show practical viability and speed advantages of several orders of magnitude over a leading commercial optimization package. The contribution therefore combines an exact specialized computation with both theoretical and measured efficiency gains.
summary.tldr: A specialized exact Bellman-operator algorithm makes a structured class of robust MDP computations quasi-linear rather than cubic.

title: Fast Algorithms for $L_\infty$-constrained S-rectangular Robust MDPs

abstract: Soft-argmax operation is commonly adopted in detection-based methods to localize the target position in a differentiable manner. However, training the neural network with soft-argmax makes the shape of the probability map unconstrained. Consequently, the model lacks pixel-wise supervision through the map during training, leading to performance degradation. In this work, we propose sampling-argmax, a differentiable training method that imposes implicit constraints to the shape of the probability map by minimizing the expectation of the localization error. To approximate the expectation, we introduce a continuous formulation of the output distribution and develop a differentiable sampling process. The expectation can be approximated by calculating the average error of all samples drawn from the output distribution. We show that sampling-argmax can seamlessly replace the conventional soft-argmax operation on various localization tasks. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of the proposed method. Code is available at https://github.com/Jeff-sjtu/sampling-argmax

paragraphs: Localization models often predict a probability map and use soft-argmax to turn it into a target position while keeping training differentiable. The paper identifies a weakness in this setup: training through that position leaves the map’s shape unconstrained. As a result, the map does not receive pixel-level supervision through this operation, which can degrade localization performance.

Sampling-argmax changes the training objective to minimize expected localization error under the predicted distribution. This implicitly constrains the map because the objective depends on errors at sampled locations. To make the approach trainable, the authors introduce a continuous version of the output distribution and a differentiable procedure for drawing samples.

The expected error is approximated by averaging the localization errors of those samples. This connects training to the distribution of possible predicted locations, giving the probability map a more informative learning signal. The authors show that sampling-argmax can replace conventional soft-argmax across various localization tasks, with experiments supporting its effectiveness and flexibility.
summary.tldr: Sampling-argmax improves localization training by minimizing sampled position errors, implicitly constraining the predicted probability map.

title: Localization with Sampling-Argmax

abstract: With the advent of real-world quantum computing, the idea that parametrized quantum computations can be used as hypothesis families in a quantum-classical machine learning system is gaining increasing traction. Such hybrid systems have already shown the potential to tackle real-world tasks in supervised and generative learning, and recent works have established their provable advantages in special artificial tasks. Yet, in the case of reinforcement learning, which is arguably most challenging and where learning boosts would be extremely valuable, no proposal has been successful in solving even standard benchmarking tasks, nor in showing a theoretical learning advantage over classical algorithms. In this work, we achieve both. We propose a hybrid quantum-classical reinforcement learning model using very few qubits, which we show can be effectively trained to solve several standard benchmarking environments. Moreover, we demonstrate, and formally prove, the ability of parametrized quantum circuits to solve certain learning tasks that are intractable to classical models, including current state-of-art deep neural networks, under the widely-believed classical hardness of the discrete logarithm problem.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether parametrized quantum computations can serve as useful policies in reinforcement learning. It proposes a hybrid quantum-classical model using very few qubits. The work addresses two distinct questions: whether such a model can learn standard benchmark tasks and whether quantum policies can offer a provable advantage on particular learning problems.

For practical trainability, the authors show that their model can be trained effectively in several standard benchmark environments. This establishes that the proposed quantum-classical policy representation can support learning beyond specially constructed theoretical examples. The reported benchmark result concerns solving those environments; the abstract does not equate it with a demonstrated quantum advantage on them.

Separately, the authors demonstrate and formally prove that parametrized quantum circuits can solve certain learning tasks that are intractable for classical models, including state-of-the-art deep neural networks. This separation depends on the widely believed classical hardness of the discrete logarithm problem. The theoretical advantage is therefore conditional and task-specific, accompanying the distinct evidence of benchmark trainability.
summary.tldr: Quantum-classical policies solve standard benchmarks and offer a conditional, provable advantage on certain learning tasks.

title: Parametrized Quantum Policies for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A $k$-decision tree $t$ (or $k$-tree) is a recursive partition of a matrix (2D-signal) into $k\geq 1$ block matrices (axis-parallel rectangles, leaves) where each rectangle is assigned a real label. Its regression or classification loss to a given matrix $D$ of $N$ entries (labels) is the sum of squared differences over every label in $D$ and its assigned label by $t$.Given an error parameter $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, a $(k,\varepsilon)$-coreset $C$ of $D$ is a small summarization that provably approximates this loss to \emph{every} such tree, up to a multiplicative factor of $1\pm\varepsilon$. In particular, the optimal $k$-tree of $C$ is a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation to the optimal $k$-tree of $D$.We provide the first algorithm that outputs such a $(k,\varepsilon)$-coreset for \emph{every} such matrix $D$. The size $|C|$ of the coreset is polynomial in $k\log(N)/\varepsilon$, and its construction takes $O(Nk)$ time.This is by forging a link between decision trees from machine learning -- to partition trees in computational geometry. Experimental results on \texttt{sklearn} and \texttt{lightGBM} show that applying our coresets on real-world data-sets boosts the computation time of random forests and their parameter tuning by up to x$10$, while keeping similar accuracy. Full open source code is provided.

paragraphs: This paper studies decision trees that divide a two-dimensional signal into rectangular regions and assign each region a numeric value. Their loss measures squared differences between those assigned values and the original matrix entries. The goal is to summarize a large matrix while preserving the ability to evaluate these trees accurately.

The authors construct a coreset: a small summary whose loss approximates the full matrix's loss for every tree with the specified number of leaves. The approximation is multiplicative, controlled by an error parameter. The abstract also states that optimizing a tree on the summary yields a near-optimal tree for the original matrix.

The construction connects machine-learning decision trees to partition trees from computational geometry. It works for every input matrix, takes O(Nk) time, and produces a summary polynomial in k log(N)/ε. Experiments with sklearn and LightGBM report speedups of up to tenfold for random forests and parameter tuning while maintaining similar accuracy. These empirical gains accompany a uniform theoretical loss-preservation guarantee.
summary.tldr: Provably small matrix summaries preserve decision-tree losses and deliver up to tenfold empirical speedups while retaining similar accuracy.

title: Coresets for Decision Trees of Signals

abstract: One-shot image segmentation (OSS) methods enable semantic labeling of image pixels without supervised training with an extensive dataset. They require just one example (image, mask) pair per target class. Most neural-network-based methods train on a large subset of dataset classes and are evaluated on a disjoint subset of classes. We posit that the data used for training induces negative biases and affects the accuracy of these methods. Specifically, we present evidence for a \textit{Class Negative Bias} (CNB) arising from treating non-target objects as background during training, and \textit{Salience Bias} (SB), affecting the segmentation accuracy for non-salient target class pixels. We also demonstrate that by eliminating CNB and SB, significant gains can be made over the existing state-of-the-art. Next, we argue that there is a significant disparity between real-world expectations from an OSS method and its accuracy reported on existing benchmarks. To this end, we propose a new evaluation dataset - Tiered One-shot Segmentation (TOSS) - based on the PASCAL $5^i$ and FSS-1000 datasets, and associated metrics for each tier. The dataset enforces uniformity in the measurement of accuracy for existing methods and affords fine-grained insights into the applicability of a method to real applications. The paper includes extensive experiments with the TOSS dataset on several existing OSS methods. The intended impact of this work is to point to biases in training and introduce nuances and uniformity in reporting results for the OSS problem. The evaluation splits of the TOSS dataset and instructions for use are available at \url{https://github.com/fewshotseg/toss}.

paragraphs: One-shot image segmentation assigns pixel labels for a target category using a single example image and its mask. Many methods first train on other categories, then are evaluated on categories excluded from that training. This paper investigates how the training data can introduce biases that undermine performance in this setting.

The authors present evidence for two biases. Class Negative Bias arises when non-target objects are treated as background during training. Salience Bias affects accuracy on target pixels that are less visually prominent. They report significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art results when these biases are eliminated, highlighting the importance of how training examples and labels are constructed.

The paper also argues that existing benchmark scores do not adequately match real-world expectations. It introduces Tiered One-shot Segmentation, built from PASCAL 5i and FSS-1000, with evaluation metrics for each tier. Experiments on several methods aim to make accuracy reporting more uniform while revealing finer distinctions in where a method may be applicable.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies two data-induced segmentation biases and introduces tiered evaluation to reveal differences obscured by existing benchmark scores.

title: What Ails One-Shot Image Segmentation: A Data Perspective

abstract: We analyze graph smoothing with mean aggregation, where each node successively receives the average of the features of its neighbors. Indeed, it has quickly been observed that Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which generally follow some variant of Message-Passing (MP) with repeated aggregation, may be subject to the oversmoothing phenomenon: by performing too many rounds of MP, the node features tend to converge to a non-informative limit. In the case of mean aggregation, for connected graphs, the node features become constant across the whole graph. At the other end of the spectrum, it is intuitively obvious that some MP rounds are necessary, but existing analyses do not exhibit both phenomena at once: beneficial ``finite'' smoothing and oversmoothing in the limit. In this paper, we consider simplified linear GNNs, and rigorously analyze two examples for which a finite number of mean aggregation steps provably improves the learning performance, before oversmoothing kicks in. We consider a latent space random graph model, where node features are partial observations of the latent variables and the graph contains pairwise relationships between them. We show that graph smoothing restores some of the lost information, up to a certain point, by two phenomena: graph smoothing shrinks non-principal directions in the data faster than principal ones, which is useful for regression, and shrinks nodes within communities faster than they collapse together, which improves classification.

paragraphs: Graph smoothing repeatedly replaces a node's features with an average of its neighbors' features. Some averaging can help learning, but excessive averaging removes useful distinctions. On connected graphs, repeated mean aggregation eventually makes features constant across the graph. This paper develops an analysis that captures both the initial benefit and the later loss.

The authors study simplified linear graph neural networks under a latent-space random graph model. Node features reveal only part of the underlying latent variables, while graph edges provide pairwise information about them. In two examples, a finite number of averaging steps provably improves learning by recovering some of the information missing from the features.

For classification, nodes within communities become similar faster than the communities collapse together. These results explain why an intermediate amount of smoothing helps in the studied models, while continuing the same operation eventually destroys that advantage.
summary.tldr: The analysis proves how finite graph smoothing can improve learning in two models before excessive averaging erases useful distinctions.

title: Not too little, not too much: a theoretical analysis of graph (over)smoothing

abstract: Spike camera is an emerging bio-inspired vision sensor with ultra-high temporal resolution. It records scenes by accumulating photons and outputting continuous binary spike streams. Optical flow is a key task for spike cameras and their applications. A previous attempt has been made for spike-based optical flow. However, the previous work only focuses on motion between two moments, and it uses graphics-based data for training, whose generalization is limited. In this paper, we propose a tailored network, Spike2Flow that extracts information from binary spikes with temporal-spatial representation based on the differential of spike firing time and spatial information aggregation. The network utilizes continuous motion clues through joint correlation decoding. Besides, a new dataset with real-world scenes is proposed for better generalization. Experimental results show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on existing synthetic datasets and real data captured by spike cameras. The source code and dataset are available at \url{https://github.com/ruizhao26/Spike2Flow}.

paragraphs: Spike cameras record light through continuous streams of binary events, providing very high temporal resolution. Estimating optical flow means recovering motion from those streams. This paper addresses limitations of an earlier approach that considered motion between only two moments and relied on graphics-generated training data with limited generalization.

The proposed Spike2Flow network builds a representation from differences in spike firing times together with aggregated spatial information. This combines clues about when spikes occur with information about their surrounding locations. A joint correlation decoding mechanism then uses continuous motion clues, making the ongoing stream part of the motion-estimation process.

The authors also introduce a dataset containing real-world scenes to support better generalization. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on existing synthetic datasets and on real data recorded by spike cameras. The contribution combines a representation tailored to binary spike timing, a decoder that uses continuity, and additional real-scene data. Together, these address both how motion is extracted from the sensor output and how the model is trained for real observations.
summary.tldr: Spike2Flow combines spike-timing and spatial information with continuous motion decoding, supported by a new real-world scene dataset.

title: Learning Optical Flow from Continuous Spike Streams

abstract: Class-incremental learning (CIL) learns a classification model with training data of different classes arising progressively. Existing CIL either suffers from serious accuracy loss due to catastrophic forgetting, or invades data privacy by revisiting used exemplars. Inspired by learning of linear problems, we propose an analytic class-incremental learning (ACIL) with absolute memorization of past knowledge while avoiding breaching of data privacy (i.e., without storing historical data). The absolute memorization is demonstrated in the sense that the CIL using ACIL given present data would give identical results to that from its joint-learning counterpart that consumes both present and historical samples. This equality is theoretically validated. The data privacy is ensured by showing that no historical data are involved during the learning process. Empirical validations demonstrate ACIL's competitive accuracy performance with near-identical results for various incremental task settings (e.g., 5-50 phases). This also allows ACIL to outperform the state-of-the-art methods for large-phase scenarios (e.g., 25 and 50 phases).

paragraphs: Class-incremental learning trains a classifier as examples from new classes arrive over time. Updating the model can erase knowledge of earlier classes, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Keeping old examples available for retraining can help, but requires retaining historical data. ACIL addresses this tension through an analytic learning approach inspired by linear problems.

The paper gives “absolute memorization” a precise meaning: an ACIL update using current data produces the same result as its corresponding joint-learning procedure using both current and historical samples. The authors prove this equality theoretically. The guarantee concerns equivalence to that joint-learning counterpart, so it provides a concrete reference for what preserving past knowledge means.

The privacy claim is specifically tied to avoiding storage and reuse of historical examples. Experiments report competitive accuracy and nearly identical results across incremental settings ranging from 5 to 50 phases. ACIL also outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods in the reported 25- and 50-phase scenarios. These findings suggest particular value when learning is divided into many successive updates.
summary.tldr: ACIL preserves equivalence to its joint-learning counterpart while learning new classes without retaining historical examples.

title: ACIL: Analytic Class-Incremental Learning with Absolute Memorization and Privacy Protection

abstract: We consider the online restless bandits with average-reward and multiple actions, where the state of each arm evolves according to a Markov decision process (MDP), and the reward of pulling an arm depends on both the current state of the corresponding MDP and the action taken. Since finding the optimal control is typically intractable for restless bandits, existing learning algorithms are often computationally expensive or with a regret bound that is exponential in the number of arms and states. In this paper, we advocate \textit{index-aware reinforcement learning} (RL) solutions to design RL algorithms operating on a much smaller dimensional subspace by exploiting the inherent structure in restless bandits. Specifically, we first propose novel index policies to address dimensionality concerns, which are provably optimal. We then leverage the indices to develop two low-complexity index-aware RL algorithms, namely, (i) GM-R2MAB, which has access to a generative model; and (ii) UC-R2MAB, which learns the model using an upper confidence style online exploitation method. We prove that both algorithms achieve a sub-linear regret that is only polynomial in the number of arms and states. A key differentiator between our algorithms and existing ones stems from the fact that our RL algorithms contain a novel exploitation that leverages our proposed provably optimal index policies for decision-makings.

Each arm has a state governed by a Markov decision process, and rewards depend on both that state and the chosen action. Finding optimal control is typically intractable, while existing learning approaches can incur high computation or regret bounds that grow exponentially.

The authors propose index-aware reinforcement learning, using the problem's structure to work in a much smaller-dimensional subspace. They first develop index policies with optimality guarantees, then incorporate those policies into two learning algorithms. GM-R2MAB assumes access to a generative model, whereas UC-R2MAB learns the model online using an upper-confidence approach.

Both algorithms have sublinear regret bounds whose dependence on the numbers of arms and states is polynomial. Sublinear regret means the accumulated performance gap grows more slowly than the learning horizon. The distinguishing feature is how the algorithms exploit what they have learned: decisions use the proposed optimal index policies. This links computational simplification to the structure of the control problem itself.
summary.tldr: Index-aware reinforcement learning uses provably optimal index policies to obtain low-complexity restless-bandit algorithms with sublinear, polynomially scaling regret.

title: Learning Infinite-Horizon Average-Reward Restless Multi-Action Bandits via Index Awareness

abstract: Communication compression is a crucial technique for modern distributed learning systems to alleviate their communication bottlenecks over slower networks. Despite recent intensive studies of gradient compression for data parallel-style training, compressing the activations for models trained with pipeline parallelism is still an open problem. In this paper, we propose AQ-SGD, a novel activation compression algorithm for communication-efficient pipeline parallelism training over slow networks. Different from previous efforts in activation compression, instead of compressing activation values directly, AQ-SGD compresses the changes of the activations. This allows us to show, to the best of our knowledge for the first time, that one can still achieve $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence rate for non-convex objectives under activation compression, without making assumptions on gradient unbiasedness that do not hold for deep learning models with non-linear activation functions. We then show that AQ-SGD can be optimized and implemented efficiently, without additional end-to-end runtime overhead. We evaluated AQ-SGD to fine-tune language models with up to 1.5 billion parameters, compressing activation to 2-4 bits. AQ-SGD provides up to $4.3\times$ end-to-end speed-up in slower networks, without sacrificing model quality. Moreover, we also show that AQ-SGD can be combined with state-of-the-art gradient compression algorithms to enable end-to-end communication compression: All communications between machines, including model gradients, forward activations, and backward gradients are compressed into lower precision. This provides up to $4.9\times$ end-to-end speed-up, without sacrificing model quality.

title: Fine-tuning Language Models over Slow Networks using Activation Quantization with Guarantees

abstract: The beauty of physics is that there is usually a conserved quantity in an always-changing system, known as the constant of motion. Finding the constant of motion is important in understanding the dynamics of the system, but typically requires mathematical proficiency and manual analytical work. In this paper, we present a neural network that can simultaneously learn the dynamics of the system and the constants of motion from data. By exploiting the discovered constants of motion, it can produce better predictions on dynamics and can work on a wider range of systems than Hamiltonian-based neural networks. In addition, the training progresses of our method can be used as an indication of the number of constants of motion in a system which could be useful in studying a novel physical system.

paragraphs: A physical system can change continuously while some quantities remain constant. Discovering these constants of motion helps explain the system's dynamics, but usually requires mathematical analysis performed by hand. This paper presents a neural network that learns both how a system evolves and which quantities remain conserved, using data as the basis for both tasks.

The discovered constants also contribute to the network's predictions. By exploiting them, the method can make better predictions of the system's dynamics. This connects learning a useful physical description with learning to forecast motion. The abstract further states that the approach can handle a wider range of systems than neural networks based on Hamiltonian formulations.

The authors also identify a possible diagnostic use for the learning process itself. How training progresses can indicate the number of constants of motion in a system. That indication could help researchers investigating unfamiliar physical systems, alongside the learned dynamics and conserved quantities. It is presented as a potentially useful signal, rather than a guaranteed exact count for every system.
summary.tldr: A neural network jointly learns physical dynamics and conserved quantities, using those quantities to improve predictions.

title: Constants of motion network

abstract: Tensor decompositions are powerful tools for dimensionality reduction and feature interpretation of multidimensional data such as signals. Existing tensor decomposition objectives (e.g., Frobenius norm) are designed for fitting raw data under statistical assumptions, which may not align with downstream classification tasks. In practice, raw input tensor can contain irrelevant information while data augmentation techniques may be used to smooth out class-irrelevant noise in samples. This paper addresses the above challenges by proposing augmented tensor decomposition (ATD), which effectively incorporates data augmentations and self-supervised learning (SSL) to boost downstream classification. To address the non-convexity of the new augmented objective, we develop an iterative method that enables the optimization to follow an alternating least squares (ALS) fashion. We evaluate our proposed ATD on multiple datasets. It can achieve 0.8%~2.5% accuracy gain over tensor-based baselines. Also, our ATD model shows comparable or better performance (e.g., up to 15% in accuracy) over self-supervised and autoencoder baselines while using less than 5% of learnable parameters of these baseline models.

paragraphs: Tensor decomposition compresses multidimensional data into simpler components that can also help interpret its features. However, accurately fitting the original measurements is not necessarily the same as preserving what a classifier needs. Raw signals can contain irrelevant information, so a reconstruction-focused objective may spend capacity representing details unrelated to the eventual classification task.

Augmented Tensor Decomposition, or ATD, incorporates data augmentation and self-supervised learning into the decomposition objective. The approach uses these additional learning signals to improve the usefulness of the resulting features for classification. Because the augmented objective is non-convex, the authors develop an iterative optimization method that follows the alternating least squares style used in tensor decomposition.

Across multiple datasets, ATD reports accuracy gains of 0.8%–2.5% over tensor-based baselines. Against self-supervised and autoencoder baselines, it achieves comparable or better performance, with improvements reaching 15% in accuracy while using less than 5% of their learnable parameters. These findings support changing the decomposition objective to favor classification-relevant structure while retaining a compact model.
summary.tldr: ATD adds augmentation and self-supervised learning to tensor decomposition, improving downstream classification with relatively few learnable parameters.

title: ATD: Augmenting CP Tensor Decomposition by Self Supervision

abstract: Learning adversarially robust models require invariant predictions to a small neighborhood of its natural inputs, often encountering insufficient model capacity. There is research showing that learning multiple sub-models in an ensemble could mitigate this insufficiency, further improving the generalization and the robustness. However, the ensemble's voting-based strategy excludes the possibility that the true predictions remain with the minority. Therefore, this paper further improves the ensemble through a collaboration scheme---Synergy-of-Experts (SoE). Compared with the voting-based strategy, the SoE enables the possibility of correct predictions even if there exists a single correct sub-model. In SoE, every sub-model fits its specific vulnerability area and reserves the rest of the sub-models to fit other vulnerability areas, which effectively optimizes the utilization of the model capacity. Empirical experiments verify that SoE outperforms various ensemble methods against white-box and transfer-based adversarial attacks.
