paragraphs: Adversarial robustness requires a model to preserve its predictions around natural inputs despite small perturbations. The paper starts from the observation that model capacity can be insufficient for this demand, and that ensembles can help. However, majority voting can discard a correct prediction when only a minority of the component models produce it.

Synergy-of-Experts replaces this voting-based approach with a collaboration scheme. Each component model focuses on a particular area of vulnerability, leaving other areas to the remaining components. This division aims to use the available model capacity more effectively. It also allows the combined system to produce a correct answer even when only one component is correct, without claiming that one correct component always guarantees success.

Experiments compare the method with various ensemble approaches under white-box and transfer-based adversarial attacks. The reported results favor Synergy-of-Experts. They support the idea that how component models divide responsibility and combine their outputs can matter for robustness, beyond simply having several models available to vote on the same input.
summary.tldr: Synergy-of-Experts assigns models different vulnerability areas and combines them collaboratively to improve reported adversarial robustness.

title: Synergy-of-Experts: Collaborate to Improve Adversarial Robustness

abstract: Recently complex-valued neural networks have received increasing attention due to successful applications in various tasks and the potential advantages of better theoretical properties and richer representational capacity. However, the training dynamics of complex networks compared to real networks remains an open problem. In this paper, we investigate the dynamics of deep complex networks during real-valued backpropagation in the infinite-width limit via neural tangent kernel (NTK). We first extend the Tensor Program to the complex domain, to show that the dynamics of any basic complex network architecture is governed by its NTK under real-valued backpropagation. Then we propose a way to investigate the comparison of training dynamics between complex and real networks by studying their NTKs. As a result, we surprisingly prove that for most complex activation functions, the commonly used real-valued backpropagation reduces the training dynamics of complex networks to that of ordinary real networks as the widths tend to infinity, thus eliminating the characteristics of complex-valued neural networks. Finally, the experiments validate our theoretical findings numerically.

paragraphs: Complex-valued neural networks offer potentially richer representations and attractive theoretical properties, but their training behavior relative to ordinary real-valued networks is less understood. This paper investigates whether commonly used real-valued backpropagation preserves distinctive complex-network dynamics. The analysis focuses on the limit where network widths become infinite.

The authors extend the Tensor Program framework to complex numbers. They use it to show that the training dynamics of basic complex architectures under real-valued backpropagation are governed by their neural tangent kernels. Comparing these kernels then provides a mathematical route to comparing complex and real networks during training.

For most complex activation functions, the authors prove that the limiting training dynamics reduce to those of ordinary real networks. In that regime, the training procedure removes the distinctive dynamics that complex-valued computation might otherwise provide. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. The conclusion is specifically about the studied backpropagation procedure and infinite-width behavior, making the interaction between representation and training method central to the result.
summary.tldr: For most complex activations, real-valued backpropagation makes infinite-width complex networks train like ordinary real networks.

title: Real-Valued Backpropagation is Unsuitable for Complex-Valued Neural Networks

abstract: We consider prediction with expert advice for strongly convex and bounded losses, and investigate trade-offs between regret and ``variance'' (i.e., squared difference of learner's predictions and best expert predictions).With $K$ experts, the Exponentially Weighted Average (EWA) algorithm is known to achieve $O(\log K)$ regret.We prove that a variant of EWA either achieves a \textsl{negative} regret (i.e., the algorithm outperforms the best expert), or guarantees a $O(\log K)$ bound on \textsl{both} variance and regret.Building on this result, we show several examples of how variance of predictions can be exploited in learning.In the online to batch analysis, we show that a large empirical variance allows to stop the online to batch conversion early and outperform the risk of the best predictor in the class. We also recover the optimal rate of model selection aggregation when we do not consider early stopping.In online prediction with corrupted losses, we show that the effect of corruption on the regret can be compensated by a large variance.In online selective sampling, we design an algorithm that samples less when the variance is large, while guaranteeing the optimal regret bound in expectation.In online learning with abstention, we use a similar term as the variance to derive the first high-probability $O(\log K)$ regret bound in this setting.Finally, we extend our results to the setting of online linear regression.

paragraphs: This paper examines prediction with expert advice under strongly convex, bounded losses. It connects regret, the learner's loss relative to the best expert, with a particular notion of variance: squared differences between the learner's predictions and that expert's predictions. Here, variance measures prediction disagreement rather than uncertainty in an ordinary statistical estimate.

The main result concerns a variant of the Exponentially Weighted Average algorithm. Either it outperforms the best expert, producing negative regret, or both its regret and its variance are bounded by a quantity growing logarithmically with the number of experts. This gives prediction disagreement a useful interpretation: substantial disagreement can accompany an advantage over the comparison class.

The authors use this relationship in several settings. Large empirical variance can support early stopping during online-to-batch conversion and better risk than the best predictor in the class. It can also compensate for corruption effects or permit less sampling while preserving optimal expected regret. Related reasoning yields a high-probability logarithmic regret bound with abstention, and the results extend to online linear regression.
summary.tldr: An expert-learning algorithm either beats the best expert or controls both regret and prediction disagreement, enabling several improvements in online learning.

title: A Regret-Variance Trade-Off in Online Learning

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) under changing environment models many real-world applications via nonstationary Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), and hence gains considerable interest. However, theoretical studies on nonstationary MDPs in the literature have mainly focused on tabular and linear (mixture) MDPs, which do not capture the nature of unknown representation in deep RL. In this paper, we make the first effort to investigate nonstationary RL under episodic low-rank MDPs, where both transition kernels and rewards may vary over time, and the low-rank model contains unknown representation in addition to the linear state embedding function. We first propose a parameter-dependent policy optimization algorithm called PORTAL,and further improve PORTAL to its parameter-free version of Ada-PORTAL, which is able to tune its hyper-parameters adaptively without any prior knowledge of nonstationarity. For both algorithms, we provide upper bounds on the average dynamic suboptimality gap, which show that as long as the nonstationarity is not significantly large, PORTAL and Ada-PORTAL are sample-efficient and can achieve arbitrarily small average dynamic suboptimality gap with polynomial sample complexity.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning environments can change over time, affecting both rewards and the consequences of actions. This paper studies episodic low-rank Markov decision processes with such changes. Its model includes an unknown representation alongside a linear state embedding, addressing a representation-learning aspect absent from the tabular and linear settings emphasized in earlier theory.

The authors introduce PORTAL, a policy-optimization algorithm whose configuration depends on problem parameters. They then develop Ada-PORTAL, which adjusts its hyperparameters without prior knowledge of nonstationarity. This adaptive version addresses the practical difficulty of specifying in advance how much an environment will change.

For both algorithms, the paper bounds the average dynamic suboptimality gap, measuring performance shortfalls as the environment varies. When nonstationarity is not too large, the bounds establish sample efficiency and allow arbitrarily small average gaps with polynomial sample complexity. The guarantee therefore combines unknown representations and changing dynamics, with the degree of environmental change remaining a stated condition on the result.
summary.tldr: PORTAL and adaptive Ada-PORTAL provide sample-efficiency guarantees for changing low-rank MDPs when nonstationarity is sufficiently limited.

title: Provably Efficient Algorithm for Nonstationary Low-Rank MDPs

abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) is a promising learning-based approach for solving challenging combinatorial optimization problems without specialized algorithm design by experts. However, most constructive NCO methods cannot solve problems with large-scale instance sizes, which significantly diminishes their usefulness for real-world applications. In this work, we propose a novel Light Encoder and Heavy Decoder (LEHD) model with a strong generalization ability to address this critical issue. The LEHD model can learn to dynamically capture the relationships between all available nodes of varying sizes, which is beneficial for model generalization to problems of various scales. Moreover, we develop a data-efficient training scheme and a flexible solution construction mechanism for the proposed LEHD model. By training on small-scale problem instances, the LEHD model can generate nearly optimal solutions for the Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) and the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) with up to 1000 nodes, and also generalizes well to solve real-world TSPLib and CVRPLib problems. These results confirm our proposed LEHD model can significantly improve the state-of-the-art performance for constructive NCO.

paragraphs: Neural combinatorial optimization learns to construct solutions to difficult discrete problems, reducing dependence on specialized algorithm design. A major obstacle is scale: many constructive models struggle when problem instances become large. This paper focuses on learning from small instances while retaining the ability to solve much larger ones.

The proposed Light Encoder and Heavy Decoder, or LEHD, dynamically captures relationships among all currently available nodes across different instance sizes. This design supports adapting the solution-construction process to problems of varying scale. The authors complement the architecture with a data-efficient training scheme and a flexible mechanism for constructing solutions.

After training on small problems, LEHD produces nearly optimal solutions for the Travelling Salesman Problem and Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem with up to 1,000 nodes. It also generalizes well to real-world instances from TSPLib and CVRPLib. These reported results improve the state of the art for constructive neural combinatorial optimization and support shifting modeling capacity toward decoding. The demonstrated near-optimality is an empirical finding, rather than an exact optimality guarantee.
summary.tldr: LEHD uses a light encoder and heavy decoder to generalize from small training instances to routing problems with up to 1,000 nodes.

title: Neural Combinatorial Optimization with Heavy Decoder: Toward Large Scale Generalization

abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and the intensifying popularity of ChatGPT-like applications have blurred the boundary of high-quality text generation between humans and machines. However, in addition to the anticipated revolutionary changes to our technology and society, the difficulty of distinguishing LLM-generated texts (AI-text) from human-generated texts poses new challenges of misuse and fairness, such as fake content generation, plagiarism, and false accusations of innocent writers. While existing works show that current AI-text detectors are not robust to LLM-based paraphrasing, this paper aims to bridge this gap by proposing a new framework called RADAR, which jointly trains a $\underline{r}$obust $\underline{A}$I-text $\underline{d}$etector via $\underline{a}$dversarial lea$\underline{r}$ning. RADAR is based on adversarial training of a paraphraser and a detector. The paraphraser's goal is to generate realistic content to evade AI-text detection.RADAR uses the feedback from the detector to update the paraphraser, and vice versa.Evaluated with 8 different LLMs (Pythia, Dolly 2.0, Palmyra, Camel, GPT-J, Dolly 1.0, LLaMA, and Vicuna) across 4 datasets, experimental results show that RADAR significantly outperforms existing AI-text detection methods, especially when paraphrasing is in place. We also identify the strong transferability of RADAR from instruction-tuned LLMs to other LLMs, and evaluate the improved capability of RADAR via GPT-3.5-Turbo.

paragraphs: AI-text detectors can become unreliable when generated text is paraphrased by another language model. RADAR addresses this weakness by making paraphrasing an active part of detector training. The aim is to improve discrimination between human and machine writing even when the machine-generated wording has been deliberately changed to evade detection.

The framework jointly trains a paraphraser and a detector in an adversarial process. The paraphraser tries to produce realistic text that the detector fails to recognize as AI-generated. Feedback from the detector updates the paraphraser, while the paraphraser's outputs help update the detector. This creates an ongoing interaction in which the detector encounters evolving attempts to bypass its decisions.

Experiments using eight language models across four datasets show significant improvements over existing detection methods, particularly when paraphrasing is involved. The authors also report strong transfer from instruction-tuned models to other language models and evaluate improved capability using GPT-3.5-Turbo. These findings support adversarial paraphrasing as a useful training strategy for the tested detection settings, including transfer beyond the models used in a particular training configuration.
summary.tldr: RADAR jointly trains a paraphraser and detector to improve AI-text detection, especially after machine-generated text is paraphrased.

title: RADAR: Robust AI-Text Detection via Adversarial Learning

abstract: In generative modeling, numerous successful approaches leverage a low-dimensional latent space, e.g., Stable Diffusion models the latent space induced by an encoder and generates images through a paired decoder. Although the selection of the latent space is empirically pivotal, determining the optimal choice and the process of identifying it remain unclear. In this study, we aim to shed light on this under-explored topic by rethinking the latent space from the perspective of model complexity. Our investigation starts with the classic generative adversarial networks (GANs). Inspired by the GAN training objective, we propose a novel "distance" between the latent and data distributions, whose minimization coincides with that of the generator complexity. The minimizer of this distance is characterized as the optimal data-dependent latent that most effectively capitalizes on the generator's capacity. Then, we consider parameterizing such a latent distribution by an encoder network and propose a two-stage training strategy called Decoupled Autoencoder (DAE), where the encoder is only updated in the first stage with an auxiliary decoder and then frozen in the second stage while the actual decoder is being trained. DAE can improve the latent distribution and as a result, improve the generative performance. Our theoretical analyses are corroborated by comprehensive experiments on various models such as VQGAN and Diffusion Transformer, where our modifications yield significant improvements in sample quality with decreased model complexity.

paragraphs: Many generative models work in a compressed latent space and use a decoder to turn latent representations into data. The choice of latent space strongly affects performance, but choosing it is not straightforward. This paper studies that choice through the complexity required of the generator.

Starting from the GAN training objective, the authors define a distance between latent and data distributions whose minimization coincides with minimizing generator complexity. Within this formulation, the best data-dependent latent distribution makes effective use of the generator’s capacity. They turn this idea into a training method called the Decoupled Autoencoder: first train the encoder with an auxiliary decoder, then freeze the encoder while training the actual decoder.

Separating these stages allows the learned latent distribution to shape the subsequent decoder-training problem. Experiments with models including VQGAN and Diffusion Transformer support the theoretical analysis, reporting significant improvements in sample quality together with reduced model complexity. The findings suggest that improving the latent representation can make generation easier, rather than relying solely on increasing the generator’s capacity.
summary.tldr: A complexity-based analysis motivates training and freezing the encoder before the final decoder, improving reported sample quality with lower model complexity.

title: Complexity Matters: Rethinking the Latent Space for Generative Modeling

abstract: Text-to-image generation models represent the next step of evolution in image synthesis, offering a natural way to achieve flexible yet fine-grained control over the result.One emerging area of research is the fast adaptation of large text-to-image models to smaller datasets or new visual concepts.However, many efficient methods of adaptation have a long training time, which limits their practical applications, slows down experiments, and spends excessive GPU resources.In this work, we study the training dynamics of popular text-to-image personalization methods (such as Textual Inversion or DreamBooth), aiming to speed them up.We observe that most concepts are learned at early stages and do not improve in quality later, but standard training convergence metrics fail to indicate that.Instead, we propose a simple drop-in early stopping criterion that only requires computing the regular training objective on a fixed set of inputs for all training iterations.Our experiments on Stable Diffusion for 48 different concepts and three personalization methods demonstrate the competitive performance of our approach, which makes adaptation up to 8 times faster with no significant drops in quality.

paragraphs: Personalizing a text-to-image model for a new concept can require lengthy training even with adaptation methods intended to be efficient. This paper investigates whether that training continues after useful learning has largely finished. It examines the learning dynamics of approaches including Textual Inversion and DreamBooth.

The authors observe that most concepts are learned early and do not improve in quality later, while standard convergence measures fail to reveal this. They propose a simple early-stopping rule based on evaluating the usual training objective on a fixed collection of inputs throughout training. Holding those inputs fixed provides the basis for tracking the objective's evolution and deciding when to stop.

Experiments use Stable Diffusion with 48 concepts and three personalization methods. The proposed stopping approach achieves competitive results while making adaptation up to eight times faster, without significant quality drops in the reported evaluation. Its practical contribution is a drop-in way to reduce unnecessary training using the existing objective, rather than requiring a separate personalization method.
summary.tldr: Tracking training loss on fixed inputs enables earlier stopping and up to eightfold faster image-model personalization without significant quality loss.

title: Is This Loss Informative? Faster Text-to-Image Customization by Tracking Objective Dynamics

abstract: Although equivariant machine learning has proven effective at many tasks, success depends heavily on the assumption that the ground truth function is symmetric over the entire domain matching the symmetry in an equivariant neural network. A missing piece in the equivariant learning literature is the analysis of equivariant networks when symmetry exists only partially in the domain. In this work, we present a general theory for such a situation. We propose pointwise definitions of correct, incorrect, and extrinsic equivariance, which allow us to quantify continuously the degree of each type of equivariance a function displays. We then study the impact of various degrees of incorrect or extrinsic symmetry on model error. We prove error lower bounds for invariant or equivariant networks in classification or regression settings with partially incorrect symmetry. We also analyze the potentially harmful effects of extrinsic equivariance. Experiments validate these results in three different environments.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks encode rules about how predictions should respond when inputs are transformed. Their success often depends on those rules matching the symmetry of the function being learned across its entire domain. This paper examines the more complicated situation in which the assumed symmetry holds in some places but fails elsewhere.

The authors introduce pointwise definitions of correct, incorrect, and extrinsic equivariance. Defining these properties locally lets them describe degrees of symmetry rather than treating a function as simply symmetric or nonsymmetric. They then investigate how varying amounts of incorrect or extrinsic symmetry affect prediction error.

The theory establishes lower bounds on error for invariant and equivariant networks performing classification or regression when their imposed symmetry is partially incorrect. It also analyzes potentially harmful effects of extrinsic equivariance. Experiments in three environments support the results. The central implication is that architectural symmetry can impose an error floor when it conflicts with the target function, making the extent of that mismatch important.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a theory of partially valid symmetry assumptions and shows how incorrect equivariance can impose lower bounds on prediction error.

title: A General Theory of Correct, Incorrect, and Extrinsic Equivariance

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning suffers from the extrapolation error and value overestimation caused by out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. To mitigate this issue, value regularization approaches aim to penalize the learned value functions to assign lower values to OOD actions. However, existing value regularization methods lack a proper distinction between the regularization effects on in-distribution (ID) and OOD actions, and fail to guarantee optimal convergence results of the policy. To this end, we propose Supported Value Regularization (SVR), which penalizes the Q-values for all OOD actions while maintaining standard Bellman updates for ID ones. Specifically, we utilize the bias of importance sampling to compute the summation of Q-values over the entire OOD region, which serves as the penalty for policy evaluation. This design automatically separates the regularization for ID and OOD actions without manually distinguishing between them. In tabular MDP, we show that the policy evaluation operator of SVR is a contraction, whose fixed point outputs unbiased Q-values for ID actions and underestimated Q-values for OOD actions. Furthermore, the policy iteration with SVR guarantees strict policy improvement until convergence to the optimal support-constrained policy in the dataset. Empirically, we validate the theoretical properties of SVR in a tabular maze environment and demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on a range of continuous control tasks in the D4RL benchmark.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning can overestimate the value of actions poorly represented in its fixed dataset. Value penalties aim to control this problem, but they can also affect actions that the data support. Supported Value Regularization separates these effects: it penalizes out-of-distribution action values while preserving standard Bellman updates for in-distribution actions.

The method uses the bias of importance sampling to compute a sum of Q-values across the out-of-distribution region. That sum supplies the policy-evaluation penalty and automatically creates the desired separation. In tabular Markov decision processes, the authors prove that the evaluation operator is a contraction, with a fixed point giving unbiased supported-action values and underestimated unsupported-action values.

Also in the tabular setting, policy iteration strictly improves the policy until it reaches the optimal policy constrained to the dataset's support. This is a support-constrained guarantee, so its target depends on which actions the dataset supports. Experiments validate the theoretical properties in a tabular maze and report state-of-the-art performance on a range of D4RL continuous control tasks.
summary.tldr: Supported Value Regularization penalizes unsupported actions while preserving supported-action updates, with tabular guarantees of convergence to the optimal support-constrained policy.

title: Supported Value Regularization for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Virtual screening, which identifies potential drugs from vast compound databases to bind with a particular protein pocket, is a critical step in AI-assisted drug discovery. Traditional docking methods are highly time-consuming, and can only work with a restricted search library in real-life applications. Recent supervised learning approaches using scoring functions for binding-affinity prediction, although promising, have not yet surpassed docking methods due to their strong dependency on limited data with reliable binding-affinity labels. In this paper, we propose a novel contrastive learning framework, DrugCLIP, by reformulating virtual screening as a dense retrieval task and employing contrastive learning to align representations of binding protein pockets and molecules from a large quantity of pairwise data without explicit binding-affinity scores. We also introduce a biological-knowledge inspired data augmentation strategy to learn better protein-molecule representations. Extensive experiments show that DrugCLIP significantly outperforms traditional docking and supervised learning methods on diverse virtual screening benchmarks with highly reduced computation time, especially in zero-shot setting.

paragraphs: Virtual screening searches compound collections for molecules that may bind to a particular protein pocket. Traditional docking is computationally expensive, while supervised binding predictors depend heavily on scarce, reliable affinity labels. DrugCLIP approaches this problem by learning representations that make screening a retrieval task.

The framework uses contrastive learning to align representations of protein pockets and molecules from paired data. This training does not require explicit numerical binding-affinity scores. Screening can then use the learned representations to retrieve candidate molecules for a pocket. The authors also introduce a data augmentation strategy inspired by biological knowledge to improve the representations learned from these pairs.

Across diverse virtual screening benchmarks, DrugCLIP is reported to significantly outperform both traditional docking and supervised learning methods while greatly reducing computation time. The gains are especially pronounced in the zero-shot setting. These findings support representation-based retrieval as an effective screening approach in the evaluated settings, addressing both the computational burden of docking and dependence on explicit affinity labels.
summary.tldr: DrugCLIP learns aligned protein-pocket and molecule representations for faster virtual screening without explicit binding-affinity scores.

title: DrugCLIP: Contrastive Protein-Molecule Representation Learning for Virtual Screening

abstract: Embodied agents face significant challenges when tasked with performing actions in diverse environments, particularly in generalizing across object types and executing suitable actions to accomplish tasks. Furthermore, agents should exhibit robustness, minimizing the execution of illegal actions. In this work, we present Egocentric Planning, an innovative approach that combines symbolic planning and Object-oriented POMDPs to solve tasks in complex environments, harnessing existing models for visual perception and natural language processing. We evaluated our approach in ALFRED, a simulated environment designed for domestic tasks, and demonstrated its high scalability, achieving an impressive 36.07\% unseen success rate in the ALFRED benchmark and winning the ALFRED challenge at CVPR Embodied AI workshop. Our method requires reliable perception and the specification or learning of a symbolic description of the preconditions and effects of the agent's actions, as well as what object types reveal information about others. It can naturally scale to solve new tasks beyond ALFRED, as long as they can be solved using the available skills. This work offers a solid baseline for studying end-to-end and hybrid methods that aim to generalize to new tasks, including recent approaches relying on LLMs, but often struggle to scale to long sequences of actions or produce robust plans for novel tasks.

paragraphs: An embodied agent must choose actions that fit its surroundings, work across object types, and avoid actions that are invalid in the current situation. Egocentric Planning combines symbolic planning with an object-oriented model of decision-making under partial observability. It also uses existing visual perception and natural language processing models to support task execution.

The symbolic component describes the preconditions and effects of actions: what must hold before an action and what it can change. The approach also needs information about which object types reveal information about others. These requirements make its dependence on reliable perception and specified or learned symbolic knowledge explicit.

On ALFRED, a simulated benchmark for domestic tasks, the approach achieves a 36.07% unseen success rate and won the associated challenge at the CVPR Embodied AI workshop. The authors argue that it can scale to new tasks beyond ALFRED when those tasks are solvable using available skills. Its contribution is a hybrid planning baseline for studying generalization and robustness, including tasks that require long action sequences.
summary.tldr: Egocentric Planning combines symbolic action knowledge and object-oriented decision-making to perform embodied tasks, achieving 36.07% unseen success on ALFRED.

title: Egocentric Planning for Scalable Embodied Task Achievement

abstract: What are the functionals of the reward that can be computed and optimized exactly in Markov Decision Processes?In the finite-horizon, undiscounted setting, Dynamic Programming (DP) can only handle these operations efficiently for certain classes of statistics. We summarize the characterization of these classes for policy evaluation, and give a new answer for the planning problem. Interestingly, we prove that only generalized means can be optimized exactly, even in the more general framework of Distributional Reinforcement Learning (DistRL).DistRL permits, however, to evaluate other functionals approximately. We provide error bounds on the resulting estimators, and discuss the potential of this approach as well as its limitations.These results contribute to advancing the theory of Markov Decision Processes by examining overall characteristics of the return, and particularly risk-conscious strategies.

paragraphs: Average return captures only one aspect of a decision-making strategy's outcomes. A risk-conscious decision maker may care about other summaries of the reward distribution. This paper asks which such summaries can be evaluated and optimized exactly in Markov Decision Processes, focusing on finite-horizon problems without discounting.

Dynamic programming solves a sequential problem through smaller linked computations, but this structure supports efficient exact treatment only for certain statistics. The authors summarize the relevant characterization for policy evaluation and establish a new result for planning: within the framework studied, only generalized means can be optimized exactly. Moving to distributional reinforcement learning does not remove that restriction.

Distributional reinforcement learning nevertheless allows approximate evaluation of other functionals, or numerical summaries, of return. The paper supplies error bounds for these estimators and discusses their potential and limits. Its contribution separates what richer return information can help estimate from what the studied planning machinery can optimize exactly, providing a theoretical foundation for assessing risk-conscious objectives.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes limits on exact return-based planning and bounds approximate evaluation of richer objectives in finite-horizon, undiscounted Markov Decision Processes.

title: Beyond Average Return in Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Missing values in real-world data pose a significant and unique challenge to algorithmic fairness. Different demographic groups may be unequally affected by missing data, and the standard procedure for handling missing values where first data is imputed, then the imputed data is used for classification—a procedure referred to as "impute-then-classify"—can exacerbate discrimination. In this paper, we analyze how missing values affect algorithmic fairness. We first prove that training a classifier from imputed data can significantly worsen the achievable values of group fairness and average accuracy. This is because imputing data results in the loss of the missing pattern of the data, which often conveys information about the predictive label. We present scalable and adaptive algorithms for fair classification with missing values. These algorithms can be combined with any preexisting fairness-intervention algorithm to handle all possible missing patterns while preserving information encoded within the missing patterns. Numerical experiments with state-of-the-art fairness interventions demonstrate that our adaptive algorithms consistently achieve higher fairness and accuracy than impute-then-classify across different datasets.

paragraphs: Missing data can affect demographic groups differently, making it relevant to both prediction quality and fairness. This paper studies the common workflow of filling in missing values before training a classifier. Its central concern is that replacing missing entries can erase information carried by the pattern of what was missing.

The authors prove that training on imputed data can substantially worsen the fairness and average accuracy that a classifier can achieve. The mechanism is informational: missingness patterns often help predict the target label, and the imputation step can discard that signal. This is a statement about what can happen, rather than a claim that every use of imputation necessarily produces discrimination.

The proposed scalable algorithms adapt fairness interventions to different missingness patterns while preserving their information. They are designed to work with any existing fairness-intervention algorithm. Across the reported datasets, combining them with state-of-the-art fairness methods consistently improves both fairness and accuracy relative to imputing first and then classifying. The results support treating missingness as part of the learning problem.
summary.tldr: Preserving information about which values are missing improves the reported fairness and accuracy of classification compared with imputing first.

title: Adapting Fairness Interventions to Missing Values

abstract: In-context learning––the ability to configure a model's behavior with different prompts––has revolutionized the field of natural language processing, alleviating the need for task-specific models and paving the way for generalist models capable of assisting with any query. Computer vision, in contrast, has largely stayed in the former regime: specialized decoders and finetuning protocols are generally required to perform dense tasks such as semantic segmentation and depth estimation. In this work we explore a simple mechanism for in-context learning of such scene understanding tasks: nearest neighbor retrieval from a prompt of annotated features. We propose a new pretraining protocol––leveraging attention within and across images––which yields representations particularly useful in this regime. The resulting Hummingbird model, suitably prompted, performs various scene understanding tasks without modification while approaching the performance of specialists that have been finetuned for each task. Moreover, Hummingbird can be configured to perform new tasks much more efficiently than finetuned models, raising the possibility of scene understanding in the interactive assistant regime.

paragraphs: Dense scene-understanding tasks, such as segmentation and depth estimation, commonly require specialized decoders or task-specific fine-tuning. This paper explores configuring those tasks through prompts instead. Its prompt consists of annotated features, allowing the model to use supplied examples to determine the requested output.

The proposed mechanism is nearest-neighbor retrieval from those prompted features. To make that mechanism effective, the authors introduce a pretraining protocol that uses attention both within individual images and across images. The resulting Hummingbird representations are designed to support scene understanding through feature matching, linking the pretraining objective to the intended prompting procedure.

With suitable prompts, Hummingbird performs multiple scene-understanding tasks without modifying the model. Its performance approaches that of specialists fine-tuned for individual tasks, and configuring it for new tasks is much more efficient than fine-tuning in the reported comparison. These findings support prompting as a route toward flexible visual systems. The paper presents interactive scene-understanding assistants as a possibility enabled by this efficiency, rather than as an already established universal capability.
summary.tldr: Hummingbird uses retrieval from annotated feature prompts to perform scene-understanding tasks without task-specific model modification.

title: Towards In-context Scene Understanding

abstract: Generative priors of large-scale text-to-image diffusion models enable a wide range of new generation and editing applications on diverse visual modalities. However, when adapting these priors to complex visual modalities, often represented as multiple images (e.g., video or 3D scene), achieving consistency across a set of images is challenging. In this paper, we address this challenge with a novel method, Collaborative Score Distillation (CSD). CSD is based on the Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD). Specifically, we propose to consider multiple samples as “particles” in the SVGD update and combine their score functions to distill generative priors over a set of images synchronously. Thus, CSD facilitates the seamless integration of information across 2D images, leading to a consistent visual synthesis across multiple samples. We show the effectiveness of CSD in a variety of editing tasks, encompassing the visual editing of panorama images, videos, and 3D scenes. Our results underline the competency of CSD as a versatile method for enhancing inter-sample consistency, thereby broadening the applicability of text-to-image diffusion models.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models contain useful visual knowledge for generation and editing. Applying that knowledge to videos, panoramas, or three-dimensional scenes creates an additional challenge: several related images must agree with one another. An edit that works for an individual image does not by itself solve consistency across the complete visual representation.

Collaborative Score Distillation addresses this by updating multiple samples together. The method builds on Stein Variational Gradient Descent, treating the samples as interacting particles. It combines their score functions so that the diffusion model's generative guidance is distilled across the image collection synchronously. This provides a mechanism for information to pass between samples during editing.

The researchers demonstrate the method on panorama, video, and three-dimensional scene editing. Their results support its ability to improve consistency between samples across these different applications. The approach matters because it adapts image-based generative knowledge to tasks whose success depends on relationships among images, extending the usefulness of text-to-image models beyond isolated outputs.
summary.tldr: Collaborative Score Distillation jointly guides related images to improve consistency in panorama, video, and 3D scene editing.

title: Collaborative Score Distillation for Consistent Visual Editing

abstract: Asynchronous stochastic gradient descent (ASGD) has evolved into an indispensable optimization algorithm for training modern large-scale distributed machine learning tasks. Therefore, it is imperative to explore the generalization performance of the ASGD algorithm. However, the existing results are either pessimistic and vacuous or restricted by strict assumptions that fail to reveal the intrinsic impact of asynchronous training on generalization. In this study, we establish sharper stability and generalization bounds for ASGD under much weaker assumptions. Firstly, this paper studies the on-average model stability of ASGD and provides a non-vacuous upper bound on the generalization error, without relying on the Lipschitz assumption. Furthermore, we investigate the excess generalization error of the ASGD algorithm, revealing the effects of asynchronous delay, model initialization, number of training samples and iterations on generalization performance. Secondly, for the first time, this study explores the generalization performance of ASGD in the non-smooth case. We replace smoothness with the much weaker Hölder continuous assumption and achieve similar generalization results as in the smooth case. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings by training numerous machine learning models, including convex problems and non-convex tasks in computer vision and natural language processing.

paragraphs: Asynchronous stochastic gradient descent supports distributed training, but understanding its performance on unseen data requires accounting for asynchronous updates. Earlier theoretical results can give uninformative bounds or depend on restrictive assumptions. This paper develops sharper stability and generalization results intended to better expose how asynchronous training affects learning.

The authors analyze on-average model stability and obtain a non-vacuous upper bound on generalization error without the Lipschitz assumption. They also study excess generalization error, making explicit the roles of asynchronous delay, initialization, training-set size, and iteration count. This connects several practical aspects of training to the theoretical assessment of generalization.

The analysis additionally covers a nonsmooth setting by replacing smoothness with the weaker assumption of Hölder continuity. Under that condition, the authors obtain generalization results similar to those in the smooth case. Experiments involving convex models and nonconvex computer-vision and natural-language tasks validate the theoretical findings. The contribution broadens the settings in which asynchronous training has informative generalization guarantees while retaining explicit assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper derives sharper generalization bounds for asynchronous SGD under weaker assumptions, including a nonsmooth setting with Hölder continuity.

title: Stability and Generalization of Asynchronous SGD: Sharper Bounds Beyond Lipschitz and Smoothness

abstract: Large Language Models are known to capture real-world knowledge, allowing them to excel in many downstream tasks. Despite recent advances, these models are still prone to what are commonly known as hallucinations, causing them to emit unwanted and factually incorrect text. In this work, we propose a novel calibration method that can be used to combat hallucinations. We add a special [IDK] (“I Don't Know”) token to the model's vocabulary and introduce an objective function that shifts probability mass to the [IDK] token for incorrect predictions. This approach allows the model to express uncertainty in its output explicitly. We evaluate our proposed method across multiple model architectures and factual downstream tasks.We find that models trained with our method are able to express uncertainty in places where they would previously make mistakes while suffering only a small loss of encoded knowledge. We further perform extensive ablation studies of multiple variations of our approach and provide a detailed analysis of the precision-recall tradeoff of our method.

paragraphs: Language models can contain substantial factual knowledge and still produce incorrect statements. This paper proposes giving them an explicit way to signal uncertainty through a special [IDK] token, meaning “I Don’t Know.” The aim is to reduce mistaken outputs by making uncertainty an available prediction within the model’s vocabulary.

The training objective moves probability toward [IDK] when a prediction is incorrect. This directly connects factual errors to an alternative output the model can learn to choose. The method therefore changes how the model allocates probability, providing a mechanism for expressing uncertainty at places where it might otherwise generate a wrong answer.

Across multiple architectures and factual tasks, trained models express uncertainty where they previously made mistakes, with only a small reported loss of encoded knowledge. The authors also compare variations of the method through ablations and analyze its precision-recall tradeoff. These findings support explicit uncertainty modeling while recognizing that avoiding incorrect answers and retaining useful factual responses involve a tradeoff.
summary.tldr: Training language models to assign incorrect predictions’ probability to an [IDK] token helps them express uncertainty with a small reported knowledge loss.

title: I Don't Know: Explicit Modeling of Uncertainty with an [IDK] Token

abstract: Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has gained massive attention in the recent generative AI research. One of the main advantages of LoRA is its ability to be fused with pretrained models, adding no overhead during inference. However, from a mobile deployment standpoint, we can either avoid inference overhead in the fused mode but lose the ability to switch adapters rapidly, or suffer significant (up to 30% higher) inference latency while enabling rapid switching in the unfused mode. LoRA also exhibits concept-loss when multiple adapters are used concurrently. In this paper, we propose Sparse High Rank Adapters (SHiRA), a new paradigm which incurs no inference overhead, enables rapid switching, and significantly reduces concept-loss. Specifically, SHiRA can be trained by directly tuning only 1-2% of the base model weights while leaving others unchanged. This results in a highly sparse adapter which can be switched directly in the fused mode. We further provide theoretical and empirical insights on how high sparsity in SHiRA can aid multi-adapter fusion by reducing concept loss. Our extensive experiments on LVMs and LLMs demonstrate that finetuning only a small fraction of the parameters in the base model significantly outperforms LoRA while enabling both rapid switching and multi-adapter fusion. Finally, we provide a latency- and memory-efficient SHiRA implementation based on Parameter-Efficient Finetuning (PEFT) Library which trains at nearly the same speed as LoRA while consuming up to 16% lower peak GPU memory, thus making SHiRA easy to adopt for practical use cases. To demonstrate rapid switching benefits during inference, we show that loading SHiRA on a base model can be 5x-16x faster than LoRA fusion on a CPU.

title: Sparse High Rank Adapters

abstract: Long-horizon manipulation tasks with general instructions often implicitly encapsulate multiple sub-tasks, posing significant challenges in instruction following.While language planning is a common approach to decompose general instructions into stepwise sub-instructions, text-only guidance may lack expressiveness and lead to potential ambiguity. Considering that humans often imagine and visualize sub-instructions reasoning out before acting, the imagined subgoal images can provide more intuitive guidance and enhance the reliability of decomposition. Inspired by this, we propose **PERIA**(**PE**rceive, **R**eason, **I**magine, **A**ct), a novel framework that integrates holistic language planning and vision planning for long-horizon manipulation tasks with complex instructions, leveraging both logical and intuitive aspects of task decomposition.Specifically, we first perform a lightweight multimodal alignment on the encoding side to empower the MLLM to perceive visual details and language instructions. The MLLM is then jointly instruction-tuned with a pretrained image-editing model to unlock capabilities of simultaneous reasoning of language instructions and generation of imagined subgoals. Furthermore, we introduce a consistency alignment loss to encourage coherent subgoal images and align with their corresponding instructions, mitigating potential hallucinations and semantic conflicts between the two planning manners.Comprehensive evaluations across three task domains demonstrate that PERIA, benefiting from holistic language and vision planning, significantly outperforms competitive baselines in both instruction following accuracy and task success rate on complex manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: Complex manipulation instructions often hide several smaller tasks. Breaking them into written steps can help, but text alone may leave ambiguity about the desired intermediate state. PERIA combines language planning with imagined subgoal images so that task decomposition includes both verbal reasoning and visual guidance.

The framework first performs lightweight multimodal alignment to help a multimodal language model perceive visual details alongside instructions. It then jointly instruction-tunes that model with a pretrained image-editing model, enabling instruction reasoning and subgoal-image generation together. A consistency alignment loss encourages the generated images to agree with their corresponding instructions and remain coherent.

That agreement matters because contradictory text and images could undermine the plan even if each appeared plausible separately. The loss is intended to mitigate hallucinations and semantic conflicts between the planning modes. Across three task domains, PERIA significantly outperforms competitive baselines in instruction-following accuracy and task success. These results support combining language and visual planning for the evaluated complex manipulation tasks, without implying that consistency errors are entirely eliminated.
summary.tldr: PERIA jointly plans verbal steps and imagined visual subgoals to improve instruction following and success in complex manipulation tasks.

title: PERIA: Perceive, Reason, Imagine, Act via Holistic Language and Vision Planning for Manipulation

abstract: Approximating invariant subspaces of generalized eigenvalue problems (GEPs) is a fundamental computational problem at the core of machine learning and scientific computing. It is, for example, the root of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction, data visualization, and noise filtering, and of Density Functional Theory (DFT), arguably the most popular method to calculate the electronic structure of materials. Given Hermitian $H,S\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$, where $S$ is positive-definite, let $\Pi_k$ be the true spectral projector on the invariant subspace that is associated with the $k$ smallest (or largest) eigenvalues of the GEP $HC=SC\Lambda$, for some $k\in[n]$. We show that we can compute a matrix $\widetilde\Pi_k$ such that $\lVert\Pi_k-\widetilde\Pi_k\rVert_2\leq \epsilon$, in $O\left( n^{\omega+\eta}\mathrm{polylog}(n,\epsilon^{-1},\kappa(S),\mathrm{gap}_k^{-1}) \right)$ bit operations in the floating point model, for some $\epsilon\in(0,1)$, with probability $1-1/n$. Here, $\eta>0$ is arbitrarily small, $\omega\lesssim 2.372$ is the matrix multiplication exponent, $\kappa(S)=\lVert S\rVert_2\lVert S^{-1}\rVert_2$, and $\mathrm{gap}_k$ is the gap between eigenvalues $k$ and $k+1$. To achieve such provable "forward-error" guarantees, our methods rely on a new $O(n^{\omega+\eta})$ stability analysis for the Cholesky factorization, and a smoothed analysis for computing spectral gaps, which can be of independent interest.Ultimately, we obtain new matrix multiplication-type bit complexity upper bounds for PCA problems, including classical PCA and (randomized) low-rank approximation.

paragraphs: This paper develops fast algorithms for approximating invariant subspaces in generalized eigenvalue problems. These subspaces underpin tasks such as principal component analysis and electronic-structure calculations. The goal is to compute an approximate spectral projector: a matrix representing the subspace associated with a chosen number of the smallest or largest eigenvalues.

The result applies to Hermitian matrices H and S, with S positive-definite. It bounds the projector’s spectral-norm error by a requested tolerance, with success probability 1 minus 1/n. The bit-operation cost is close to the matrix-multiplication exponent, with additional polylogarithmic dependence on matrix size, inverse accuracy, the conditioning of S, and the inverse gap between the relevant neighboring eigenvalues.

To establish this numerical guarantee, the authors develop a stability analysis for Cholesky factorization and a smoothed analysis for computing spectral gaps. These ingredients explicitly support control of error in the computed projector. The resulting complexity bounds extend to classical PCA and randomized low-rank approximation, providing theoretical guarantees for both computational cost and approximation accuracy.
summary.tldr: New numerical analyses enable provably accurate invariant-subspace and PCA computations with bit complexity close to matrix multiplication.

title: Invariant subspaces and PCA in nearly matrix multiplication time

abstract: Training deep neural networks (DNNs) is costly. Fortunately, Nvidia Ampere and Hopper GPUs can accelerate matrix multiplications twice as fast as a dense equivalent by implementing 2:4 sparsity. However, previous STE-based 2:4 pre-training methods (\eg~STE with hard-thresholding, SR-STE) suffer from optimization difficulties because of discontinuous pruning function.In this study, we comprehensively analyse the bottleneck of traditional N:M sparse training and recognize three drawbacks with discontinuity: incorrect descending direction, inability to predict the amount of descent and sparse mask oscillation. In the light of this statement, we propose S-STE, a simple yet powerful 2:4 training method that contains two parts: to continuously project weights to be 2:4 sparse, and to rescale sparse weights with a per-tensor fixed scaling factor. Besides, we adopt minimum-variance unbiased estimation for activation gradient and FP8 quantization for whole process. Results show that our method surpass previous 2:4 pre-training recipes and is comparable even with full parameter models.

paragraphs: Structured 2:4 sparsity makes neural-network matrix multiplication compatible with hardware acceleration on Nvidia Ampere and Hopper GPUs. However, training with this pattern can be difficult. The paper attributes problems in earlier straight-through-estimator approaches to discontinuous pruning functions, which abruptly change the sparse weights used by the model.

The analysis identifies three consequences: incorrect descent directions, difficulty predicting how much the objective will decrease, and oscillating sparsity masks. S-STE addresses these through a continuous projection onto 2:4-sparse weights and a fixed scaling factor for each tensor. The training recipe also uses a minimum-variance unbiased estimator for activation gradients and FP8 quantization throughout the process.

The reported results surpass earlier 2:4 pretraining recipes and are comparable with full-parameter models. The significance is that enforcing a hardware-supported sparse structure depends on the behavior of the pruning operation during optimization, not just the resulting pattern. The stated twofold acceleration concerns supported matrix multiplications; the abstract’s empirical claim focuses on the quality achieved by the proposed sparse training recipe.
summary.tldr: S-STE uses continuous sparse projection and fixed rescaling to improve optimization and model quality during 2:4 sparse pretraining.

title: S-STE: Continuous Pruning Function for Efficient 2:4 Sparse Pre-training

abstract: Reconstructing and understanding 3D structures from a limited number of images is a classical problem in computer vision. Traditional approaches typically decompose this task into multiple subtasks, involving several stages of complex mappings between different data representations. For example, dense reconstruction using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) requires transforming images into key points, optimizing camera parameters, and estimating structures. Following this, accurate sparse reconstructions are necessary for further dense modeling, which is then input into task-specific neural networks. This multi-stage paradigm leads to significant processing times and engineering complexity.In this work, we introduce the Large Spatial Model (LSM), which directly processes unposed RGB images into semantic radiance fields. LSM simultaneously estimates geometry, appearance, and semantics in a single feed-forward pass and can synthesize versatile label maps by interacting through language at novel views. Built on a general Transformer-based framework, LSM predicts global geometry via pixel-aligned point maps. To improve spatial attribute regression, we adopt local context aggregation with multi-scale fusion, enhancing the accuracy of fine local details. To address the scarcity of labeled 3D semantic data and enable natural language-driven scene manipulation, we incorporate a pre-trained 2D language-based segmentation model into a 3D-consistent semantic feature field. An efficient decoder parameterizes a set of semantic anisotropic Gaussians, allowing supervised end-to-end learning. Comprehensive experiments on various tasks demonstrate that LSM unifies multiple 3D vision tasks directly from unposed images, achieving real-time semantic 3D reconstruction for the first time.

The resulting representation supports language interaction and the synthesis of label maps from new viewpoints. Experiments across several tasks show that LSM can bring multiple 3D vision capabilities into one pipeline operating directly on unposed images. The authors report real-time semantic 3D reconstruction, making processing speed and integrated scene understanding central outcomes of the approach.
summary.tldr: Large Spatial Model converts unposed images into geometry, appearance, and language-accessible 3D semantics in one feed-forward pass.

title: Large Spatial Model: End-to-end Unposed Images to Semantic 3D

abstract: We introduce Language Feedback Models (LFMs) that identify desirable behaviour --- actions that help achieve tasks specified in the instruction - for imitation learning in instruction following. To train LFMs, we obtain feedback from Large Language Models (LLMs) on visual trajectories verbalized to language descriptions. First, by using LFMs to identify desirable behaviour to imitate, we improve in task-completion rate over strong behavioural cloning baselines on three distinct language grounding environments (Touchdown, ScienceWorld, and ALFWorld). Second, LFMs outperform using LLMs as experts to directly predict actions, when controlling for the number of LLM output tokens. Third, LFMs generalize to unseen environments, improving task-completion rate by 3.5-12.0% through one round of adaptation. Finally, LFMs can be modified to provide human-interpretable feedback without performance loss, allowing human verification of desirable behaviour for imitation learning.

paragraphs: Language Feedback Models identify actions worth imitating when learning to follow instructions. The idea is to judge whether behavior helps complete the requested task, then use those judgments to improve imitation learning. To train these feedback models, the authors translate visual trajectories into language descriptions and obtain feedback about them from large language models.

Using the resulting models to select desirable behavior improves task completion over strong behavioral cloning baselines in Touchdown, ScienceWorld, and ALFWorld. The authors also compare this use of language models with asking them to predict actions directly. When the number of language-model output tokens is controlled, the feedback-model approach performs better.

The feedback models also transfer to unseen environments, where one round of adaptation raises task-completion rates by 3.5–12.0%. A modified version provides feedback that humans can interpret without losing performance, enabling people to verify which behaviors are being selected for imitation. These findings support learned behavioral evaluation as a useful route from language-model feedback to better instruction-following policies, including adaptation beyond the environments used initially.
summary.tldr: Language Feedback Models improve instruction-following policies by identifying useful behavior to imitate and supporting adaptation to unseen environments.

title: Policy Improvement using Language Feedback Models

abstract: In climate science and meteorology, high-resolution local precipitation (rain and snowfall) predictions are limited by the computational costs of simulation-based methods. Statistical downscaling, or super-resolution, is a common workaround where a low-resolution prediction is improved using statistical approaches. Unlike traditional computer vision tasks, weather and climate applications require capturing the accurate conditional distribution of high-resolution given low-resolution patterns to assure reliable ensemble averages and unbiased estimates of extreme events, such as heavy rain. This work extends recent video diffusion models to precipitation super-resolution, employing a deterministic downscaler followed by a temporally-conditioned diffusion model to capture noise characteristics and high-frequency patterns. We test our approach on FV3GFS output, an established large-scale global atmosphere model, and compare it against six state-of-the-art baselines. Our analysis, capturing CRPS, MSE, precipitation distributions, and qualitative aspects using California and the Himalayas as examples, establishes our method as a new standard for data-driven precipitation downscaling.

paragraphs: Producing local precipitation predictions at high resolution through simulation is computationally expensive. Statistical downscaling starts with a coarser prediction and estimates finer detail. For weather applications, however, plausible-looking detail is insufficient: the method needs to represent the distribution of fine-scale precipitation compatible with the coarse input, including patterns relevant to heavy rain.

This paper adapts video diffusion models to that task. A deterministic downscaler first produces an initial higher-resolution estimate. A diffusion model then uses temporal conditioning to capture noise characteristics and high-frequency patterns. The temporal component brings the relationship between successive precipitation patterns into the generation process, rather than treating downscaling solely as spatial image enhancement.

The authors test the approach using output from the FV3GFS global atmosphere model and compare it with six state-of-the-art baselines. Their evaluation includes CRPS, MSE, precipitation distributions, and qualitative examples from California and the Himalayas. They report results positioning the method as a new standard for data-driven downscaling. The evaluation’s distributional emphasis reflects the goal of supporting reliable ensemble averages and estimates of extreme precipitation.
summary.tldr: A deterministic downscaler followed by temporally conditioned diffusion generates fine-scale precipitation patterns and performs strongly against six downscaling baselines.

title: Precipitation Downscaling with Spatiotemporal Video Diffusion

abstract: This paper studies the problem of rigid dynamics modeling, which has a wide range of applications in robotics, graphics, and mechanical design. The problem is partly solved by graph neural network (GNN) simulators. However, these approaches cannot effectively handle the relationship between intrinsic continuity and instantaneous changes in rigid dynamics. Moreover, they usually neglect hierarchical structures across mesh nodes and objects in systems. In this paper, we propose a novel approach named Event-attend Graph ODE (EGODE) for effective rigid dynamics modeling. In particular, we describe the rigid system using both mesh node representations and object representations. To model continuous dynamics across hierarchical structures, we use a coupled graph ODE framework for the evolution of both types of representations over a long period. In addition, to capture instantaneous changes during the collision, we introduce an event module, which can effectively estimate the occurrence of the collision and update the states of both mesh node and object representations during evolution. Extensive experiments on a range of benchmark datasets validate the superiority of the proposed EGODE compared to various state-of-the-art baselines. The source code can be found at https://github.com/yuanjypku/EGODE.

paragraphs: Rigid-body motion combines continuous evolution with abrupt changes during collisions. The paper argues that existing graph neural network simulators struggle to capture this combination and often overlook the relationship between individual mesh nodes and whole objects. EGODE is designed to represent both the timing of motion and this hierarchy of physical structure.

The system maintains representations at two levels: mesh nodes and objects. A coupled graph ordinary differential equation evolves both representations over time, connecting their continuous dynamics. An additional event module estimates when collisions occur and updates the states at both levels to account for the resulting instantaneous changes.

This division gives the model explicit mechanisms for smooth motion and collision events while keeping local and object-level descriptions connected. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets report better performance than several leading comparison methods. The findings support the proposed combination of hierarchical representations, continuous-time evolution, and event handling for the rigid-dynamics problems evaluated in the paper.
summary.tldr: EGODE combines continuous graph dynamics with collision events at mesh-node and object levels to improve rigid-body simulation.

title: EGODE: An Event-attended Graph ODE Framework for Modeling Rigid Dynamics

abstract: With the emergence of large pre-trained multimodal video models, multiple benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate model capabilities. However, most of the benchmarks are human-centric, with evaluation data and tasks centered around human applications. Animals are an integral part of the natural world, and animal-centric video understanding is crucial for animal welfare and conservation efforts. Yet, existing benchmarks overlook evaluations focused on animals, limiting the application of the models. To address this limitation, our work established an animal-centric benchmark, namely Animal-Bench, to allow for a comprehensive evaluation of model capabilities in real-world contexts, overcoming agent-bias in previous benchmarks. Animal-Bench includes 13 tasks encompassing both common tasks shared with humans and special tasks relevant to animal conservation, spanning 7 major animal categories and 819 species, comprising a total of 41,839 data entries. To generate this benchmark, we defined a task system centered on animals and proposed an automated pipeline for animal-centric data processing. To further validate the robustness of models against real-world challenges, we utilized a video editing approach to simulate realistic scenarios like weather changes and shooting parameters due to animal movements. We evaluated 8 current multimodal video models on our benchmark and found considerable room for improvement. We hope our work provides insights for the community and opens up new avenues for research in multimodal video models. Our data and code will be released at https://github.com/PRIS-CV/Animal-Bench.

Some tasks overlap with familiar human-centered evaluations, while others address animal conservation. The authors define an animal-centered task system and build an automated data-processing pipeline, giving the benchmark a structured basis beyond simply collecting animal videos.

The evaluation also includes edited videos that simulate challenges such as changing weather and shooting conditions associated with animal movement. Tests of eight multimodal video models reveal considerable room for improvement. The contribution is therefore both a broader test collection and evidence that existing models still face substantial challenges on animal-focused tasks, including robustness under the simulated viewing conditions.
summary.tldr: Animal-Bench evaluates video models across diverse animal tasks and species, revealing substantial room for improvement.

title: Animal-Bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Video Models for Animal-centric Video Understanding

abstract: Dual-target therapeutic strategies have become a compelling approach and attracted significant attention due to various benefits, such as their potential in overcoming drug resistance in cancer therapy. Considering the tremendous success that deep generative models have achieved in structure-based drug design in recent years, we formulate dual-target drug design as a generative task and curate a novel dataset of potential target pairs based on synergistic drug combinations. We propose to design dual-target drugs with diffusion models that are trained on single-target protein-ligand complex pairs. Specifically, we align two pockets in 3D space with protein-ligand binding priors and build two complex graphs with shared ligand nodes for SE(3)-equivariant composed message passing, based on which we derive a composed drift in both 3D and categorical probability space in the generative process. Our algorithm can well transfer the knowledge gained in single-target pretraining to dual-target scenarios in a zero-shot manner. We also repurpose linker design methods as strong baselines for this task. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method compared with various baselines.

paragraphs: The paper treats designing a molecule for two protein targets as a generative task. Dual-target therapies are motivated partly by their potential to overcome drug resistance. The authors curate a dataset of potential target pairs from synergistic drug combinations and ask how models trained on single-target protein-ligand complexes can support this new task.

summary.tldr: The method composes pretrained single-target diffusion models to generate candidate dual-target molecules without dual-target retraining.

title: Reprogramming Pretrained Target-Specific Diffusion Models for Dual-Target Drug Design

abstract: Vision-language foundation models (such as CLIP) have recently shown their power in transfer learning, owing to large-scale image-text pre-training. However, target domain data in the downstream tasks can be highly different from the pre-training phase, which makes it hard for such a single model to generalize well. Alternatively, there exists a wide range of expert models that contain diversified vision and/or language knowledge pre-trained on different modalities, tasks, networks, and datasets. Unfortunately, these models are "isolated agents" with heterogeneous structures, and how to integrate their knowledge for generalizing CLIP-like models has not been fully explored. To bridge this gap, we propose a general and concise TransAgent framework, which transports the knowledge of the isolated agents in a unified manner, and effectively guides CLIP to generalize with multi-source knowledge distillation. With such a distinct framework, we flexibly collaborate with 11 heterogeneous agents to empower vision-language foundation models, without further cost in the inference phase. Finally, our TransAgent achieves state-of-the-art performance on 11 visual recognition datasets. Under the same low-shot setting, it outperforms the popular CoOp with around 10\% on average, and 20\% on EuroSAT which contains large domain shifts.

Meanwhile, other pretrained models contain useful expertise from different modalities, tasks, architectures, and datasets. TransAgent aims to bring that distributed knowledge into a single vision-language model despite the experts' heterogeneous structures.

The framework uses a unified knowledge-transfer process and multi-source distillation to guide CLIP. In the reported setup, it collaborates with 11 heterogeneous expert agents. Their knowledge strengthens the target model without adding inference-time cost, so the resulting predictions do not require an additional computational burden from the participating experts.

These results support using diverse pretrained expertise to improve transfer when labeled target examples are scarce. The contribution is both a way to unify otherwise separate models' knowledge and evidence that this transfer improves downstream recognition.
summary.tldr: TransAgent distills knowledge from 11 heterogeneous experts into a vision-language model, improving low-shot recognition without additional inference cost.

title: TransAgent: Transfer Vision-Language Foundation Models with Heterogeneous Agent Collaboration

abstract: Kernel k-means has been widely studied in machine learning. However, existing kernel k-means methods often ignore the \textit{fairness} issue, which may cause discrimination. To address this issue, in this paper, we propose a novel Fair Kernel K-Means (FKKM) framework. In this framework, we first propose a new fairness regularization term that can lead to a fair partition of data. The carefully designed fairness regularization term has a similar form to the kernel k-means which can be seamlessly integrated into the kernel k-means framework. Then, we extend this method to the multiple kernel setting, leading to a Fair Multiple Kernel K-Means (FMKKM) method. We also provide some theoretical analysis of the generalization error bound, and based on this bound we give a strategy to set the hyper-parameter, which makes the proposed methods easy to use. At last, we conduct extensive experiments on both the single kernel and multiple kernel settings to compare the proposed methods with state-of-the-art methods to demonstrate their effectiveness.
