paragraphs: Kernel k-means groups data using similarities represented by a kernel. The paper addresses a concern that conventional versions can overlook: a partition may be useful for clustering while also raising fairness issues. The authors incorporate fairness directly into the clustering framework so that it becomes part of the optimization process.

Their Fair Kernel K-Means method adds a fairness regularization term designed to have a form similar to the underlying clustering objective. This compatibility allows the term to be integrated into kernel k-means. The authors then extend the approach to a setting with multiple kernels, yielding Fair Multiple Kernel K-Means and carrying the fairness mechanism into a broader similarity representation.

The paper provides theoretical analysis of a generalization-error bound and uses it to derive a strategy for setting the hyperparameter. That connects a practical configuration choice to the theoretical analysis. Experiments in both single-kernel and multiple-kernel settings compare the proposed approaches with state-of-the-art methods and demonstrate their effectiveness. The contribution combines a fairness-aware objective, an extension across kernel settings, and guidance for configuring the method.
summary.tldr: The paper integrates a fairness regularizer into single-kernel and multiple-kernel k-means and derives guidance for setting its hyperparameter.

title: Fair Kernel K-Means: from Single Kernel to Multiple Kernel

abstract: Superconductivity is a fascinating phenomenon observed in certain materials under certain conditions. However, some critical aspects of it, such as the relationship between superconductivity and materials' chemical/structural features, still need to be understood. Recent successes of data-driven approaches in material science strongly inspire researchers to study this relationship with them, but a corresponding dataset is still lacking. Hence, we present a new dataset for data-driven approaches, namely SuperCon3D, containing both 3D crystal structures and experimental superconducting transition temperature (Tc) for the first time. Based on SuperCon3D, we propose two deep learning methods for designing high Tc superconductors. The first is SODNet, a novel equivariant graph attention model for screening known structures, which differs from existing models in incorporating both ordered and disordered geometric content. The second is a diffusion generative model DiffCSP-SC for creating new structures, which enables high Tc-targeted generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that both our proposed dataset and models are advantageous for designing new high Tc superconducting candidates.

paragraphs: Learning how material structure relates to superconductivity requires examples that connect geometry to measured superconducting behavior. SuperCon3D supplies this connection by pairing three-dimensional crystal structures with experimentally measured transition temperatures, or Tc. The dataset is intended to support data-driven investigation of the chemical and structural features associated with superconductivity.

The paper builds two complementary models on this resource. SODNet is an equivariant graph attention model for screening known structures, incorporating both ordered and disordered geometric information. DiffCSP-SC is a diffusion model for generating new structures while targeting high transition temperatures. Together, they address selecting promising existing candidates and proposing additional ones.

Experiments show advantages from the dataset and the proposed models for designing high-Tc superconducting candidates. The distinction between screening and generation matters: each uses the structural information toward a different stage of candidate discovery. The reported contribution is a linked data-and-model approach to materials design, with experimentally grounded temperature data supporting learned predictions and targeted proposals.
summary.tldr: SuperCon3D links crystal structures to measured transition temperatures and supports models for screening and generating high-temperature superconducting candidates.

title: Learning Superconductivity from Ordered and Disordered Material Structures

abstract: Estimating and disentangling epistemic uncertainty, uncertainty that is reducible with more training data, and aleatoric uncertainty, uncertainty that is inherent to the task at hand, is critically important when applying machine learning to high-stakes applications such as medical imaging and weather forecasting. Conditional diffusion models' breakthrough ability to accurately and efficiently sample from the posterior distribution of a dataset now makes uncertainty estimation conceptually straightforward: One need only train and sample from a large ensemble of diffusion models. Unfortunately, training such an ensemble becomes computationally intractable as the complexity of the model architecture grows. In this work we introduce a new approach to ensembling, hyper-diffusion models (HyperDM), which allows one to accurately estimate both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty with a single model. Unlike existing single-model uncertainty methods like Monte-Carlo dropout and Bayesian neural networks, HyperDM offers prediction accuracy on par with, and in some cases superior to, multi-model ensembles. Furthermore, our proposed approach scales to modern network architectures such as Attention U-Net and yields more accurate uncertainty estimates compared to existing methods. We validate our method on two distinct real-world tasks: x-ray computed tomography reconstruction and weather temperature forecasting.

paragraphs: This paper separates two reasons a prediction can be uncertain: insufficient training knowledge and uncertainty inherent in the task. The first, epistemic uncertainty, can decrease with more training data. The second, aleatoric uncertainty, concerns variability inherent to the problem. Distinguishing them is especially valuable in applications such as medical imaging and weather forecasting.

An ensemble of conditional diffusion models offers a conceptually straightforward way to estimate both kinds of uncertainty, but training many large models can become computationally intractable. Hyper-diffusion models, called HyperDM, introduce an approach to ensembling that estimates both uncertainty components using a single model.

The reported prediction accuracy matches multi-model ensembles and sometimes exceeds them, while uncertainty estimates improve over existing methods. The approach also scales to modern architectures such as Attention U-Net. Validation covers x-ray computed tomography reconstruction and temperature forecasting. These results support the possibility of obtaining both strong predictions and useful uncertainty separation without training a separate collection of full models in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: HyperDM estimates both data-reducible and inherent uncertainty with one model while achieving prediction accuracy comparable to multi-model ensembles.

title: Estimating Epistemic and Aleatoric Uncertainty with a Single Model

abstract: Text-guided diffusion models have significantly advanced image editing, enabling high-quality and diverse modifications driven by text prompts. However, effective editing requires inverting the source image into a latent space, a process often hindered by prediction errors inherent in DDIM inversion. These errors accumulate during the diffusion process, resulting in inferior content preservation and edit fidelity, especially with conditional inputs. We address these challenges by investigating the primary contributors to error accumulation in DDIM inversion and identify the singularity problem in traditional noise schedules as a key issue. To resolve this, we introduce the *Logistic Schedule*, a novel noise schedule designed to eliminate singularities, improve inversion stability, and provide a better noise space for image editing. This schedule reduces noise prediction errors, enabling more faithful editing that preserves the original content of the source image. Our approach requires no additional retraining and is compatible with various existing editing methods. Experiments across eight editing tasks demonstrate the Logistic Schedule's superior performance in content preservation and edit fidelity compared to traditional noise schedules, highlighting its adaptability and effectiveness. The project page is available at https://lonelvino.github.io/SYE/.

paragraphs: Text-guided diffusion editing needs a useful latent representation of the source image before making changes. DDIM inversion can introduce prediction errors that accumulate through the diffusion process, harming both preservation of the original content and fidelity to the requested edit. The paper investigates the contributors to that accumulation, particularly when conditional inputs are involved.

The authors identify singularities in traditional noise schedules as a key issue and propose a Logistic Schedule designed to remove them. Changing the schedule improves inversion stability and reduces noise-prediction errors, creating a more suitable noise space for editing. The intervention operates through the noise schedule and requires no additional model retraining.

The schedule is compatible with multiple existing editing methods. Across eight editing tasks, experiments report better content preservation and edit fidelity than traditional schedules. These findings connect the analysis of inversion instability to an actionable modification: adjusting how noise is scheduled can improve editing while allowing the existing editing method and trained model to remain in use.
summary.tldr: The Logistic Schedule improves diffusion image editing by reducing DDIM inversion instability and prediction errors without retraining.

title: Schedule Your Edit: A Simple yet Effective Diffusion Noise Schedule for Image Editing

abstract: Contrastive learning has been a leading paradigm for self-supervised learning, but it is widely observed that it comes at the price of sacrificing useful features (\eg colors) by being invariant to data augmentations. Given this limitation, there has been a surge of interest in equivariant self-supervised learning (E-SSL) that learns features to be augmentation-aware. However, even for the simplest rotation prediction method, there is a lack of rigorous understanding of why, when, and how E-SSL learns useful features for downstream tasks. To bridge this gap between practice and theory, we establish an information-theoretic perspective to understand the generalization ability of E-SSL. In particular, we identify a critical explaining-away effect in E-SSL that creates a synergy between the equivariant and classification tasks. This synergy effect encourages models to extract class-relevant features to improve its equivariant prediction, which, in turn, benefits downstream tasks requiring semantic features. Based on this perspective, we theoretically analyze the influence of data transformations and reveal several principles for practical designs of E-SSL. Our theory not only aligns well with existing E-SSL methods but also sheds light on new directions by exploring the benefits of model equivariance. We believe that a theoretically grounded understanding on the role of equivariance would inspire more principled and advanced designs in this field. Code is available at https://github.com/kaotty/Understanding-ESSL.

paragraphs: Self-supervised contrastive learning often encourages representations to ignore data augmentations, which can discard useful information such as color. Equivariant self-supervised learning instead makes features aware of those transformations. This paper develops an information-theoretic account of why such awareness can help models learn features useful for later tasks.

The analysis identifies an explaining-away effect that links the transformation-prediction task with classification. Under this account, extracting class-relevant information can help a model predict the transformation. Learning that information then benefits downstream tasks that need semantic features. This gives a mechanism for understanding the usefulness of equivariant prediction beyond simply retaining more augmentation details.

The authors use this perspective to analyze how different data transformations influence learning and derive principles for practical method design. Their theory aligns with existing equivariant self-supervised approaches and suggests additional directions involving model equivariance. The contribution is a theoretical explanation connecting augmentation-aware training, semantic feature extraction, and generalization, intended to guide more principled choices of transformations and architectures.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic analysis explains how predicting transformations can encourage semantic features that help downstream tasks.

title: Understanding the Role of Equivariance in Self-supervised Learning

abstract: Pre-training techniques have greatly advanced computer vision, with CroCo’s cross-view completion approach yielding impressive results in tasks like 3D reconstruction and pose regression. However, cross-view completion is ill-posed in non-covisible regions, limiting its effectiveness. We introduce Alligat0R, a novel pre-training approach that replaces cross-view learning with a covisibility segmentation task. Our method predicts whether each pixel in one image is covisible in the second image, occluded, or outside the field of view, making the pre-training effective in both covisible and non-covisible regions, and provides interpretable predictions. To support this, we present Cub3, a large-scale dataset with 5M image pairs and dense covisibility annotations derived from the nuScenes and ScanNet datasets. Cub3 includes diverse scenarios with varying degrees of overlap. The experiments show that our novel pre-training method Alligat0R significantly outperforms CroCo in relative pose regression. Alligat0R and Cub3 will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Learning from two views of a scene can help a vision model estimate how the cameras are positioned relative to one another. However, a task that asks the model to complete one view using another becomes ambiguous where the views do not share visible content. Alligat0R changes the pre-training task to address that problem directly.

For every pixel in one image, the model predicts whether its scene content is also visible in the second image, hidden behind something, or beyond the second camera's field of view. These categories provide a meaningful training target even where image overlap is absent. They also make the predictions interpretable as statements about visibility.

The authors introduce Cub3 to support this training, with five million image pairs and dense visibility annotations derived from nuScenes and ScanNet. Its pairs cover different degrees of overlap. Experiments report significantly better relative camera pose regression than CroCo. The finding supports visibility classification as useful preparation for pose estimation, with the pre-training objective explicitly accounting for both shared and unshared regions.
summary.tldr: Alligat0R improves relative camera pose learning by pre-training models to classify visibility relationships between two images.

title: Alligat0R: Pre-Training through Covisibility Segmentation for Relative Camera Pose Regression

abstract: One persistent challenge in LLM research is the development of attention mechanisms that are able to generalise from training on shorter contexts to inference on longer contexts. We propose two conditions that we expect all effective long-context attention mechanisms to have: scale-invariant total attention, and scale-invariant attention sparsity. Under a Gaussian assumption, we show that a simple position-dependent transformation of the attention logits is sufficient for these conditions to hold. Experimentally we find that the resulting scale-invariant attention scheme gives considerable benefits in terms of validation loss when zero-shot generalising from training on short contexts to validation on longer contexts, and is effective at long-context retrieval.

paragraphs: Language models trained on shorter contexts can struggle when given longer ones. This paper studies how an attention mechanism should behave as context length changes. The authors propose two properties they expect effective long-context attention to possess: scale invariance in total attention and in attention sparsity.

They then show that, under a Gaussian assumption, a simple position-dependent transformation of attention logits is sufficient to satisfy both properties. Logits are the scores from which attention weights are formed, so the intervention acts directly on how attention is allocated. The theoretical statement establishes sufficiency under the assumption; the proposed properties are motivated expectations about effective mechanisms.

Experiments find considerable validation-loss benefits when models trained on short contexts are evaluated zero-shot on longer contexts. The resulting attention scheme also performs effectively at long-context retrieval. Together, these findings support the proposed transformation as a way to improve length generalization, connecting desired scaling behavior with a concrete modification to attention and empirical tests on longer inputs.
summary.tldr: A position-dependent attention-logit transformation satisfies two proposed scaling properties under a Gaussian assumption and improves empirical generalization to longer contexts.

title: Scale-invariant attention

abstract: Local convergence has emerged as a fundamental tool for analyzing sparse random graph models. We introduce a new notion of local convergence, _color convergence_, based on the Weisfeiler–Leman algorithm. Color convergence fully characterizes the class of random graphs that are well-behaved in the limit for message-passing graph neural networks. Building on this, we propose the _Refined Configuration Model_ (RCM), a random graph model that generalizes the configuration model. The RCM is universal with respect to local convergence among locally tree-like random graph models, including Erdős–Rényi, stochastic block and configuration models. Finally, this framework enables a complete characterization of the random trees that arise as local limits of such graphs.

paragraphs: Local convergence studies how the neighborhoods of sparse random graphs behave as the graphs grow. This paper introduces color convergence, a new formulation based on the Weisfeiler–Leman algorithm. Its central result connects a graph-theoretic notion of limiting behavior with the behavior of message-passing graph neural networks.

Specifically, color convergence fully characterizes the random graphs that are well-behaved in the limit for these neural networks. This provides a criterion tied to the kind of local information processing that message-passing models perform. The authors also introduce the Refined Configuration Model, extending the existing configuration model into a broader random-graph construction.

The new model is universal with respect to local convergence within the class of locally tree-like random graph models. That class includes Erdős–Rényi, stochastic block, and configuration models. The framework further completely characterizes the random trees arising as local limits of such graphs. Its universality is therefore a precise statement about this local-convergence setting, linking a broad family of graph models through their limiting neighborhood structure.
summary.tldr: Color convergence characterizes well-behaved graph limits for message-passing networks, while the Refined Configuration Model unifies locally tree-like random graphs under local convergence.

title: On Local Limits of Sparse Random Graphs: Color Convergence and the Refined Configuration Model

abstract: We present a systematic theoretical framework that interprets masked diffusion models (MDMs) as solutions to energy minimization problems in discrete optimal transport. Specifically, we prove that three distinct energy formulations—kinetic, conditional kinetic, and geodesic energy—are mathematically equivalent under the structure of MDMs, and that MDMs minimize all three when the mask schedule satisfies a closed-form optimality condition. This unification not only clarifies the theoretical foundations of MDMs, but also motivates practical improvements in sampling. By parameterizing interpolation schedules via Beta distributions, we reduce the schedule design space to a tractable 2D search, enabling efficient post-training tuning without model modification. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that our energy-inspired schedules outperform hand-crafted baselines, particularly in low-step sampling settings.

This paper gives that process an interpretation through energy minimization in discrete optimal transport. The aim is to connect the model’s theoretical structure with practical choices about how generation progresses.

They further show that the models minimize all three when the mask schedule meets a closed-form optimality condition. The schedule condition is essential to this minimization result; the equivalence does not make every possible schedule optimal.

The theory motivates a practical schedule family parameterized by Beta distributions. This turns schedule selection into a two-dimensional search that can be performed after training without modifying the model. On synthetic and real-world benchmarks, these energy-inspired schedules outperform handcrafted alternatives, especially when sampling uses few steps. The findings link a formal account of generation to an inexpensive way of improving its execution.
summary.tldr: An energy-minimization theory for masked diffusion motivates post-training schedule tuning that improves sampling, particularly with few steps.

title: Masked Diffusion Models as Energy Minimization

abstract: Data valuation techniques quantify each training example's contribution to model performance, providing a principled basis for data cleaning, acquisition, and selection. Existing valuation methods remain inadequate: \emph{model-based} techniques depend on a single fitted model and inherit its biases, while \emph{algorithm-based} approaches like Data Shapley scale poorly due to their need to train multiple models. Recent work has proposed model-agnostic alternatives based on Wasserstein distance between the training set and a clean reference set, but exact computation is expensive and approximations often misrank examples. We introduce KAIROS, a model-agnostic framework that values examples by their contribution to the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between the training set and a clean reference distribution. Unlike Wasserstein methods, MMD admits a closed-form solution that requires no approximations and is scalable to large datasets. Additionally, KAIROS enables efficient online valuation: adding a new batch of $m$ examples requires only $O(mN)$ computation to update all scores, compared to $O(N^2)$ in prior work where $N$ is the training set size. Empirical evaluations on noise, mislabeling, and poisoning benchmarks show that KAIROS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both accuracy and runtime. On ImageNet, KAIROS achieves up to 15 $\times$ speedup over the fastest baseline while maintaining superior data valuation quality. Our results demonstrate that model-agnostic methods can match or exceed model-based approaches in performance while scaling to large datasets.

title: KAIROS: Scalable Model-Agnostic Data Valuation

abstract: Recent advances in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have showcased strong reasoning abilities across multiple modalities, achieving significant breakthroughs in various real-world applications. Despite this great success, the safety guardrail of LVLMs may not cover the unforeseen domains introduced by the visual modality. Existing studies primarily focus on eliciting LVLMs to generate harmful responses via carefully crafted image-based jailbreaks designed to bypass alignment defenses. In this study, we reveal that a safe image can be exploited to achieve the same jailbreak consequence when combined with additional safe images and prompts. This stems from two fundamental properties of LVLMs: universal reasoning capabilities and safety snowball effect. Building on these insights, we propose Safety Snowball Agent (SSA), a novel agent-based framework leveraging agents' autonomous and tool-using abilities to jailbreak LVLMs. SSA operates through two principal stages: (1) initial response generation, where tools generate or retrieve jailbreak images based on potential harmful intents, and (2) harmful snowballing, where refined subsequent prompts induce progressively harmful outputs. Our experiments demonstrate that SSA can use nearly any image to induce LVLMs to produce unsafe content, achieving high success jailbreaking rates against the latest LVLMs. Unlike prior works that exploit alignment flaws, SSA leverages the inherent properties of LVLMs, presenting a profound challenge for enforcing safety in generative multimodal systems.

paragraphs: A vision-language model may receive individually safe images and prompts yet produce unsafe content from their combination. This paper investigates that compositional failure, extending attention beyond specially crafted malicious images. The authors connect it to broad reasoning capabilities and a safety snowball effect, in which responses become progressively more harmful over an interaction.

Their Safety Snowball Agent framework uses autonomous agents and tools to study this behavior. At a high level, it first obtains an initial response using generated or retrieved imagery, then refines subsequent prompts to intensify unsafe outputs. The framework tests how the evolving interaction can turn otherwise safe visual material into part of a jailbreak.

The experiments report high jailbreak success rates against the evaluated vision-language models and show that nearly any image can be used in the tested process. The authors interpret this as a challenge rooted in general model capabilities. The safety implication is that evaluating individual inputs alone can miss risks created by combinations and the progression of a conversation.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how combinations of safe visual inputs and evolving prompts can elicit unsafe outputs from vision-language models.

title: Safe + Safe = Unsafe? Exploring How Safe Images Can Be Exploited to Jailbreak Large Vision-Language Models

abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) methods such as Grouped Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) have strengthened the reasoning capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). However, due to the inherent entanglement between visual and textual modalities, applying GRPO to LVLMs often leads to reward convergence across different responses to the same sample as training progresses, hindering effective gradient updates and causing the enhancement of chain-of-thought reasoning to stagnate or even collapse. To address this issue, we propose a progressive instruction evolution framework, EvolvedGRPO, to gradually generate more complex questions via editing instructions in an adversarial way, progressively aligned with the model’s evolving capabilities. Specifically, we design two instruction editing strategies across modalities, incorporating incrementally increasing editing instructions and RL-based adversarial data augmentation to improve the effectiveness of model training. To address GRPO's limitations on overly difficult problems, we first train on basic subproblem versions of complex multi-modal questions in both the visual and textual modalities, progressively increasing difficulty to enable prefix-style process rewards, effectively combining the strengths of both process rewards and group-wise relative rewards. Finally, EvolvedGRPO achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source RL models on multi-modal reasoning tasks, even approaching the closed-source GPT-4o in reasoning capabilities, and demonstrates better performance on unseen LVLM general benchmarks. The Code for EvolvedGRPO is available at https://github.com/SHENZHEBEI/EvolvedGRPO.

paragraphs: Grouped Relative Policy Optimization learns from reward differences among responses to the same input. For vision-language models, the authors observe that these rewards often become similar as training progresses. The resulting weak gradient signal can cause improvements in step-by-step reasoning to stall or collapse, motivating training questions that evolve with the model.

EvolvedGRPO progressively edits instructions to make questions more challenging as capabilities improve. Its two editing strategies span visual and textual modalities, using increasingly demanding instructions and reinforcement-learning-based adversarial data augmentation. To handle questions that are initially too difficult, training begins with simpler subproblems and increases their difficulty over time.

This progression enables prefix-style process rewards alongside group-relative rewards, combining feedback about intermediate reasoning with comparisons among responses. The authors report state-of-the-art multimodal reasoning performance among open-source reinforcement-learning models, approaching GPT-4o, plus stronger performance on unseen general vision-language benchmarks. The findings support adapting question difficulty throughout training to sustain useful learning signals.
summary.tldr: EvolvedGRPO progressively adjusts multimodal question difficulty to sustain reinforcement-learning signals and improve vision-language reasoning.

title: EvolvedGRPO: Unlocking Reasoning in LVLMs via Progressive Instruction Evolution

abstract: Recently, Sharma et al. (2024) suggested a method called LAyer- SElective-Rank reduction (LASER) which demonstrated that pruning high‑order components of carefully chosen LLM’s weight matrices can boost downstream accuracy—without any gradient‑based fine‑tuning. Yet LASER’s exhaustive, per‑matrix search (each requiring full‑dataset forward passes) makes it impractical for rapid deployment. We demonstrate that this overhead can be removed and find that: (i) Only a small, carefully chosen subset of matrices needs to be inspected—eliminating the layer‑by‑layer sweep, (ii) The gradient of each matrix’s singular values pinpoints which matrices merit reduction, (iii) Increasing the factorization search space by allowing matrices rows to cluster around multiple subspaces and then decomposing each cluster separately further reduces overfitting on the original training data and further lifts accuracy by up to 24.6 percentage points, and finally, (iv) we discover that evaluating on just 100 samples rather than the full training data—both for computing the indicative gradients and for measuring the final accuracy—suffices to further reduce the search time; we explain that as adaptation to downstream tasks is dominated by prompting style, not dataset size. As a results, we show that combining these findings yields a fast and robust adaptation algorithm for downstream tasks. Overall, with a single gradient step on 100 examples and a quick scan of the top candidate layers and factorization techniques, we can adapt LLMs to new datasets—entirely without fine‑tuning.

paragraphs: Reducing the rank of selected language-model weight matrices can improve downstream accuracy without conventional fine-tuning. The practical obstacle is finding which matrices to modify: the earlier LASER approach requires an expensive search with repeated evaluations over a full dataset. This paper develops a faster way to identify promising compression changes.

The method uses gradients of matrix singular values to identify a small set of candidates, avoiding an exhaustive sweep through the layers. It also expands the available factorizations by clustering matrix rows around multiple subspaces and decomposing each cluster separately. The authors report that this added flexibility reduces overfitting to the original training data and raises accuracy by up to 24.6 percentage points.

In the studied settings, 100 examples suffice for computing the indicative gradients and evaluating candidate accuracy. The authors attribute this finding to adaptation being driven mainly by prompting style rather than dataset size. Combining a single gradient step with a short search over candidate layers and factorizations produces their adaptation algorithm. The gradient serves the selection process, while adaptation is achieved through matrix reduction without fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: A single gradient step on 100 examples guides selective matrix compression that adapts language models without conventional fine-tuning.

title: Compress to Impress: Efficient LLM Adaptation Using a Single Gradient Step on 100 Samples

abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to leverage labeled samples from known categories to cluster unlabeled data that may include both known and unknown categories. While existing methods have achieved impressive results under standard conditions, their performance often deteriorates in the presence of distribution shifts. In this paper, we explore a more realistic task: Domain-Shifted Generalized Category Discovery (DS\_GCD), where the unlabeled data includes not only unknown categories but also samples from unknown domains. To tackle this challenge, we propose a \textbf{\underline{F}}requency-guided Gene\textbf{\underline{r}}alized Cat\textbf{\underline{e}}gory Discov\textbf{\underline{e}}ry framework (FREE) that enhances the model's ability to discover categories under distributional shift by leveraging frequency-domain information. Specifically, we first propose a frequency-based domain separation strategy that partitions samples into known and unknown domains by measuring their amplitude differences. We then propose two types of frequency-domain perturbation strategies: a cross-domain strategy, which adapts to new distributions by exchanging amplitude components across domains, and an intra-domain strategy, which enhances robustness to intra-domain variations within the unknown domain. Furthermore, we extend the self-supervised contrastive objective and semantic clustering loss to better guide the training process. Finally, we introduce a clustering-difficulty-aware resampling technique to adaptively focus on harder-to-cluster categories, further enhancing model performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method effectively mitigates the impact of distributional shifts across various benchmark datasets and achieves superior performance in discovering both known and unknown categories.

paragraphs: Generalized category discovery uses labeled examples from known categories to organize unlabeled data that may also contain unknown categories. This paper adds another difficulty: the unlabeled examples can come from unfamiliar domains as well. A system must therefore discover categories while handling distribution changes that can disrupt its clustering.

The proposed FREE framework uses frequency-domain information to address these shifts. It first separates samples into known and unknown domains according to differences in their amplitude components. It then exchanges amplitude components across domains to help adaptation and applies additional perturbations within the unknown domain to improve robustness to variation there.

FREE also extends the self-supervised contrastive objective and semantic clustering loss, and resamples data to give harder-to-cluster categories more attention. These elements connect domain adaptation with the actual difficulty of discovering categories. Across benchmark datasets, the authors report that the framework reduces the impact of distribution shifts and improves discovery of both known and unknown categories. The results support frequency information as a useful basis for category discovery when domain identity is also uncertain.
summary.tldr: FREE uses frequency-based domain separation, perturbations, and adaptive resampling to improve category discovery under domain shifts.

title: Generalized Category Discovery under Domain Shift: A Frequency Domain Perspective

abstract: In typical graph neural networks (GNNs), feature representation learning naturally evolves through iteratively updating node features and exchanging information based on graph topology. In this context, we conceptualize that the learning process in GNNs is a mean-field game (MFG), where each graph node is an agent, interacting with its topologically connected neighbors. However, current GNNs often employ the identical MFG strategy across different graph datasets, regardless of whether the graph exhibits homophilic or heterophilic characteristics. To address this challenge, we propose to formulate the learning mechanism into a variational framework of the MFG inverse problem, introducing an in-context selective message passing paradigm for each agent, which promotes the best overall outcome for the graph. Specifically, we seek for the application-adaptive transportation function (controlling information exchange throughout the graph) and reaction function (controlling feature representation learning on each agent), *on the fly*, which allows us to uncover the most suitable selective mechanism of message passing by solving an MFG variational problem through the lens of Hamiltonian flows. Taken together, our variational framework unifies existing GNN models into various mean-field games with distinct equilibrium states, each characterized by the learned in-context message passing operators. Furthermore, we present an agnostic end-to-end deep model, coined *Game-of-GNN*, to jointly identify the message passing mechanism and fine-tune the GNN hyper-parameters on top of the elucidated message passing operators. *Game-of-GNN* has achieved SOTA performance on diverse graph data, including popular benchmark datasets and human connectomes. More importantly, the mathematical insight of MFG framework provides a new window to understand the foundational principles of graph learning as an interactive dynamical system, which allows us to reshape the idea of designing next-generation GNN models.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks learn by updating node features and exchanging information along graph connections. This paper views that process as a mean-field game, with nodes acting as interacting agents. The motivation is that different graphs may need different exchange strategies, particularly when neighboring nodes tend to be similar in some datasets and dissimilar in others.

The authors formulate an inverse problem that learns the interaction mechanism from context. A transportation function controls information exchange, while a reaction function controls feature learning within each node. Solving a variational problem through Hamiltonian flows selects these functions for the application. The framework also interprets existing GNN models as games with different equilibrium states.

The resulting end-to-end model, Game-of-GNN, jointly identifies message-passing mechanisms and tunes GNN hyperparameters. It reports state-of-the-art results across diverse graph datasets, including human connectomes. The broader contribution is a mathematical perspective that makes the choice of message-passing behavior part of learning itself, while connecting graph learning to the dynamics of interacting agents.
summary.tldr: Game-of-GNN uses a mean-field-game formulation to learn context-dependent message passing and reports leading results across diverse graphs.

title: Explore In-Context Message Passing Operator for Graph Neural Networks in A Mean Field Game

abstract: In visual generation, the quadratic complexity of attention mechanisms results in high memory and computational costs, especially for longer token sequences required in high-resolution image or multi-frame video generation. To address this, prior research has explored techniques such as sparsification and quantization. However, these techniques face significant challenges under low density and reduced bitwidths. Through systematic analysis, we identify that the core difficulty stems from the dispersed and irregular characteristics of visual attention patterns. Therefore, instead of introducing specialized sparsification and quantization design to accommodate such patterns, we propose an alternative strategy: "reorganizing" the attention pattern to alleviate the challenges. Inspired by the local aggregatin nature of visual feature extraction, we design a novel **P**attern-**A**ware token **R**e**O**rdering (**PARO**) technique, which unifies the diverse attention patterns into a hardware-friendly block-wise pattern. This unification substantially simplifies and enhances both sparsification and quantization. We evaluate the performance-efficiency trade-offs of various design choices and finalize a methodology tailored for the unified pattern. Our approach, **PAROAttention**, achieves video and image generation with lossless metrics, and nearly identical results from full-precision (FP) baselines, while operating at notably lower density (**20%-30%**) and bitwidth (**INT8/INT4**), achieving a **1.9 - 2.7x** end-to-end latency speedup.

paragraphs: Attention becomes costly when image and video generation require long token sequences. Sparsity reduces the attention entries computed, while quantization lowers numerical precision, but both become difficult when visual attention is scattered and irregular. This paper identifies that pattern structure as a central obstacle to combining aggressive sparsity with low precision.

PAROAttention addresses the obstacle by reordering tokens according to their attention patterns. The reordering organizes diverse patterns into blocks that are easier for hardware to process. With this common structure in place, the authors evaluate different sparsification and quantization choices and select a method suited to the reorganized attention. The approach therefore changes the organization of the computation before applying compression.

The reported system operates at 20–30% density with INT8 or INT4 precision and achieves 1.9–2.7× end-to-end latency speedups. In the evaluated image and video generation settings, metrics show no loss and outputs are nearly identical to full-precision baselines. These findings show that attention layout can materially affect how efficiently sparsity and quantization work together.
summary.tldr: PAROAttention reorganizes visual attention into hardware-friendly blocks, enabling sparse, low-precision generation with reported speedups and preserved evaluation metrics.

title: PAROAttention: Pattern-Aware ReOrdering for Efficient Sparse and Quantized Attention in Visual Generation Models

abstract: Temporal Graph Learning (TGL) aims to discover patterns in evolving networks or temporal graphs and leverage these patterns to predict future interactions. However, most existing research focuses on learning from a single network in isolation, leaving the challenges of within-domain and cross-domain generalization largely unaddressed. In this study, we introduce a new benchmark of 84 real-world temporal transaction networks and propose **Temporal Multi-network Transfer (MiNT)**, a pre-training framework designed to capture transferable temporal dynamics across diverse networks. We train MiNT models on up to 64 transaction networks and evaluate their generalization ability on 20 held-out, unseen networks. Our results show that MiNT consistently outperforms individually trained models, revealing a strong relation between the number of pre-training networks and transfer performance. These findings highlight scaling trends in temporal graph learning and underscore the importance of network diversity in improving generalization. This work establishes the first large-scale benchmark for studying transferability in TGL and lays the groundwork for developing Temporal Graph Foundation Models. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/benjaminnNgo/ScalingTGNs}

paragraphs: Temporal graph learning uses evolving networks to predict future interactions. Most existing work trains on a single network, leaving open how well learned patterns transfer to other networks within or across domains. This paper introduces both a larger evaluation setting and a pretraining framework aimed at learning temporal dynamics that transfer.

The benchmark contains 84 real-world temporal transaction networks. The Temporal Multi-network Transfer framework, called MiNT, is trained on as many as 64 networks and evaluated on 20 held-out networks. Testing on unseen networks makes generalization across networks a central part of the evaluation, rather than measuring only predictions within the network used for training.

MiNT consistently outperforms models trained individually, and transfer performance has a strong relationship with the number of pretraining networks. The authors interpret these results as evidence of scaling trends and the importance of network diversity. The work provides a foundation for studying temporal graph foundation models by making multi-network training and transfer measurable at a larger scale.
summary.tldr: MiNT introduces an 84-network benchmark and shows that multi-network pretraining improves temporal graph transfer to unseen networks.

title: MiNT: Multi-Network Transfer Benchmark for Temporal Graph Learning

abstract: Adversarial optimization algorithms that explicitly search for flaws in agents' policies have been successfully applied to finding robust and diverse policies in the context of multi-agent learning. However, the success of adversarial optimization has been largely limited to zero-sum settings because its naive application in cooperative settings leads to a critical failure mode: agents are irrationally incentivized to *self-sabotage*, blocking the completion of tasks and halting further learning. To address this, we introduce *Rationality-preserving Policy Optimization (RPO)*, a formalism for adversarial optimization that avoids self-sabotage by ensuring agents remain *rational*—that is, their policies are optimal with respect to some possible partner policy. To solve RPO, we develop *Rational Policy Gradient (RPG)*, which trains agents to maximize their own reward in a modified version of the original game in which we use *opponent shaping* techniques to optimize the adversarial objective. RPG enables us to extend a variety of existing adversarial optimization algorithms that, no longer subject to the limitations of self-sabotage, can find adversarial examples, improve robustness and adaptability, and learn diverse policies. We empirically validate that our approach achieves strong performance in several popular cooperative and general-sum environments. Our project page can be found at https://rational-policy-gradient.github.io.

However, the success of adversarial optimization has been largely limited to zero-sum settings because its naive application in cooperative settings leads to a critical failure mode: agents are irrationally incentivized to *self-sabotage*, blocking the completion of tasks and halting further learning. To address this, we introduce *Rationality-preserving Policy Optimization (RPO)*, a formalism for adversarial optimization that avoids self-sabotage by ensuring agents remain *rational*—that is, their policies are optimal with respect to some possible partner policy. To solve RPO, we develop *Rational Policy Gradient (RPG)*, which trains agents to maximize their own reward in a modified version of the original game in which we use *opponent shaping* techniques to optimize the adversarial objective. RPG enables us to extend a variety of existing adversarial optimization algorithms that, no longer subject to the limitations of self-sabotage, can find adversarial examples, improve robustness and adaptability, and learn diverse policies. We empirically validate that our approach achieves strong performance in several popular cooperative and general-sum environments. Our project page can be found at https://rational-policy-gradient.github.io.

paragraphs: Adversarial optimization searches for weaknesses in agents' policies, but applying it naively to cooperative tasks can encourage self-sabotage. Agents may block task completion, preventing useful learning from continuing. This paper develops a way to retain the benefits of adversarial search while avoiding that failure mode.

Rationality-preserving Policy Optimization requires agents to remain rational in a specific sense: each policy must be optimal for some possible partner policy. The authors develop Rational Policy Gradient to solve this formulation. It trains agents to maximize their own rewards in a modified game, using opponent shaping to optimize the adversarial objective.

This construction allows a range of existing adversarial optimization methods to be extended beyond the self-sabotaging behavior described in the paper. The resulting methods can find adversarial examples, improve robustness and adaptability, and learn diverse policies. Evaluations in several cooperative and general-sum environments report strong performance, supporting rationality preservation as a useful constraint when searching for challenging interactions between agents.
summary.tldr: Rational Policy Gradient supports adversarial multi-agent learning while constraining agents to avoid self-sabotaging policies.

title: Robust and Diverse Multi-Agent Learning via Rational Policy Gradient

abstract: Zero-shot denoising aims to denoise observations without access to training samples or clean reference images. This setting is particularly relevant in practical imaging scenarios involving specialized domains such as medical imaging or biology. In this work, we propose the *Zero-Shot Neural Compression Denoiser* (ZS-NCD), a novel denoising framework based on neural compression. ZS-NCD treats a neural compression network as an untrained model, optimized directly on patches extracted from a single noisy image. The final reconstruction is then obtained by aggregating the outputs of the trained model over overlapping patches. Thanks to the built-in entropy constraints of compression architectures, our method naturally avoids overfitting and does not require manual regularization or early stopping. Through extensive experiments, we show that ZS-NCD achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot denoisers for both Gaussian and Poisson noise, and generalizes well to both natural and non-natural images. Additionally, we provide new finite-sample theoretical results that characterize upper bounds on the achievable reconstruction error of general maximum-likelihood compression-based denoisers. These results further establish the theoretical foundations of compression-based denoising. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Computational-Imaging-RU/ZS-NCDenoiser.

paragraphs: Zero-shot denoising removes noise without a training dataset or clean reference image. This setting is relevant when suitable examples are difficult to obtain, including specialized imaging domains. The paper introduces ZS-NCD, which uses a neural compression architecture to recover an image directly from its noisy observation.

The compression network starts untrained and is optimized on patches extracted from that single image. Its outputs for overlapping patches are then aggregated into the final reconstruction. The architecture’s built-in entropy constraints provide the mechanism for avoiding overfitting. The paper also derives finite-sample upper bounds on reconstruction error for a broader class of maximum-likelihood compression-based denoisers. These two contributions connect a practical single-image algorithm with theoretical analysis of how compression can support denoising when clean training examples are unavailable.
summary.tldr: ZS-NCD denoises a single image using an initially untrained compression network whose entropy constraints control overfitting.

title: Zero-shot Denoising via Neural Compression: Theoretical and algorithmic framework

abstract: Decision tree learning is a popular approach for classification and regression in machine learning and statistics, and Bayesian formulations - which introduce a prior distribution over decision trees, and formulate learning as posterior inference given data - have been shown to produce competitive performance. Unlike classic decision tree learning algorithms like ID3, C4.5 and CART, which work in a top-down manner, existing Bayesian algorithms produce an approximation to the posterior distribution by evolving a complete tree (or collection thereof) iteratively via local Monte Carlo modifications to the structure of the tree, e.g., using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). We present a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithm that instead works in a top-down manner, mimicking the behavior and speed of classic algorithms. We demonstrate empirically that our approach delivers accuracy comparable to the most popular MCMC method, but operates more than an order of magnitude faster, and thus represents a better computation-accuracy tradeoff.

paragraphs: Bayesian decision-tree learning places a prior over possible trees and updates it using data to obtain a posterior distribution. Existing Bayesian approaches commonly approximate that distribution by repeatedly modifying complete trees through Monte Carlo steps. This differs from familiar decision-tree algorithms that build a tree from the top down.

The paper introduces a sequential Monte Carlo algorithm that also proceeds from the top down. Its construction follows the broad behavior of classic tree-building methods while retaining the Bayesian goal of posterior inference. The change addresses the computational route used to explore trees, seeking the speed of top-down construction within a probabilistic learning framework.

Experiments show accuracy comparable to the most popular Markov chain Monte Carlo method while running more than an order of magnitude faster. This establishes a better computation–accuracy tradeoff in the reported evaluation. The result matters because competitive Bayesian tree prediction need not require the same expense as iteratively revising complete trees; sequential construction offers an empirically effective alternative.
summary.tldr: Top-down sequential Monte Carlo makes Bayesian decision-tree inference over an order of magnitude faster in experiments while retaining comparable accuracy.

title: Top-down particle filtering for Bayesian decision trees

abstract: We consider a stochastic bandit problem with infinitely many arms. In this setting, the learner has no chance of trying all the arms even once and has to dedicate its limited number of samples only to a certain number of arms. All previous algorithms for this setting were designed for minimizing the cumulative regret of the learner. In this paper, we propose an algorithm aiming at minimizing the simple regret. As in the cumulative regret setting of infinitely many armed bandits, the rate of the simple regret will depend on a parameter βcharacterizing the distribution of the near-optimal arms. We prove that depending on β, our algorithm is minimax optimal either up to a multiplicative constant or up to a \log(n) factor. We also provide extensions to several important cases: when βis unknown, in a natural setting where the near-optimal arms have a small variance, and in the case of unknown time horizon.

paragraphs: With infinitely many bandit arms, a learner cannot try every available option, even once. A finite sampling budget must therefore be divided among a limited selection of arms. This paper focuses on simple regret: the quality of the option ultimately selected, rather than the accumulated cost of choices made during exploration.

The proposed algorithm targets that final-selection objective. Its rate depends on a parameter, beta, describing the distribution of near-optimal arms. This dependence captures a fundamental feature of the setting: the difficulty of finding an excellent option changes with how those options are distributed. Depending on beta, the authors prove minimax optimality up to either a constant multiplier or a logarithmic factor.

The paper also extends the approach to cases where beta is unknown, where near-optimal arms naturally have small variance, and where the time horizon is unknown. These extensions broaden the situations covered by the method. The contribution establishes a theoretically grounded treatment of final recommendation quality in an exploration space too large to exhaust.
summary.tldr: An infinite-armed bandit algorithm targets final-choice quality with minimax guarantees that depend on the distribution of near-optimal arms.

title: Simple regret for infinitely many armed bandits

abstract: This paper presents a novel distributed variational inference framework that unifies many parallel sparse Gaussian process regression (SGPR) models for scalable hyperparameter learning with big data. To achieve this, our framework exploits a structure of correlated noise process model that represents the observation noises as a finite realization of a high-order Gaussian Markov random process. By varying the Markov order and covariance function for the noise process model, different variational SGPR models result. This consequently allows the correlation structure of the noise process model to be characterized for which a particular variational SGPR model is optimal. We empirically evaluate the predictive performance and scalability of the distributed variational SGPR models unified by our framework on two real-world datasets.

To achieve this, our framework exploits a structure of correlated noise process model that represents the observation noises as a finite realization of a high-order Gaussian Markov random process. By varying the Markov order and covariance function for the noise process model, different variational SGPR models result. This consequently allows the correlation structure of the noise process model to be characterized for which a particular variational SGPR model is optimal. We empirically evaluate the predictive performance and scalability of the distributed variational SGPR models unified by our framework on two real-world datasets.

paragraphs: The paper develops a common framework for several parallel sparse Gaussian process regression models. Its goal is to make learning model hyperparameters scalable to large datasets while explaining how different approximation methods relate to one another. The framework uses distributed variational inference, bringing these models into a shared mathematical formulation.

The central modeling choice concerns correlations in observation noise. The authors represent that noise as a finite realization of a high-order Gaussian Markov process. Changing the Markov order and the covariance function produces different variational regression models. These choices therefore provide a way to connect particular approximations to particular assumptions about the noise.

This connection also lets the authors characterize the noise correlation structure for which a particular model is optimal. Optimality is tied to that structure, rather than presented as a universal ranking of models. Experiments on two real-world datasets evaluate prediction and scalability. The stated contribution is both a unifying account of existing approaches and a framework for studying their computational and predictive behavior.
summary.tldr: A distributed inference framework connects sparse Gaussian process models through their assumptions about correlated observation noise.

title: A Distributed Variational Inference Framework for Unifying Parallel Sparse Gaussian Process Regression Models

abstract: We consider the problem of selecting a strong pool of individuals from several populations with incomparable skills (e.g. soccer players, mathematicians, and singers) in a fair manner. The quality of an individual is defined to be their relative rank (by cumulative distribution value) within their own population, which permits cross-population comparisons. We study algorithms which attempt to select the highest quality subset despite the fact that true CDF values are not known, and can only be estimated from the finite pool of candidates. Specifically, we quantify the regret in quality imposed by “meritocratic” notions of fairness, which require that individuals are selected with probability that is monotonically increasing in their true quality. We give algorithms with provable fairness and regret guarantees, as well as lower bounds, and provide empirical results which suggest that our algorithms perform better than the theory suggests. We extend our results to a sequential batch setting, in which an algorithm must repeatedly select subsets of individuals from new pools of applicants, but has the benefit of being able to compare them to the accumulated data from previous rounds.

paragraphs: Selecting people across populations is difficult when their skills are not directly comparable. This paper defines individual quality through relative standing within a person's own population, using the cumulative distribution value of their skill. That definition creates a common scale for comparing candidates whose underlying abilities are measured differently.

The learner does not know these true relative ranks and must estimate them from a finite candidate pool. The paper studies meritocratic fairness requirements under which selection probability increases monotonically with true quality. It quantifies the loss in selection quality, or regret, associated with satisfying these requirements despite uncertainty about candidates' ranks.

The authors provide algorithms with provable fairness and regret guarantees, together with lower bounds that characterize unavoidable difficulty. Empirical results suggest better performance than the theoretical bounds indicate. They also extend the analysis to repeated batches of new applicants, where previous rounds supply additional comparison data. The result is a formal treatment of fair cross-population selection under a specific definition of merit and uncertainty about that merit.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies selection-quality tradeoffs when fairness requires higher within-population rank to imply at least as much selection probability.

title: Meritocratic Fairness for Cross-Population Selection

abstract: Tree search algorithms, such as branch-and-bound, are the most widely used tools for solving combinatorial problems. These algorithms recursively partition the search space to find an optimal solution. To keep the tree small, it is crucial to carefully decide, when expanding a tree node, which variable to branch on at that node to partition the remaining space. Many partitioning techniques have been proposed, but no theory describes which is optimal. We show how to use machine learning to determine an optimal weighting of any set of partitioning procedures for the instance distribution at hand using samples. Via theory and experiments, we show that learning to branch is both practical and hugely beneficial.

paragraphs: Tree-search methods such as branch-and-bound solve combinatorial problems by repeatedly dividing the remaining search space. At each node, choosing which variable to branch on affects the size of the resulting tree. A good branching decision therefore matters for how much search is needed to find an optimal solution.

Many procedures exist for making these decisions, but the paper notes the lack of a theory identifying which is optimal. The authors use machine learning to determine an optimal weighting of a supplied set of partitioning procedures for the distribution of problem instances at hand. Samples from that distribution provide the information used to learn the weighting.

The paper supports learning to branch through both theoretical analysis and experiments, reporting that it is practical and highly beneficial. Its central contribution is to make branching choices responsive to the kinds of instances a solver encounters. The optimality claim concerns the learned weighting for that instance distribution, tying the method's target directly to its available procedures and training samples.
summary.tldr: Learning to Branch uses samples to optimize the weighting of branching procedures for a particular distribution of combinatorial problems.

title: Learning to Branch

abstract: Gibbs sampling is the de facto Markov chain Monte Carlo method used for inference and learning on large scale graphical models. For complicated factor graphs with lots of factors, the performance of Gibbs sampling can be limited by the computational cost of executing a single update step of the Markov chain. This cost is proportional to the degree of the graph, the number of factors adjacent to each variable. In this paper, we show how this cost can be reduced by using minibatching: subsampling the factors to form an estimate of their sum. We introduce several minibatched variants of Gibbs, show that they can be made unbiased, prove bounds on their convergence rates, and show that under some conditions they can result in asymptotic single-update-run-time speedups over plain Gibbs sampling.

paragraphs: Gibbs sampling can become expensive on graphical models where each variable is connected to many factors. Even one update may require work proportional to the number of adjacent factors. This paper targets that local computational bottleneck, asking whether an update can use a sampled subset of factors while preserving useful sampling guarantees.

The proposed approach uses minibatches to estimate the sum of factor contributions. The authors introduce several Gibbs variants based on this idea and show that they can be made unbiased. They also establish bounds on convergence rates, addressing how the modified update mechanism affects the progress of the sampling procedure.

Under some conditions, the variants achieve asymptotic speedups in the runtime of a single update compared with ordinary Gibbs sampling. The result is specifically about per-update cost, while the convergence analysis addresses a separate part of overall sampling behavior. Together, the contributions provide a theoretical basis for reducing work in densely connected graphical models without treating subsampling as an unexamined approximation.
summary.tldr: Minibatched Gibbs variants subsample factors, can be made unbiased, and offer faster individual updates under specified conditions.

title: Minibatch Gibbs Sampling on Large Graphical Models

abstract: We study how to effectively leverage expert feedback to learn sequential decision-making policies. We focus on problems with sparse rewards and long time horizons, which typically pose significant challenges in reinforcement learning. We propose an algorithmic framework, called hierarchical guidance, that leverages the hierarchical structure of the underlying problem to integrate different modes of expert interaction. Our framework can incorporate different combinations of imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) at different levels, leading to dramatic reductions in both expert effort and cost of exploration. Using long-horizon benchmarks, including Montezuma’s Revenge, we demonstrate that our approach can learn significantly faster than hierarchical RL, and be significantly more label-efficient than standard IL. We also theoretically analyze labeling cost for certain instantiations of our framework.

Our framework can incorporate different combinations of imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) at different levels, leading to dramatic reductions in both expert effort and cost of exploration. paragraphs: Learning a long sequence of decisions is difficult when useful rewards occur only rarely. An agent may spend substantial effort exploring before receiving evidence that its behavior is promising. Expert guidance can help, but obtaining that guidance also has a cost. This paper studies how to use expert feedback effectively in such settings.

The proposed framework, hierarchical guidance, uses the problem's hierarchical structure to combine different forms of expert interaction. Imitation learning and reinforcement learning can be assigned in different combinations at different levels. This provides a way to distribute learning and guidance across the hierarchy, with the aim of reducing both expert effort and exploration cost.

On long-horizon benchmarks, including Montezuma's Revenge, the authors demonstrate significantly faster learning than hierarchical reinforcement learning and significantly greater label efficiency than standard imitation learning. They also analyze labeling cost theoretically for certain versions of the framework. The theoretical scope is therefore tied to those instantiations, while the benchmark results provide empirical support for the broader approach.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical guidance combines imitation and reinforcement learning across levels to reduce expert labeling and exploration effort on long-horizon tasks.

title: Hierarchical Imitation and Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Open category detection is the problem of detecting "alien" test instances that belong to categories or classes that were not present in the training data. In many applications, reliably detecting such aliens is central to ensuring the safety and accuracy of test set predictions. Unfortunately, there are no algorithms that provide theoretical guarantees on their ability to detect aliens under general assumptions. Further, while there are algorithms for open category detection, there are few empirical results that directly report alien detection rates. Thus, there are significant theoretical and empirical gaps in our understanding of open category detection. In this paper, we take a step toward addressing this gap by studying a simple, but practically-relevant variant of open category detection. In our setting, we are provided with a "clean" training set that contains only the target categories of interest and an unlabeled "contaminated” training set that contains a fraction alpha of alien examples. Under the assumption that we know an upper bound on alpha we develop an algorithm with PAC-style guarantees on the alien detection rate, while aiming to minimize false alarms. Empirical results on synthetic and standard benchmark datasets demonstrate the regimes in which the algorithm can be effective and provide a baseline for further advancements.

paragraphs: Open category detection asks whether a test example belongs to a class absent from the known training categories. This paper seeks guarantees for detecting these unfamiliar examples, which it calls aliens. It studies a particular training setup that makes the problem more structured than detection under general assumptions.

The algorithm receives two datasets: a clean set containing only target categories and an unlabeled contaminated set containing some alien examples. The alien fraction is denoted by alpha, and the method assumes a known upper bound on that fraction. Under this assumption, the authors develop PAC-style guarantees on the alien detection rate while aiming to keep false alarms low.

This separates the guaranteed detection objective from the additional goal of avoiding unnecessary alarms. Experiments on synthetic and standard benchmark datasets identify regimes where the algorithm can be effective and establish a baseline for further work. The contribution is a theoretically supported step for the stated two-dataset setting, rather than a guarantee for every open-category problem.
summary.tldr: Given clean and contaminated training sets plus a bound on contamination, an algorithm provides PAC-style guarantees for detecting unfamiliar categories.

title: Open Category Detection with PAC Guarantees

abstract: GANs excel at learning high dimensional distributions, but they can update generator parameters in directions that do not correspond to the steepest descent direction of the objective. Prominent examples of problematic update directions include those used in both Goodfellow’s original GAN and the WGAN-GP. To formally describe an optimal update direction, we introduce a theoretical framework which allows the derivation of requirements on both the divergence and corresponding method for determining an update direction, with these requirements guaranteeing unbiased mini-batch updates in the direction of steepest descent. We propose a novel divergence which approximates the Wasserstein distance while regularizing the critic’s first order information. Together with an accompanying update direction, this divergence fulfills the requirements for unbiased steepest descent updates. We verify our method, the First Order GAN, with image generation on CelebA, LSUN and CIFAR-10 and set a new state of the art on the One Billion Word language generation task.

paragraphs: A GAN’s generator update need not point in the direction that most steeply decreases its objective. This paper identifies that mismatch in prominent GAN formulations, including the original GAN and WGAN-GP. It asks what properties an objective and its update rule must jointly satisfy to obtain the desired direction.

The authors introduce a theoretical framework that derives requirements guaranteeing unbiased minibatch updates in the steepest descent direction. They then propose a divergence that approximates Wasserstein distance while regularizing the critic’s first-order information. Paired with its accompanying update direction, this divergence satisfies the framework’s requirements. The objective and update rule therefore form a deliberately matched construction.

The resulting First Order GAN is evaluated on image generation using CelebA, LSUN, and CIFAR-10. The authors also report a new state-of-the-art result on the One Billion Word language generation task. These experiments complement the theoretical contribution: the method connects a formal property of generator updates with demonstrated performance in both image and language generation.
summary.tldr: First Order GAN pairs a new divergence with an update rule that satisfies guarantees for unbiased steepest descent minibatch updates.

title: First Order Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: The Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) is a state-of-the art metric for comparing discrete probability distributions, but its high distinguishability comes at a high cost in computational complexity. Even though linear-complexity approximation algorithms have been proposed to improve its scalability, these algorithms are either limited to vector spaces with only a few dimensions or they become ineffective when the degree of overlap between the probability distributions is high. We propose novel approximation algorithms that overcome both of these limitations, yet still achieve linear time complexity. All our algorithms are data parallel, and therefore, we can take advantage of massively parallel computing engines, such as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs). On the popular text-based 20 Newsgroups dataset, the new algorithms are four orders of magnitude faster than a multi-threaded CPU implementation of Word Mover’s Distance and match its search accuracy. On MNIST images, the new algorithms are four orders of magnitude faster than Cuturi’s GPU implementation of the Sinkhorn’s algorithm while offering a slightly higher search accuracy.

paragraphs: Earth Mover’s Distance provides a powerful way to compare discrete probability distributions, but computing it is costly. Existing linear-time approximations face two obstacles identified by this paper: some are restricted to low-dimensional vector spaces, while others become ineffective when the distributions overlap heavily. These restrictions limit where efficient approximations remain useful.

The authors propose approximation algorithms that address both obstacles while retaining linear time complexity. All of the algorithms are data parallel, allowing their computation to use massively parallel hardware such as GPUs. The approach therefore combines reduced computational growth with a structure suited to parallel execution.

On 20 Newsgroups text data, the algorithms are four orders of magnitude faster than a multithreaded CPU implementation of Word Mover’s Distance while matching search accuracy. On MNIST, they are four orders of magnitude faster than Cuturi’s GPU Sinkhorn implementation and achieve slightly higher search accuracy. These are benchmark-specific comparisons showing substantial speed gains without reduced retrieval accuracy in the reported tests.
summary.tldr: Parallel linear-time Earth Mover’s Distance approximations deliver large benchmark speedups while matching or slightly improving the reported search accuracy.

title: Linear-Complexity Data-Parallel Earth Mover’s Distance Approximations

abstract: We consider the problem of selective prediction (also known as reject option) in deep neural networks, and introduce SelectiveNet, a deep neural architecture with an integrated reject option. Existing rejection mechanisms are based mostly on a threshold over the prediction confidence of a pre-trained network. In contrast, SelectiveNet is trained to optimize both classification (or regression) and rejection simultaneously, end-to-end. The result is a deep neural network that is optimized over the covered domain. In our experiments, we show a consistently improved risk-coverage trade-off over several well-known classification and regression datasets, thus reaching new state-of-the-art results for deep selective classification.
