Existing rejection mechanisms are based mostly on a threshold over the prediction confidence of a pre-trained network. In contrast, SelectiveNet is trained to optimize both classification (or regression) and rejection simultaneously, end-to-end. The result is a deep neural network that is optimized over the covered domain. In our experiments, we show a consistently improved risk-coverage trade-off over several well-known classification and regression datasets, thus reaching new state-of-the-art results for deep selective classification.

paragraphs: Selective prediction allows a model to decline some predictions instead of answering on every input. The central trade-off is between coverage, the portion of inputs it accepts, and risk on those accepted inputs. This paper introduces SelectiveNet, a deep network architecture that makes rejection part of the learning process itself.

Many existing rejection methods place a confidence threshold on a network that has already been trained. SelectiveNet jointly learns the prediction task and the rejection decision through end-to-end training. It supports classification or regression, and the resulting network is optimized for the covered domain: the inputs on which it chooses to provide an answer.

Experiments across several classification and regression datasets show consistently better risk–coverage trade-offs, including new state-of-the-art results for deep selective classification. The significance is that deciding where to answer can influence training, rather than being added only afterward. The reported findings support learning prediction and selection together when the objective is accuracy over a chosen portion of the input domain.
summary.tldr: SelectiveNet jointly learns predictions and rejection, improving reported error–coverage trade-offs on classification and regression tasks.

title: SelectiveNet: A Deep Neural Network with an Integrated Reject Option

abstract: Nearest Neighbor Search (NNS) over generalized weighted space is a fundamental problem which has many applications in various fields. However, to the best of our knowledge, there is no sublinear time solution to this problem. Based on the idea of Asymmetric Locality-Sensitive Hashing (ALSH), we introduce a novel spherical asymmetric transformation and propose the first two novel weight-oblivious hashing schemes SL-ALSH and S2-ALSH accordingly. We further show that both schemes enjoy a quality guarantee and can answer the NNS queries in sublinear time. Evaluations over three real datasets demonstrate the superior performance of the two proposed schemes.

paragraphs: The paper studies nearest neighbor search in generalized weighted spaces, where the search must account for weights in comparing objects. The goal is to answer a query without requiring time that grows linearly with the collection size. The authors identify the absence of a known sublinear solution as the gap their work addresses.

Their construction builds on asymmetric locality-sensitive hashing. They introduce a spherical asymmetric transformation and use it to design two weight-oblivious hashing schemes, SL-ALSH and S2-ALSH. The transformation is the central technical ingredient connecting the weighted search problem to hashing schemes that can support faster queries.

The authors prove that both schemes provide a quality guarantee and answer nearest neighbor queries in sublinear time. This pairs a statement about search efficiency with a statement about result quality. Evaluations on three real datasets report superior performance for the proposed schemes. The contribution thus combines a theoretical solution to the stated search problem with empirical evidence that the construction is useful in practice.
summary.tldr: Two hashing schemes use a spherical asymmetric transformation to provide quality-guaranteed, sublinear nearest neighbor search in generalized weighted spaces.

title: Sublinear Time Nearest Neighbor Search over Generalized Weighted Space

abstract: The focus of this paper is on intrinsic methods to detect overfitting. By intrinsic methods, we mean methods that rely only on the model and the training data, as opposed to traditional methods (we call them extrinsic methods) that rely on performance on a test set or on bounds from model complexity. We propose a family of intrinsic methods called Counterfactual Simulation (CFS) which analyze the flow of training examples through the model by identifying and perturbing rare patterns. By applying CFS to logic circuits we get a method that has no hyper-parameters and works uniformly across different types of models such as neural networks, random forests and lookup tables. Experimentally, CFS can separate models with different levels of overfit using only their logic circuit representations without any access to the high level structure. By comparing lookup tables, neural networks, and random forests using CFS, we get insight into why neural networks generalize. In particular, we find that stochastic gradient descent in neural nets does not lead to "brute force" memorization, but finds common patterns (whether we train with actual or randomized labels), and neural networks are not unlike forests in this regard. Finally, we identify a limitation with our proposal that makes it unsuitable in an adversarial setting, but points the way to future work on robust intrinsic methods.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether overfitting can be detected using only a trained model and its training data. The proposed approach, Counterfactual Simulation, follows training examples through the model, identifies rarely occurring patterns, and perturbs them. This examines the model’s internal handling of its examples rather than relying on performance on a separate test set or bounds derived from model complexity.

Applying the procedure to logic circuits gives a version with no hyperparameters that works across neural networks, random forests, and lookup tables. In experiments, these circuit representations alone distinguish models with different degrees of overfitting. The method does not need access to the original high-level architecture, making circuits a common representation for comparing otherwise different kinds of models.

Those comparisons also suggest that stochastic gradient descent finds shared patterns rather than simply performing brute-force memorization, even when neural networks are trained on randomized labels. In this respect, the observed networks resemble forests. The authors also identify a limitation that makes their proposal unsuitable in an adversarial setting, so its empirical diagnostic success does not establish robustness against deliberate manipulation.
summary.tldr: Counterfactual Simulation detects differences in overfitting by perturbing rare patterns inside circuit representations of models using only training data.

title: Circuit-Based Intrinsic Methods to Detect Overfitting

abstract: The combination of inducing point methods with stochastic variational inference has enabled approximate Gaussian Process (GP) inference on large datasets. Unfortunately, the resulting predictive distributions often exhibit substantially underestimated uncertainties. Notably, in the regression case the predictive variance is typically dominated by observation noise, yielding uncertainty estimates that make little use of the input-dependent function uncertainty that makes GP priors attractive. In this work we propose two simple methods for scalable GP regression that address this issue and thus yield substantially improved predictive uncertainties. The first applies variational inference to FITC (Fully Independent Training Conditional; Snelson et. al. 2006). The second bypasses posterior approximations and instead directly targets the posterior predictive distribution. In an extensive empirical comparison with a number of alternative methods for scalable GP regression, we find that the resulting predictive distributions exhibit significantly better calibrated uncertainties and higher log likelihoods–often by as much as half a nat per datapoint.

paragraphs: Scalable Gaussian-process methods make regression feasible on large datasets, but their uncertainty estimates can be too small. The paper identifies a particular problem: predictive variance can be dominated by observation noise, leaving too little contribution from uncertainty about the function itself. That weakens the input-dependent uncertainty modeling that makes Gaussian processes appealing.

The authors propose two methods to address this. The first applies variational inference to the Fully Independent Training Conditional approximation, or FITC. The second directly targets the posterior predictive distribution instead of constructing a posterior approximation first. Both are intended to improve predictive uncertainty while retaining scalability.

An extensive empirical comparison with alternative scalable Gaussian-process regressors finds better-calibrated uncertainty and higher predictive log likelihoods. The reported likelihood gains are often as large as half a nat per data point. These findings concern the quality of the predictive distribution, including how uncertainty is assigned, rather than merely whether its central prediction is close to the observed value.
summary.tldr: Two scalable Gaussian-process regression methods improve uncertainty calibration and predictive likelihood in extensive empirical comparisons.

title: Parametric Gaussian Process Regressors

abstract: We propose a modeling framework for event data and aim to answer questions such as \emph{when} and \emph{why} the next event would happen. Our proposed model excels in small data regime with the ability to incorporate domain knowledge in terms of logic rules. We model the dynamics of the event starts and ends via intensity function with the structures informed by a set of first-order temporal logic rules. Using the softened representation of temporal relations, and a weighted combination of logic rules, our probabilistic model can deal with uncertainty in events. Furthermore, many well-known point processes (e.g., Hawkes process, self-correcting point process) can be interpreted as special cases of our model given simple temporal logic rules. Our model, therefore, riches the family of point processes. We derive a maximum likelihood estimation procedure for our model and show that it can lead to accurate predictions when data are sparse and domain knowledge is critical.

paragraphs: Event models often need to predict both when something will happen and why the preceding events make it likely. This paper proposes a probabilistic framework that incorporates domain knowledge as temporal logic rules. That is especially useful when observations are sparse and the available data alone may provide limited guidance about the relationships between events.

The model describes event starts and ends through an intensity function, whose structure is informed by first-order temporal logic. Softened temporal relations and weighted combinations of rules let the model represent uncertainty instead of requiring every relationship to hold rigidly. The rules give the event dynamics an interpretable structure, while their probabilistic treatment accommodates uncertain observations and relationships.

The authors derive maximum likelihood estimation and show that the model can produce accurate predictions when data are limited and domain knowledge is important. They also show that familiar models, including Hawkes and self-correcting point processes, arise as special cases under simple rules. This places established approaches within a broader framework that can express additional rule-informed event dynamics.
summary.tldr: Temporal logic rules structure a probabilistic event model that incorporates domain knowledge and supports accurate prediction in sparse-data settings.

title: Temporal Logic Point Processes

abstract: Neural networks have a remarkable capacity for contextual processing{—}using recent or nearby inputs to modify processing of current input. For example, in natural language, contextual processing is necessary to correctly interpret negation (e.g. phrases such as "not bad"). However, our ability to understand how networks process context is limited. Here, we propose general methods for reverse engineering recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to identify and elucidate contextual processing. We apply these methods to understand RNNs trained on sentiment classification. This analysis reveals inputs that induce contextual effects, quantifies the strength and timescale of these effects, and identifies sets of these inputs with similar properties. Additionally, we analyze contextual effects related to differential processing of the beginning and end of documents. Using the insights learned from the RNNs we improve baseline Bag-of-Words models with simple extensions that incorporate contextual modification, recovering greater than 90% of the RNN’s performance increase over the baseline. This work yields a new understanding of how RNNs process contextual information, and provides tools that should provide similar insight more broadly.

paragraphs: Sentiment depends on context: a word’s contribution can change when nearby text modifies its meaning, as happens with negation. This paper develops methods for reverse engineering how recurrent neural networks implement such contextual processing. The authors apply those methods to networks trained to classify sentiment.

Their analysis identifies inputs that trigger contextual effects, measures how strong those effects are and how long they persist, and groups inputs with similar properties. It also examines how processing differs at the beginning and end of documents. These measurements turn the broad idea of using context into specific behaviors that can be inspected within trained networks.

The authors then use these insights to extend baseline Bag-of-Words models with simple contextual modifications. The extensions recover more than 90% of the RNN’s performance improvement over the baseline, rather than 90% of its total performance. This result connects the interpretation work to a practical model change, while the proposed analysis tools are intended to offer broader insight into contextual processing.
summary.tldr: Reverse engineering sentiment RNNs reveals contextual mechanisms that help simple models recover over 90% of the RNN’s improvement over baseline.

title: How recurrent networks implement contextual processing in sentiment analysis

abstract: Clustering is a fundamental problem in data analysis. In differentially private clustering, the goal is to identify k cluster centers without disclosing information on individual data points. Despite significant research progress, the problem had so far resisted practical solutions. In this work we aim at providing simple implementable differentrially private clustering algorithms when the the data is "easy," e.g., when there exists a significant separation between the clusters. For the easy instances we consider, we have a simple implementation based on utilizing non-private clustering algorithms, and combining them privately. We are able to get improved sample complexity bounds in some cases of Gaussian mixtures and k-means. We complement our theoretical algorithms with experiments of simulated data.

paragraphs: Private clustering seeks a set of cluster centers while protecting information about individual data points. Although the problem has received substantial theoretical attention, practical algorithms have remained difficult to obtain. This paper focuses on data with favorable structure, such as substantial separation between clusters, to develop simpler algorithms that can be implemented.

The approach builds on non-private clustering algorithms and combines their results through a private procedure. This makes existing clustering methods part of the construction while placing privacy protection in the overall combination. The favorable structure of the considered instances is essential to the scope of the results: the paper targets particular easy cases rather than arbitrary clustering data.

The authors improve sample-complexity bounds for some Gaussian-mixture and k-means settings, meaning the guarantees can require fewer data points in those cases. They supplement the theoretical algorithms with experiments on simulated data. The work shows how structural assumptions about clusters can support both simpler private procedures and stronger data requirements within the analyzed settings.
summary.tldr: For suitably structured clustering data, privately combining non-private methods yields simple algorithms and improved sample-complexity bounds.

title: Differentially-Private Clustering of Easy Instances

abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) provide an effective and simple method for modeling complex distributions. However, training VAEs often requires considerable hyperparameter tuning to determine the optimal amount of information retained by the latent variable. We study the impact of calibrated decoders, which learn the uncertainty of the decoding distribution and can determine this amount of information automatically, on the VAE performance. While many methods for learning calibrated decoders have been proposed, many of the recent papers that employ VAEs rely on heuristic hyperparameters and ad-hoc modifications instead. We perform the first comprehensive comparative analysis of calibrated decoder and provide recommendations for simple and effective VAE training. Our analysis covers a range of datasets and several single-image and sequential VAE models. We further propose a simple but novel modification to the commonly used Gaussian decoder, which computes the prediction variance analytically. We observe empirically that using heuristic modifications is not necessary with our method.

paragraphs: Training a variational autoencoder often involves tuning how much information its latent variable retains. This paper studies calibrated decoders, which learn the uncertainty of the decoding distribution and can determine that information level automatically. The authors investigate whether this mechanism can simplify training that otherwise relies on heuristic hyperparameters.

The study compares calibrated-decoder approaches across a range of datasets and multiple VAE models, including single-image and sequential models. Its aim is to establish practical recommendations for simple, effective training. The comparison directly examines a component of the probabilistic model that can influence the information retained in its latent representation.

The authors also propose a modification to the commonly used Gaussian decoder that calculates prediction variance analytically. In their empirical evaluation, heuristic modifications are unnecessary when this method is used. This is an experimental finding about the proposed approach, rather than a claim that every VAE requires no tuning. The contribution combines comparative analysis with a concrete decoder change that supports a simpler training procedure.
summary.tldr: Calibrated decoders, including an analytically computed Gaussian variance, can simplify VAE training and reduce reliance on heuristic adjustments.

title: Simple and Effective VAE Training with Calibrated Decoders

abstract: Capsule networks aim to parse images into a hierarchy of objects, parts and relations. While promising, they remain limited by an inability to learn effective low level part descriptions. To address this issue we propose a way to learn primary capsule encoders that detect atomic parts from a single image. During training we exploit motion as a powerful perceptual cue for part definition, with an expressive decoder for part generation within a layered image model with occlusion. Experiments demonstrate robust part discovery in the presence of multiple objects, cluttered backgrounds, and occlusion. The learned part decoder is shown to infer the underlying shape masks, effectively filling in occluded regions of the detected shapes. We evaluate FlowCapsules on unsupervised part segmentation and unsupervised image classification.

paragraphs: Capsule networks aim to represent images through objects, parts, and their relationships, but learning useful low-level parts remains difficult. FlowCapsules addresses this by learning primary capsule encoders that detect atomic parts from a single image. The method focuses on building the part representations needed by a larger compositional account of an image.

During training, motion provides a perceptual cue for defining parts. An expressive decoder generates those parts within a layered image model that includes occlusion. This combination connects evidence about movement with a representation of how visible and hidden parts contribute to an image. Although training uses motion, the learned encoder detects parts from one image.

Experiments demonstrate robust part discovery with multiple objects, background clutter, and occlusion. The decoder also infers underlying shape masks, effectively completing hidden regions of detected shapes. The authors evaluate unsupervised part segmentation and image classification. These findings support the use of motion-guided training to learn part descriptions that remain useful when objects overlap or their boundaries are only partly visible.
summary.tldr: FlowCapsules uses motion during training to discover image parts and infer their shapes through clutter and occlusion.

title: Unsupervised Part Representation by Flow Capsules

abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) aims to improve the generalization of several related tasks by learning them jointly. As a comparison, in addition to the joint training scheme, modern meta-learning allows unseen tasks with limited labels during the test phase, in the hope of fast adaptation over them. Despite the subtle difference between MTL and meta-learning in the problem formulation, both learning paradigms share the same insight that the shared structure between existing training tasks could lead to better generalization and adaptation. In this paper, we take one important step further to understand the close connection between these two learning paradigms, through both theoretical analysis and empirical investigation. Theoretically, we first demonstrate that MTL shares the same optimization formulation with a class of gradient-based meta-learning (GBML) algorithms. We then prove that for over-parameterized neural networks with sufficient depth, the learned predictive functions of MTL and GBML are close. In particular, this result implies that the predictions given by these two models are similar over the same unseen task. Empirically, we corroborate our theoretical findings by showing that, with proper implementation, MTL is competitive against state-of-the-art GBML algorithms on a set of few-shot image classification benchmarks. Since existing GBML algorithms often involve costly second-order bi-level optimization, our first-order MTL method is an order of magnitude faster on large-scale datasets such as mini-ImageNet. We believe this work could help bridge the gap between these two learning paradigms, and provide a computationally efficient alternative to GBML that also supports fast task adaptation.

This paper examines how closely these approaches are connected. Both aim to extract shared structure from training tasks, but their differing formulations can make them appear to require substantially different learning procedures.

summary.tldr: Under specified network conditions, multi-task learning closely matches a class of gradient-based meta-learning methods and offers efficient few-shot adaptation.

title: Bridging Multi-Task Learning and Meta-Learning: Towards Efficient Training and Effective Adaptation

abstract: Sequence learning has attracted much research attention from the machine learning community in recent years. In many applications, a sequence learning task is usually associated with multiple temporally correlated auxiliary tasks, which are different in terms of how much input information to use or which future step to predict. For example, (i) in simultaneous machine translation, one can conduct translation under different latency (i.e., how many input words to read/wait before translation); (ii) in stock trend forecasting, one can predict the price of a stock in different future days (e.g., tomorrow, the day after tomorrow). While it is clear that those temporally correlated tasks can help each other, there is a very limited exploration on how to better leverage multiple auxiliary tasks to boost the performance of the main task. In this work, we introduce a learnable scheduler to sequence learning, which can adaptively select auxiliary tasks for training depending on the model status and the current training data. The scheduler and the model for the main task are jointly trained through bi-level optimization. Experiments show that our method significantly improves the performance of simultaneous machine translation and stock trend forecasting.

paragraphs: Sequence-learning problems often come with related tasks that differ in timing. A translation system can work with different amounts of input before producing output, while a forecasting model can predict different future days. These auxiliary tasks share temporal structure with the main task, creating opportunities for them to help train the same model.

The paper introduces a learnable scheduler that decides which auxiliary tasks to use during training. Its choices depend on the model's current state and the training data currently being processed. The scheduler and main-task model are trained jointly through bi-level optimization, allowing auxiliary-task selection to adapt as learning progresses.

Experiments show significant improvements in simultaneous machine translation and stock trend forecasting. The contribution is a mechanism for deciding when related tasks are useful, beyond simply recognizing that they exist. The reported findings support adaptive selection as a way to turn temporal relationships among tasks into better main-task performance in these two sequence-learning applications.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained scheduler adaptively selects temporally related auxiliary tasks, improving translation and stock-trend forecasting in experiments.

title: Temporally Correlated Task Scheduling for Sequence Learning

abstract: There has been a surge of interest in continual learning and federated learning, both of which are important in deep neural networks in real-world scenarios. Yet little research has been done regarding the scenario where each client learns on a sequence of tasks from a private local data stream. This problem of federated continual learning poses new challenges to continual learning, such as utilizing knowledge from other clients, while preventing interference from irrelevant knowledge. To resolve these issues, we propose a novel federated continual learning framework, Federated Weighted Inter-client Transfer (FedWeIT), which decomposes the network weights into global federated parameters and sparse task-specific parameters, and each client receives selective knowledge from other clients by taking a weighted combination of their task-specific parameters. FedWeIT minimizes interference between incompatible tasks, and also allows positive knowledge transfer across clients during learning. We validate our FedWeIT against existing federated learning and continual learning methods under varying degrees of task similarity across clients, and our model significantly outperforms them with a large reduction in the communication cost.

paragraphs: Federated continual learning combines two demands: clients learn from private local data, and each client encounters a sequence of tasks over time. Knowledge from other clients may help with a new task, but unrelated knowledge can interfere. The paper addresses how clients can share useful information selectively within this evolving setting.

FedWeIT separates network weights into globally shared federated parameters and sparse parameters specific to individual tasks. A client receives knowledge from other clients through a weighted combination of their task-specific parameters. This gives the framework a way to control which task knowledge contributes to local learning, supporting positive transfer while reducing interference between incompatible tasks.

The authors compare FedWeIT with existing federated-learning and continual-learning methods under different levels of task similarity across clients. They report significantly better performance together with a large reduction in communication cost. These findings support distinguishing shared knowledge from task-specific knowledge and making inter-client transfer selective when tasks vary across both clients and time.
summary.tldr: FedWeIT selectively combines sparse task-specific knowledge across clients, improving federated continual learning while reducing reported communication costs.

title: Federated Continual Learning with Weighted Inter-client Transfer

abstract: Myopic exploration policies such as epsilon-greedy, softmax, or Gaussian noise fail to explore efficiently in some reinforcement learning tasks and yet, they perform well in many others. In fact, in practice, they are often selected as the top choices, due to their simplicity. But, for what tasks do such policies succeed? Can we give theoretical guarantees for their favorable performance? These crucial questions have been scarcely investigated, despite the prominent practical importance of these policies. This paper presents a theoretical analysis of such policies and provides the first regret and sample-complexity bounds for reinforcement learning with myopic exploration. Our results apply to value-function-based algorithms in episodic MDPs with bounded Bellman Eluder dimension. We propose a new complexity measure called myopic exploration gap, denoted by alpha, that captures a structural property of the MDP, the exploration policy and the given value function class. We show that the sample-complexity of myopic exploration scales quadratically with the inverse of this quantity, 1 / alpha^2. We further demonstrate through concrete examples that myopic exploration gap is indeed favorable in several tasks where myopic exploration succeeds, due to the corresponding dynamics and reward structure.

The result provides a conditional theoretical explanation for why inexpensive exploration methods can perform well in suitable environments.
summary.tldr: A new exploration-gap measure yields conditional learning guarantees that explain when simple myopic exploration can succeed.

title: Guarantees for Epsilon-Greedy Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation

abstract: Test-time adaptation provides an effective means of tackling the potential distribution shift between model training and inference, by dynamically updating the model at test time. This area has seen fast progress recently, at the effectiveness of handling test shifts. Nonetheless, prior methods still suffer two key limitations: 1) these methods rely on performing backward computation for each test sample, which takes a considerable amount of time; and 2) these methods focus on improving the performance on out-of-distribution test samples and ignore that the adaptation on test data may result in a catastrophic forgetting issue, \ie, the performance on in-distribution test samples may degrade. To address these issues, we propose an efficient anti-forgetting test-time adaptation (EATA) method. Specifically, we devise a sample-efficient entropy minimization loss to exclude uninformative samples out of backward computation, which improves the overall efficiency and meanwhile boosts the out-of-distribution accuracy. Afterward, we introduce a regularization loss to ensure that critical model weights tend to be preserved during adaptation, thereby alleviating the forgetting issue. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R verify the effectiveness and superiority of our EATA.

paragraphs: A model can encounter inputs during deployment that differ from its training data. Test-time adaptation addresses this by updating the model as those inputs arrive. The paper identifies two problems with existing approaches: updating on every sample is expensive, and adaptation to unfamiliar data can reduce performance on data resembling the original training distribution.

EATA addresses the computational problem through a sample-efficient entropy-minimization objective. It excludes uninformative samples from backward computation, reducing the number of costly updates. The authors report that this selection also improves accuracy on shifted data, so the efficiency gain accompanies a predictive benefit in their experiments.

A second objective discourages changes to weights that are important to the existing model. These weights tend to be preserved during adaptation, helping alleviate forgetting while other updates accommodate the new inputs. Experiments on CIFAR-10-C, ImageNet-C, and ImageNet-R support the combined method. Its contribution is to treat adaptation efficiency and retention of earlier capabilities as connected requirements of deployment-time learning.
summary.tldr: EATA selectively updates on informative test samples and protects important weights to improve adaptation efficiency while reducing forgetting.

title: Efficient Test-Time Model Adaptation without Forgetting

abstract: We introduce the Lossy Implicit Network Activation Coding (LINAC) defence, an input transformation which successfully hinders several common adversarial attacks on CIFAR-10 classifiers for perturbations up to 8/255 in Linf norm and 0.5 in L2 norm. Implicit neural representations are used to approximately encode pixel colour intensities in 2D images such that classifiers trained on transformed data appear to have robustness to small perturbations without adversarial training or large drops in performance. The seed of the random number generator used to initialise and train the implicit neural representation turns out to be necessary information for stronger generic attacks, suggesting its role as a private key. We devise a Parametric Bypass Approximation (PBA) attack strategy for key-based defences, which successfully invalidates an existing method in this category. Interestingly, our LINAC defence also hinders some transfer and adaptive attacks, including our novel PBA strategy. Our results emphasise the importance of a broad range of customised attacks despite apparent robustness according to standard evaluations.

summary.tldr: LINAC hinders several tested adversarial attacks through image re-encoding, while a new bypass attack highlights the need for customized robustness evaluations.

title: Hindering Adversarial Attacks with Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: Non-parametric two-sample tests (TSTs) that judge whether two sets of samples are drawn from the same distribution, have been widely used in the analysis of critical data. People tend to employ TSTs as trusted basic tools and rarely have any doubt about their reliability. This paper systematically uncovers the failure mode of non-parametric TSTs through adversarial attacks and then proposes corresponding defense strategies. First, we theoretically show that an adversary can upper-bound the distributional shift which guarantees the attack’s invisibility. Furthermore, we theoretically find that the adversary can also degrade the lower bound of a TST’s test power, which enables us to iteratively minimize the test criterion in order to search for adversarial pairs. To enable TST-agnostic attacks, we propose an ensemble attack (EA) framework that jointly minimizes the different types of test criteria. Second, to robustify TSTs, we propose a max-min optimization that iteratively generates adversarial pairs to train the deep kernels. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets validate the adversarial vulnerabilities of non-parametric TSTs and the effectiveness of our proposed defense. Source code is available at https://github.com/GodXuxilie/Robust-TST.git.

paragraphs: Two-sample tests assess whether two collections of observations come from the same distribution. This paper investigates how non-parametric versions of these tests can fail when someone deliberately manipulates their inputs. The target is a statistical decision tool that users may otherwise treat as a reliable component of data analysis.

The theoretical analysis shows that an adversary can bound the distributional shift in a way that guarantees the attack’s invisibility. It also shows how the adversary can weaken a lower bound on test power, the ability to detect a distributional difference. This motivates repeatedly minimizing the test criterion to find adversarial sample pairs. An ensemble attack jointly targets different criteria to support attacks without committing to a single test.

For defense, the authors alternate adversarial-pair generation with training deep kernels through a max-min objective. The attack therefore also supplies challenging examples for strengthening the test. Experiments on simulated and real data demonstrate both the vulnerability and the effectiveness of the proposed defense.
summary.tldr: Adversarial sample pairs can undermine non-parametric two-sample tests, while training deep kernels against such pairs improves their robustness in experiments.

title: Adversarial Attack and Defense for Non-Parametric Two-Sample Tests

abstract: Strong adversarial attacks are important for evaluating the true robustness of deep neural networks. Most existing attacks search in the input space, e.g., using gradient descent, and may miss adversarial examples due to non-convexity. In this work, we systematically search adversarial examples in the activation space of ReLU networks to tackle hard instances where none of the existing adversarial attacks succeed. Unfortunately, searching the activation space typically relies on generic mixed integer programming (MIP) solvers and is limited to small networks and easy problem instances. To improve scalability and practicability, we use branch and bound (BaB) with specialized GPU-based bound propagation methods, and propose a top-down beam-search approach to quickly identify the subspace that may contain adversarial examples. Moreover, we build an adversarial candidates pool using cheap attacks to further assist the search in activation space via diving techniques and a bottom-up large neighborhood search. Our adversarial attack framework, BaB-Attack, opens up a new opportunity for designing novel adversarial attacks not limited to searching the input space, and enables us to borrow techniques from integer programming theory and neural network verification. In experiments, we can successfully generate adversarial examples when existing attacks on input space fail. Compared to off-the-shelf MIP solver based attacks that requires significant computations, we outperform in both success rates and efficiency.

This paper targets difficult cases in ReLU networks by searching through activation patterns. That changes how the attack organizes the problem, moving beyond direct search over input values.

The proposed BaB-Attack uses branch and bound with specialized GPU-based bound propagation to make this search more practical. These findings support activation-space search as a useful additional tool for robustness evaluation, while demonstrating how techniques from integer programming and network verification can help construct stronger attacks.
summary.tldr: BaB-Attack searches ReLU activation patterns to find adversarial examples missed by existing input-space attacks.

title: A Branch and Bound Framework for Stronger Adversarial Attacks of ReLU Networks

abstract: Diffusion-based generative graph models have been proven effective in generating high-quality small graphs. However, they need to be more scalable for generating large graphs containing thousands of nodes desiring graph statistics. In this work, we propose EDGE, a new diffusion-based generative graph model that addresses generative tasks with large graphs. To improve computation efficiency, we encourage graph sparsity by using a discrete diffusion process that randomly removes edges at each time step and finally obtains an empty graph. EDGE only focuses on a portion of nodes in the graph at each denoising step. It makes much fewer edge predictions than previous diffusion-based models. Moreover, EDGE admits explicitly modeling the node degrees of the graphs, further improving the model performance. The empirical study shows that EDGE is much more efficient than competing methods and can generate large graphs with thousands of nodes. It also outperforms baseline models in generation quality: graphs generated by our approach have more similar graph statistics to those of the training graphs.

paragraphs: EDGE addresses the computational difficulty of generating large graphs with diffusion models. Earlier diffusion approaches had demonstrated strong results on small graphs, but scaling to thousands of nodes while reproducing training-graph statistics remained challenging. The paper changes the diffusion process to make sparse graph structure central to generation.

Its forward process repeatedly removes randomly selected edges until the graph is empty. During denoising, EDGE concentrates on only a portion of the nodes at each step, substantially reducing the number of edge predictions. It also explicitly models node degrees, meaning the number of connections associated with each node, to improve generation performance.

The empirical study reports substantially greater efficiency than competing methods and successful generation of graphs containing thousands of nodes. Generated graphs also have statistics closer to those of the training graphs than baseline outputs do. Together, these findings support the approach's ability to reduce computation while improving the measured structural resemblance of generated graphs.
summary.tldr: EDGE uses edge-removal diffusion, selective denoising, and degree modeling to generate large graphs more efficiently with better statistical resemblance.

title: Efficient and Degree-Guided Graph Generation via Discrete Diffusion Modeling

abstract: Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) has recently enjoyed great success as an efficient self-supervised representation learning approach. However, the existing methods have focused on designing of contrastive modes and used data augmentation with a rigid and inefficient one-to-one sampling strategy. We adopted node neighborhoods to extend positive samplings and made avoided resorting to data augmentation to create different views. We also considered the homophily problem in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) between the inter-class node pairs. The key novelty of our method hinged upon analyzing this GNNs problem and integrating the GCL sampling strategy with homophily discrimination, where we solved these two significant problems using one approach. We introduced a new parameterized neighbor sampling component to replace the conventional sub-optimal samplings. By keeping and updating the neighbor sets, both the positive sampling of GCL and the message passing of GNNs can be optimized. Moreover, we theoretically proved that the new method provided a lower bound of mutual information for unsupervised semantic learning, and it can also keep the lower bound with downstream tasks. In essence, our method is a new self-supervised approach, which we refer to as group discrimination, and it can make the downstream fine-tuning efficient. Our extensive empirical results demonstrate that the new method can significantly outperform the existing GCL methods because the former can solve the homophily problem in a self-supervised way with the new group discrimination method used.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning learns representations by deciding which examples should be treated as related. Existing approaches often construct different augmented views and use one-to-one positive pairs. This paper replaces that setup with neighborhood-based groups, while also addressing the difficulty of passing information between connected nodes that belong to different classes.

The central component is a parameterized neighbor sampler that maintains and updates neighbor sets. Those same sets guide both positive sampling for contrastive learning and message passing in the graph network. This connects two decisions that otherwise can be handled separately: which nodes provide related learning examples and which neighbors should contribute information to a node’s representation.

The authors call the resulting self-supervised approach group discrimination. They prove a mutual-information lower bound for unsupervised semantic learning and show that a lower bound can also be maintained with downstream tasks. Their experiments report substantial improvements over existing graph contrastive methods and efficient downstream fine-tuning. The stated explanation is that learned group selection addresses the homophily problem while improving the contrastive sampling strategy.
summary.tldr: Learned neighbor groups jointly improve contrastive sampling and graph message passing, with mutual-information guarantees and reported empirical gains.

title: Contrastive Learning Meets Homophily: Two Birds with One Stone

abstract: Lossy image compression aims to represent images in as few bits as possible while maintaining fidelity to the original. Theoretical results indicate that optimizing distortion metrics such as PSNR or MS-SSIM necessarily leads to a discrepancy in the statistics of original images from those of reconstructions, in particular at low bitrates, often manifested by the blurring of the compressed images. Previous work has leveraged adversarial discriminators to improve statistical fidelity. Yet these binary discriminators adopted from generative modeling tasks may not be ideal for image compression. In this paper, we introduce a non-binary discriminator that is conditioned on quantized local image representations obtained via VQ-VAE autoencoders. Our evaluations on the CLIC2020, DIV2K and Kodak datasets show that our discriminator is more effective for jointly optimizing distortion (e.g., PSNR) and statistical fidelity (e.g., FID) than the PatchGAN of the state-of-the-art HiFiC model. On CLIC2020, we obtain the same FID as HiFiC with 30-40% fewer bits.

paragraphs: Lossy image compression balances file size against the quality of reconstructed images. Optimizing distortion measures alone can produce reconstructions whose statistics differ from those of original images, especially at low bitrates, where blur is a common symptom. Adversarial discriminators have been used to address this, but the paper questions whether a binary discriminator is the best fit.

The goal is to improve statistical fidelity while also maintaining performance on distortion measures, so the reconstruction objective accounts for both kinds of quality.

summary.tldr: A locally conditioned non-binary discriminator improves neural image compression, matching HiFiC’s FID on CLIC2020 with 30–40% fewer bits.

title: Improving Statistical Fidelity for Neural Image Compression with Implicit Local Likelihood Models

abstract: Differential private optimization for nonconvex smooth objective is considered. In the previous work, the best known utility bound is $\widetilde O(\sqrt{d}/(n\varepsilon_\mathrm{DP}))$ in terms of the squared full gradient norm, which is achieved by Differential Private Gradient Descent (DP-GD) as an instance, where $n$ is the sample size, $d$ is the problem dimensionality and $\varepsilon_\mathrm{DP}$ is the differential privacy parameter. To improve the best known utility bound, we propose a new differential private optimization framework called DIFF2 (DIFFerential private optimization via gradient DIFFerences) that constructs a differential private global gradient estimator with possibly quite small variance based on communicated gradient differences rather than gradients themselves. It is shown that DIFF2 with a gradient descent subroutine achieves the utility of $\widetilde O(d^{2/3}/(n\varepsilon_\mathrm{DP})^{4/3})$, which can be significantly better than the previous one in terms of the dependence on the sample size $n$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first fundamental result to improve the standard utility $\widetilde O(\sqrt{d}/(n\varepsilon_\mathrm{DP}))$ for nonconvex objectives. Additionally, a more computational and communication efficient subroutine is combined with DIFF2 and its theoretical analysis is also given. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the superiority of DIFF2 framework.

paragraphs: DIFF2 studies differentially private optimization of smooth, nonconvex objectives in distributed learning. The quality measure is the squared norm of the full gradient: the theoretical goal is to make that quantity small while preserving privacy. The paper seeks to improve the previously best-known bound achieved, for example, by differentially private gradient descent.

The central idea is to communicate differences between gradients instead of the gradients themselves. DIFF2 uses those differences to construct a private global gradient estimator with potentially much smaller variance. With a gradient-descent subroutine, its utility bound scales as d^(2/3)/(nε)^(4/3), suppressing logarithmic factors, where d is dimensionality, n is sample size, and ε controls privacy.

Compared with the earlier square-root-d divided by nε bound, this improves the dependence on sample size and can yield a substantially better guarantee. The benefit is qualified by the full expression, including dimensionality. The paper also analyzes a subroutine designed to reduce computation and communication costs, and reports numerical experiments supporting the framework’s advantages.
summary.tldr: DIFF2 uses private gradient differences to improve the sample-size dependence of utility guarantees for smooth nonconvex distributed optimization.

title: DIFF2: Differential Private Optimization via Gradient Differences for Nonconvex Distributed Learning

abstract: While efficient distribution learning is no doubt behind the groundbreaking success of diffusion modeling, its theoretical guarantees are quite limited. In this paper, we provide the first rigorous analysis on approximation and generalization abilities of diffusion modeling for well-known function spaces. The highlight of this paper is that when the true density function belongs to the Besov space and the empirical score matching loss is properly minimized, the generated data distribution achieves the nearly minimax optimal estimation rates in the total variation distance and in the Wasserstein distance of order one. Furthermore, we extend our theory to demonstrate how diffusion models adapt to low-dimensional data distributions. We expect these results advance theoretical understandings of diffusion modeling and its ability to generate verisimilar outputs.

The highlight of this paper is that when the true density function belongs to the Besov space and the empirical score matching loss is properly minimized, the generated data distribution achieves the nearly minimax optimal estimation rates in the total variation distance and in the Wasserstein distance of order one. paragraphs: Diffusion models have become effective generators, but their statistical efficiency needs theoretical explanation. This paper studies how accurately a learned diffusion process can approximate an unknown data distribution from samples. It analyzes both approximation and generalization for established classes of functions.

When the true density belongs to a Besov space and empirical score matching is sufficiently well optimized, the generated distribution achieves nearly minimax-optimal estimation rates. The guarantees cover total variation distance and first-order Wasserstein distance, giving two ways to quantify how close the generated and true distributions are.

The theory also addresses adaptation to low-dimensional data distributions. These results support the statistical foundations of diffusion modeling by comparing its estimation performance with the best possible rates for the analyzed setting. The assumptions matter: the theorem requires an appropriate density class and successful loss minimization, and does not automatically guarantee optimal behavior for every practical architecture or training run.
summary.tldr: Under function-class and optimization assumptions, diffusion models achieve nearly minimax-optimal distribution-estimation rates.

title: Diffusion Models are Minimax Optimal Distribution Estimators

abstract: In this work, we propose introduce a variant of online stochastic gradient descent and prove it converges to Nash equilibria and simultaneously it has sublinear regret for the class of congestion games in the semi-bandit feedback setting. Our proposed method admits convergence rates depending only polynomially on the number of players and the number of facilities, but not on the size of the action set, which can be exponentially large in terms of the number of facilities. Moreover, the running time of our method has polynomial-time dependence on the implicit description of the game. Our analysis exploits techniques from convex geometry, in particular Caratheodory’s theorem and recent advances in non-convex stochastic optimization. This work improves upon and answers an open question from (Cui et al 2022).
originalAbstract: In this work, we propose introduce a variant of online stochastic gradient descent and prove it converges to Nash equilibria and simultaneously it has sublinear regret for the class of congestion games in the semi-bandit feedback setting. Our proposed method admits convergence rates depending only polynomially on the number of players and the number of facilities, but not on the size of the action set, which can be exponentially large in terms of the number of facilities. Moreover, the running time of our method has polynomial-time dependence on the implicit description of the game. Our analysis exploits techniques from convex geometry, in particular Caratheodory’s theorem and recent advances in non-convex stochastic optimization. This work improves upon and answers an open question from (Cui et al 2022).

paragraphs: This paper studies learning in congestion games under semi-bandit feedback, where participants receive limited information about their decisions. The authors propose a variant of online stochastic gradient descent and prove two properties together: convergence to Nash equilibria and sublinear regret. The latter means accumulated regret grows more slowly than the number of rounds.

A central issue is that the number of possible actions can be exponentially large relative to the number of facilities. The proposed method’s convergence rates depend polynomially on the numbers of players and facilities, without depending on the action-set size. Its running time is also polynomial in the game’s implicit description, making compact problem structure important to the result.

The analysis combines ideas from convex geometry, including Carathéodory’s theorem, with advances in non-convex stochastic optimization. The contribution is a joint guarantee: players can approach equilibrium while also controlling their learning regret under limited feedback. The scaling results show that these guarantees need not carry an explicit dependence on an exponentially large list of actions.
summary.tldr: A stochastic-gradient learning rule achieves equilibrium convergence and sublinear regret in congestion games without scaling with action-set size.

title: Semi Bandit dynamics in Congestion Games: Convergence to Nash Equilibrium and No-Regret Guarantees.

abstract: Driven by the need from real-world applications, Auxiliary Modality Learning (AML) offers the possibility to utilize more information from auxiliary data in training, while only requiring data from one or fewer modalities in test, to save the overall computational cost and reduce the amount of input data for inferencing. In this work, we formally define “Auxiliary Modality Learning” (AML), systematically classify types of auxiliary modality (in visual computing) and architectures for AML, and analyze their performance. We also analyze the conditions under which AML works well from the optimization and data distribution perspectives. To guide various choices to achieve optimal performance using AML, we propose a novel method to assist in choosing the best auxiliary modality and estimating an upper bound performance before executing AML. In addition, we propose a new AML method using generalized curriculum distillation to enable more effective curriculum learning. Our method achieves the best performance compared to other SOTA methods.

paragraphs: Auxiliary Modality Learning uses additional kinds of input during training while requiring fewer kinds at test time. Its attraction is practical: a model can benefit from richer training information while reducing the inputs and overall computation needed when making predictions. The paper gives this setting a formal definition and organizes auxiliary modalities and model architectures in visual computing.

The authors also investigate when this approach works well, considering both optimization and the distributions of the data involved. This matters because the availability of an extra modality does not by itself establish how useful it will be. They propose a method to help select an auxiliary modality and estimate an upper bound on performance before carrying out auxiliary modality learning.

The paper then introduces a learning method based on generalized curriculum distillation, intended to make curriculum learning more effective. It reports the best performance among the state-of-the-art methods compared. The contribution therefore combines guidance about choosing auxiliary information with a concrete method for transferring its benefits into a model that uses fewer modalities at inference.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes learning from extra training modalities and proposes modality selection and curriculum distillation methods.

title: Auxiliary Modality Learning with Generalized Curriculum Distillation

abstract: As machine learning becomes more prominent there is a growing demand to perform several inference tasks in parallel. Multi-task learning (MTL) addresses this challenge by learning a single model that solves several tasks simultaneously and efficiently. Often optimizing MTL models entails first computing the gradient of the loss for each task, and then aggregating all the gradients to obtain a combined update direction. However, common methods following this approach do not consider an important aspect, the sensitivity in the dimensions of the gradients. Some dimensions may be more lenient for changes while others may be more restrictive. Here, we introduce a novel gradient aggregation procedure using Bayesian inference. We place a probability distribution over the task-specific parameters, which in turn induce a distribution over the gradients of the tasks. This valuable information allows us to quantify the uncertainty associated with each of the gradients’ dimensions which is factored in when aggregating them. We empirically demonstrate the benefits of our approach in a variety of datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning trains one model to solve several tasks together. A common training approach computes a separate gradient for each task and combines those gradients into one parameter update. This paper argues that common aggregation methods overlook differences in sensitivity across gradient dimensions: some directions allow more change, while others are more restrictive.

The authors introduce a Bayesian aggregation procedure. They place probability distributions over task-specific parameters, which induce distributions over the corresponding gradients. These distributions provide uncertainty information for individual gradient dimensions, rather than treating each task’s gradient solely as a fixed vector. The aggregation procedure incorporates that information when forming the shared update.

Experiments across a variety of datasets demonstrate benefits and report state-of-the-art performance. The contribution is a more detailed basis for reconciling the training signals of different tasks. Instead of deciding how to combine tasks only from their gradient values, the method also accounts for uncertainty associated with the dimensions of those gradients, with empirical evidence that this improves multi-task learning.
summary.tldr: Bayesian gradient aggregation uses uncertainty in individual gradient dimensions to improve shared updates for multi-task learning.

title: Bayesian Uncertainty for Gradient Aggregation in Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Identifying the underlying time-delayed latent causal processes in sequential data is vital for grasping temporal dynamics and making downstream reasoning. While some recent methods can robustly identify these latent causal variables, they rely on strict assumptions about the invertible generation process from latent variables to observed data. However, these assumptions are often hard to satisfy in real-world applications containing information loss. For instance, the visual perception process translates a 3D space into 2D images, or the phenomenon of persistence of vision incorporates historical data into current perceptions. To address this challenge, we establish an identifiability theory that allows for the recovery of independent latent components even when they come from a nonlinear and non-invertible mix. Using this theory as a foundation, we propose a principled approach, CaRiNG, to learn the Causal Representation of Non-invertible Generative temporal data with identifiability guarantees. Specifically, we utilize temporal context to recover lost latent information and apply the conditions in our theory to guide the training process. Through experiments conducted on synthetic datasets, we validate that our CaRiNG method reliably identifies the causal process, even when the generation process is non-invertible. Moreover, we demonstrate that our approach considerably improves temporal understanding and reasoning in practical applications.

paragraphs: Understanding sequential data can require recovering hidden processes whose effects unfold over time. Existing approaches often assume that observations preserve enough information to reverse the mapping from hidden variables to measurements. This assumption is restrictive when observation loses information, as when a three-dimensional scene becomes a two-dimensional image or current perception incorporates earlier inputs.

The paper develops an identifiability theory for recovering independent hidden components from nonlinear, non-invertible mixtures. CaRiNG turns that theory into a learning method by using temporal context to recover information missing from individual observations. Its training procedure incorporates the theory’s conditions, so the recovery guarantees remain tied to those conditions rather than applying to every information-losing process.

Synthetic experiments show that CaRiNG can reliably identify the causal process even when the observation-generating mapping is non-invertible. The authors also report improvements in temporal understanding and reasoning in practical applications. The key implication is that information lost in a single observation need not preclude recovery when useful information remains available across time.
summary.tldr: CaRiNG uses temporal context to recover hidden causal components under theoretical conditions that allow information-losing observation processes.

title: CaRiNG: Learning Temporal Causal Representation under Non-Invertible Generation Process

abstract: This paper proposes the use of "multicalibration": to yield interpretable and reliable confidence scores for outputs generated by large language models (LLMs). Multicalibration asks for calibration not just marginally, but simultaneously across various intersecting groupings of the data. We show how to form groupings for prompt/completion pairs that are correlated with the probability of correctness via two techniques: clustering within an embedding space, and "self-annotation" - querying the LLM by asking it various yes-or-no questions about the prompt. We also develop novel variants of multicalibration algorithms that offer performance improvements by reducing their tendency to overfit. Through systematic benchmarking across various question answering datasets and LLMs, we show how our techniques can yield confidence scores that provide substantial improvements in fine-grained measures of both calibration and accuracy compared to existing methods.

paragraphs: A confidence score is useful when it reflects how often an answer is actually correct. Calibration averaged over all answers can obscure differences between kinds of questions or responses. This paper applies multicalibration to language-model outputs, asking confidence scores to remain calibrated across multiple overlapping groups of prompt-and-completion pairs.

The authors construct groups in two ways. One clusters examples in an embedding space; the other asks the language model yes-or-no questions about the prompt, producing what they call self-annotations. These groupings are correlated with the probability that a response is correct. The paper also introduces multicalibration algorithm variants designed to reduce overfitting and thereby improve performance.

Benchmarking across several question-answering datasets and language models shows substantial improvements over existing methods in fine-grained measures of calibration and accuracy. The practical contribution is confidence scoring that accounts for differences within the data, rather than relying only on an overall average. The findings concern the measured reliability and accuracy of the proposed scoring techniques in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Multicalibration improves LLM confidence scores by calibrating them across overlapping groups formed through embeddings and model-generated prompt annotations.

title: Multicalibration for Confidence Scoring in LLMs

abstract: The sparse Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform is one of the central techniques in dimensionality reduction. It supports embedding a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ into $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2} \ln n)$ dimensions while preserving all pairwise distances to within $1 \pm \varepsilon$. Each input point $x$ is embedded to $Ax$, where $A$ is an $m \times d$ matrix having $s$ non-zeros per column, allowing for an embedding time of $O(s \|x\|_0)$. Since the sparsity of $A$ governs the embedding time, much work has gone into improving the sparsity $s$. The current state-of-the-art by Kane and Nelson (2014) shows that $s = O(\varepsilon^{-1} \ln n)$ suffices. This is almost matched by a lower bound of $s = \Omega(\varepsilon^{-1} \ln n/\ln(1/\varepsilon))$ by Nelson and Nguyen (2013) for $d=\Omega(n)$. Previous work thus suggests that we have near-optimal embeddings. In this work, we revisit sparse embeddings and present a sparser embedding for instances in which $d = n^{o(1)}$, which in many applications is realistic. Formally, our embedding achieves $s = O(\varepsilon^{-1}(\ln n/\ln(1/\varepsilon)+\ln^{2/3}n \ln^{1/3} d))$. We also complement our analysis by strengthening the lower bound of Nelson and Nguyen to hold also when $d \ll n$, thereby matching the first term in our new sparsity upper bound. Finally, we also improve the sparsity of the best oblivious subspace embeddings for optimal embedding dimensionality.

paragraphs: Sparse Johnson-Lindenstrauss transforms reduce dimensionality while approximately preserving every pairwise distance among a set of points. Their computational cost depends on how many nonzero entries each projection-matrix column contains. Fewer entries mean less work when applying the transform, making matrix sparsity an important target even when the output dimension is already near optimal.

Existing upper and lower bounds suggest limited room for improvement, but the cited lower bound assumes the original dimension is at least proportional to the number of points. This paper revisits the problem when the dimension grows subpolynomially with that number. It provides a sparser embedding in that regime, retaining the stated distance-preservation and output-dimension goals.

The authors also strengthen the lower bound so that it applies when the dimension is much smaller than the number of points. This matches the first term of their new sparsity upper bound. A further result improves sparsity for oblivious subspace embeddings at optimal output dimension. Together, the results refine how attainable sparsity depends on the dimensional regime.
summary.tldr: The paper improves sparse dimensionality reduction when input dimension grows subpolynomially with the number of points and strengthens complementary lower bounds.

title: Sparse Dimensionality Reduction Revisited

abstract: Optimization objectives in the form of a sum of intractable expectations are rising in importance (e.g.,, diffusion models, variational autoencoders, and many more), a setting also known as "finite sum with infinite data." For these problems, a popular strategy is to employ SGD with doubly stochastic gradients (doubly SGD): the expectations are estimated using the gradient estimator of each component, while the sum is estimated by subsampling over these estimators. Despite its popularity, little is known about the convergence properties of doubly SGD, except under strong assumptions such as bounded variance. In this work, we establish the convergence of doubly SGD with independent minibatching and random reshuffling under general conditions, which encompasses dependent component gradient estimators. In particular, for dependent estimators, our analysis allows fined-grained analysis of the effect correlations. As a result, under a per-iteration computational budget of $b \times m$, where $b$ is the minibatch size and $m$ is the number of Monte Carlo samples, our analysis suggests where one should invest most of the budget in general. Furthermore, we prove that random reshuffling (RR) improves the complexity dependence on the subsampling noise.

paragraphs: Some learning objectives combine a finite collection of terms, each containing an expectation that cannot be computed directly. Training then involves two kinds of sampling: selecting terms and estimating their expectations. This paper analyzes stochastic gradient descent when both sources of randomness are present, a setting relevant to diffusion models and variational autoencoders.

The authors establish convergence results for independent minibatching and random reshuffling under general conditions. Their framework also permits dependence between the gradient estimators for different components. That matters because correlations can affect optimization behavior, and the analysis makes it possible to examine their effects in finer detail.

The theory also addresses how to distribute a fixed per-iteration computation budget. With minibatch size b and m Monte Carlo samples, the budget scales as b times m; the analysis provides guidance about where additional effort should go. Finally, the authors prove that random reshuffling improves the complexity dependence on subsampling noise. The contribution connects convergence theory to concrete choices about sampling and computational allocation.
summary.tldr: A convergence analysis of doubly stochastic SGD clarifies correlation effects, computation allocation, and the benefits of random reshuffling.

title: Demystifying SGD with Doubly Stochastic Gradients

abstract: We have developed a new framework based on the theory of causal inference to protect language models against backdoor attacks. Backdoor attackers can poison language models with different types of triggers, such as words, sentences, grammar, and style, enabling them to selectively modify the decision-making of the victim model. However, existing defense approaches are only effective when the backdoor attack form meets specific assumptions, making it difficult to counter diverse backdoor attacks. We propose a new defense framework Front-door Adjustment for Backdoor Elimination (FABE) based on causal reasoning that does not rely on assumptions about the form of triggers. This method effectively differentiates between spurious and legitimate associations by creating a ’front door’ that maps out the actual causal relationships. The term ’front door’ refers to a text that retains the semantic equivalence of the initial input, which is generated by an additional, fine-tuned language model, denoted as the defense model. Our defense experiments against various attack methods at the token, sentence, and syntactic levels reduced the attack success rate from 93.63% to 15.12%, improving the defense effect by 2.91 times compared to the best baseline result of 66.61%, achieving state-of-the-art results. Through ablation study analysis, we analyzed the effect of each module in FABE, demonstrating the importance of complying with the front-door criterion and front-door adjustment formula, which also explains why previous methods failed. Our code to reproduce the experiments is available at: https://github.com/lyr17/Frontdoor-Adjustment-Backdoor-Elimination.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks cause a language model to change its decisions when particular triggers appear. Triggers can involve words, sentences, grammar, or style, making defenses tied to a specific trigger form difficult to generalize. FABE approaches this problem through causal inference, aiming to separate legitimate relationships between meaning and predictions from associations introduced by an attacker.

The framework uses an additional fine-tuned language model to produce text with the same meaning as the original input. This text serves as the causal ‘front door’ through which the defense reasons about the input and the model’s decision. The method avoids assumptions about trigger form, while its causal construction still depends on following the front-door criterion and adjustment formula.

In experiments covering token, sentence, and syntactic attacks, FABE reduces attack success from 93.63% to 15.12%. Ablation studies examine the contribution of its modules and support the importance of the causal requirements. These findings indicate substantial protection across the tested attack forms, with the semantic intermediary and causal adjustment jointly central to the reported defense.
summary.tldr: FABE uses a meaning-preserving text intermediary and causal adjustment to reduce language-model backdoor attacks without assuming a particular trigger form.

title: Causality Based Front-door Defense Against Backdoor Attack on Language Models

abstract: We provide an infinite-dimensional view on optimization problems encountered in scientific machine learning (SciML) and advocate for the paradigm first optimize, then discretize for their solution. This amounts to first choosing an appropriate infinite-dimensional algorithm which is then discretized in a second step. To illustrate this point, we discuss recently proposed state-of-the-art algorithms for SciML applications and see that they can be derived within this framework. Hence, this perspective allows for a principled guide for the design of optimization algorithms for SciML. As the infinite-dimensional viewpoint is presently underdeveloped we formalize it here to foster the development of novel optimization algorithms.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that optimization in scientific machine learning should begin with the geometry of the underlying function space. Its proposed order is to choose an optimization algorithm in an infinite-dimensional setting first, then discretize that algorithm to obtain a computational procedure.

The order matters because it makes the function-level problem the starting point for algorithm design. Discretization becomes a later step that translates the chosen procedure into a finite representation. The authors formalize this viewpoint as a principled framework for designing SciML optimization methods, addressing what they describe as an underdeveloped perspective.

To illustrate the argument, the paper discusses recently proposed state-of-the-art SciML algorithms and shows that they can be derived within this framework. Those examples demonstrate how the viewpoint can explain existing methods as well as guide the search for new ones. The contribution is a design position and its formalization, supported by derivations of established approaches rather than a claim that one optimizer is best for every SciML problem.
summary.tldr: The paper advocates designing SciML optimization in function space before discretization and formalizes that approach as an algorithm-design framework.

title: Position: Optimization in SciML Should Employ the Function Space Geometry

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have a natural role in answering complex queries about data streams, but the high computational cost of LLM inference makes them infeasible in many such tasks. We propose online cascade learning, the first approach to address this challenge. The objective here is to learn a “cascade” of models, starting with lower-capacity models (such as logistic regression) and ending with a powerful LLM, along with a deferral policy that determines the model to be used on a given input. We formulate the task of learning cascades online as an imitation-learning problem, where smaller models are updated over time imitating the collected LLM demonstrations, and give a no-regret algorithm for the problem. Experimental results across four benchmarks show that our method parallels LLMs in accuracy while cutting down inference costs by as much as 90% with strong robustness against input distribution shifts, underscoring its efficacy and adaptability in stream processing. Our source code is available at https://github.com/flitternie/online_cascade_learning.
