paragraphs: Answering complex questions about a data stream with a large language model can make inference prohibitively expensive. This paper proposes learning a cascade that begins with smaller models and ends with an LLM. A deferral policy decides which model should handle each input, making model selection part of the system's learned behavior.

The authors formulate online cascade learning as imitation learning. Smaller models are updated over time using collected demonstrations from the LLM, allowing the cascade to learn while processing the stream. They provide a no-regret algorithm for this formulation. The approach therefore combines ongoing training with routing, rather than treating the cheaper models as a fixed set of alternatives.

Across four benchmarks, the method achieves accuracy comparable to the LLM while reducing inference costs by as much as 90%. The experiments also report strong robustness to shifts in the input distribution. These are empirical results for the evaluated settings, supporting the usefulness of continuously learned cascades when a stream must be processed economically without sacrificing much predictive accuracy.
summary.tldr: Online cascades learn smaller models from LLM demonstrations and route inputs to cut inference costs while maintaining comparable benchmark accuracy.

title: Online Cascade Learning for Efficient Inference over Streams

abstract: Multivariate linear regression models are broadly used to facilitate relationships between outcomes and features. However, their effectiveness is compromised by the presence of missing observations, a ubiquitous challenge in real-world applications. Considering a scenario where learners access only limited components for both outcomes and features, we develop efficient algorithms tailored for the least squares ($L_2$) and least absolute ($L_1$) loss functions, each coupled with a ridge-like and Lasso-type penalty, respectively. Moreover, we establish rigorous error bounds for all proposed algorithms. Notably, our $L_2$ loss function algorithms are probably approximately correct (PAC), distinguishing them from their $L_1$ counterparts. Extensive numerical experiments show that our approach outperforms methods that apply existing algorithms for univariate outcome individually to each coordinate of multivariate outcomes in a naive manner. Further, utilizing the $L_1$ loss function or introducing a Lasso-type penalty can enhance predictions in the presence of outliers or high dimensional features. This research contributes valuable insights into addressing the challenges posed by incomplete data.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear regression with multiple outcomes when learners can observe only some components of both the inputs and outputs. Missing information affects the quantities used to predict and the quantities being predicted. The authors develop algorithms specifically for this partially observed, multivariate setting.

The proposed methods use squared-error and absolute-error losses, with ridge-like and Lasso-type penalties as described in the formulation. The authors establish error bounds for all of their algorithms. The squared-error methods additionally have probably approximately correct guarantees, a property that the paper distinguishes from its absolute-error results.

Numerical experiments show improvements over applying existing single-outcome algorithms separately to each output coordinate. This supports treating the multivariate problem with methods designed for its observation constraints. The experiments also indicate that absolute-error loss or a Lasso-type penalty can improve predictions in the presence of outliers or high-dimensional features. These are conditional advantages: the appropriate loss and penalty depend on the data characteristics, while the theoretical results distinguish the guarantees available for the different methods.
summary.tldr: New regression algorithms handle partially observed inputs and multiple outputs, with error bounds and empirical benefits over fitting each output separately.

title: Regression Learning with Limited Observations of Multivariate Outcomes and Features

abstract: Dialog systems, such as voice assistants, are expected to engage with users in complex, evolving conversations. Unfortunately, traditional automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems deployed in such applications are usually trained to recognize each turn independently and lack the ability to adapt to the conversational context or incorporate user feedback. In this work, we introduce a general framework for ASR in dialog systems that can go beyond learning from single-turn utterances and learn over time how to adapt to both explicit supervision and implicit user feedback present in multi-turn conversations. We accomplish that by leveraging advances in student-teacher learning and context-aware dialog processing, and designing contrastive self-supervision approaches with Ohm, a new online hard-negative mining approach. We show that leveraging our new framework compared to traditional training leads to relative WER reductions of close to 10% in real-world dialog systems, and up to 26% on public synthetic data.

paragraphs: Speech recognition in a dialog system is often trained as though every utterance were an isolated event. That overlooks information available across an evolving conversation, including feedback from the user. This paper introduces a framework that lets the recognizer learn over time from multiple turns, using both explicit supervision and implicit conversational feedback.

The framework combines student-teacher learning with dialog processing that takes context into account. It also introduces contrastive self-supervision and an online hard-negative mining method called Ohm. These components provide a way to use conversational information as training signals, extending learning beyond independently labeled utterances. The aim is to improve recognition through interaction rather than treating each new turn as disconnected from previous ones.

Compared with traditional training, the authors report relative word error rate reductions close to 10% in real-world dialog systems and up to 26% on public synthetic data. These are relative reductions in recognition errors, not percentage-point gains in accuracy. The results support the practical value of incorporating context and feedback into speech recognition training.
summary.tldr: A conversational self-learning framework improves speech recognition using context and feedback, reducing real-world word error rates by close to 10% relatively.

title: An Efficient Self-Learning Framework For Interactive Spoken Dialog Systems

abstract: The rapid progress of foundation models has led to the prosperity of autonomous agents, which leverage the universal capabilities of foundation models to conduct reasoning, decision-making, and environmental interaction. However, the efficacy of agents remains limited when operating in intricate, realistic environments. In this work, we introduce the principles of **U**nified **A**lignment for **A**gents (**UA**$^2$), which advocate for the simultaneous alignment of agents with human intentions, environmental dynamics, and self-constraints such as the limitation of monetary budgets. From the perspective of **UA**$^2$, we review the current agent research and highlight the neglected factors in existing agent benchmarks and method candidates. We also conduct proof-of-concept studies by introducing realistic features to WebShop, including user profiles demonstrating intentions, personalized reranking reflecting complex environmental dynamics, and runtime cost statistics as self-constraints. We then follow the principles of **UA**$^2$ to propose an initial design of our agent and benchmark its performance with several candidate baselines in the retrofitted WebShop. The extensive experimental results further prove the importance of the principles of **UA**$^2$. Our research sheds light on the next steps of autonomous agent research with improved general problem-solving abilities.

paragraphs: Autonomous agents built from foundation models can reason, make decisions, and interact with their surroundings, yet they remain limited in complicated realistic environments. This position paper proposes Unified Alignment for Agents, or UA². Its central principle is that agents should simultaneously account for human intentions, environmental dynamics, and their own constraints, including monetary budgets.

The authors use this perspective to review agent research and identify factors neglected by existing benchmarks and candidate methods. They then modify WebShop to include user profiles expressing intentions, personalized reranking representing more complex environmental dynamics, and runtime cost statistics representing constraints on the agent. These additions make the three alignment dimensions explicit in a proof-of-concept setting.

An initial agent design follows the proposed principles and is compared with several baselines in the modified environment. The experimental results support the importance of considering these dimensions together. The paper offers both a research position and an initial demonstration, using a more realistic benchmark to investigate how alignment principles can inform agents with stronger general problem-solving abilities.
summary.tldr: UA² argues for aligning agents jointly with user intentions, environmental dynamics, and resource constraints, supported by proof-of-concept WebShop studies.

title: Position: Towards Unified Alignment Between Agents, Humans, and Environment

abstract: In this paper, we unveil that Language Models (LMs) can acquire new capabilities by assimilating parameters from homologous models without retraining or GPUs. We first introduce DARE to set most delta parameters (i.e., the disparity between fine-tuned and pre-trained parameters) to zeros without affecting the abilities of Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) LMs, which randomly Drops delta parameters with a ratio $p$ And REscales the remaining ones by $1 / (1 - p)$ to approximate the original embeddings. Then, we use DARE as a versatile plug-in to sparsify delta parameters of multiple SFT homologous models for mitigating parameter interference and merge them into a single model by parameter fusing. We experiment with encoder- and decoder-based LMs, showing that: (1) SFT delta parameter value ranges are typically small (within 0.002) with extreme redundancy, and DARE can effortlessly eliminate 90% or even 99% of them; (2) DARE can merge multiple task-specific LMs into one LM with diverse capabilities. Notably, this phenomenon is more pronounced in large-scale LMs, where the merged LM reveals the potential to surpass the performance of any source LM, providing a new discovery. We also utilize DARE to create a merged LM that ranks first among models with 7 billion parameters on the Open LLM Leaderboard.

paragraphs: This paper explores combining capabilities from language models derived from a common pretrained model, without retraining or GPUs. It focuses on delta parameters: the differences between a supervised fine-tuned model and its pretrained starting point. The authors find that these changes are typically small and highly redundant in their experiments.

Their DARE procedure randomly sets a fraction p of those differences to zero, then multiplies the remaining differences by 1/(1−p). This rescaling is intended to approximate the original embeddings. Applying DARE before merging multiple models makes their parameter changes sparse, helping reduce interference when the changes are fused into one model.

Experiments with encoder and decoder models show that DARE can remove 90%, or even 99%, of delta parameters while preserving capabilities in the reported settings. Merging yields models with multiple task-specific abilities, with larger models showing greater potential to outperform their source models. The authors also report a merged model that ranked first among seven-billion-parameter entries on the Open LLM Leaderboard in their evaluation.
summary.tldr: DARE sparsifies fine-tuning changes so related language models can merge capabilities without retraining.

title: Language Models are Super Mario: Absorbing Abilities from Homologous Models as a Free Lunch

abstract: We posit that to achieve superhuman agents, future models require superhuman feedback in order to provide an adequate training signal. Current approaches commonly train reward models from human preferences, which may then be bottlenecked by human performance level, and secondly these reward models require additional human preferences data to further improve.In this work, we study Self-Rewarding Language Models, where the language model itself is used via LLM-as-a-Judge prompting to provide its own rewards during training. We show that during Iterative DPO training, not only does instruction following ability improve, but also the ability to provide high-quality rewards to itself. Fine-tuning Llama 2 70B on three iterations of our approach yields a model that outperforms many existing systems on the AlpacaEval 2.0 leaderboard, including Claude 2, Gemini Pro, and GPT-4 0613. While there is much left still to explore, this work opens the door to the possibility of models that can continually improve in both axes.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a language model can improve both its answers and the feedback used to train it. The motivation is that reward models trained on human preferences may be constrained by human performance and require more preference data to improve further. The authors propose letting the language model itself supply training rewards.

In their approach, the model acts as a judge through prompting, evaluating responses to generate its own reward signal. Training proceeds through iterative Direct Preference Optimization. Across those iterations, the authors observe improvements in instruction following alongside improvements in the model’s ability to provide high-quality rewards for itself.

After three iterations of fine-tuning Llama 2 70B, the resulting model outperforms several systems on AlpacaEval 2.0, including Claude 2, Gemini Pro, and GPT-4 0613. These results support the possibility of jointly improving response generation and reward judgment. The paper presents continual improvement along both dimensions as a promising direction that remains to be explored, rather than an established indefinite process.
summary.tldr: A language model supplies its own training rewards, improving both instruction following and reward judgment over the reported training iterations.

title: Self-Rewarding Language Models

abstract: Scaling the capacity of language models has consistently proven to be a reliable approach for improving performance and unlocking new capabilities. Capacity can be primarily defined by two dimensions: the number of model parameters and the compute per example. While scaling typically involves increasing both, the precise interplay between these factors and their combined contribution to overall capacity remains not fully understood. We explore this relationship in the context of sparse Mixture-of-Expert models (MoEs), which allow scaling the number of parameters without proportionally increasing the FLOPs per example. We investigate how varying the sparsity level, i.e., the ratio of non-active to total parameters, affects model performance in terms of both pretraining and downstream performance. We find that under different constraints (e.g. parameter size and total training compute), there is an optimal level of sparsity that improves both training efficiency and model performance.These results provide a better understanding of the impact of sparsity in scaling laws for MoEs and complement existing works in this area, offering insights for designing more efficient architectures.

paragraphs: Language-model capacity involves both the number of parameters and the computation performed for each example. These usually increase together, making their separate contributions difficult to understand. Sparse mixture-of-experts models provide a way to investigate the relationship because they can add parameters without proportionally increasing the computation used for each example.

The paper varies sparsity, defined as the proportion of total parameters that are inactive, and studies effects on pretraining and downstream performance. It examines this choice under constraints such as model parameter size and total training compute. This framing makes sparsity a resource-allocation decision: how much model capacity should exist, and how much should participate in processing an example?

The authors find an optimal sparsity level under the constraints they investigate, improving both training efficiency and model performance. The result does not prescribe one universal sparsity setting; the relevant optimum depends on the resource constraints. By examining parameters and computation together, the work adds sparsity to the scaling-law picture and offers evidence for designing mixture-of-experts architectures around a specific budget.
summary.tldr: The study finds constraint-dependent optimal sparsity levels that improve mixture-of-experts language-model efficiency and performance.

title: Parameters vs FLOPs: Scaling Laws for Optimal Sparsity for Mixture-of-Experts Language Models

abstract: Synthetic videos nowadays is widely used to complement data scarcity and diversity of real-world videos. Current synthetic datasets primarily replicate real-world scenarios, leaving impossible, counterfactual and anti-reality video concepts underexplored. This work aims to answer two questions: 1) Can today’s video generation models effectively follow prompts to create impossible video content? 2) Are today’s video understanding models good enough for understanding impossible videos? To this end, we introduce IPV-Bench, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate and foster progress in video understanding and generation. IPV-Bench is underpinned by a comprehensive taxonomy, encompassing 4 domains, 14 categories. It features diverse scenes that defy physical, biological, geographical, or social laws. Based on the taxonomy, a prompt suite is constructed to evaluate video generation models, challenging their prompt following and creativity capabilities. In addition, a video benchmark is curated to assess Video-LLMs on their ability of understanding impossible videos, which particularly requires reasoning on temporal dynamics and world knowledge. Comprehensive evaluations reveal limitations and insights for future directions of video models, paving the way for next-generation video models.

paragraphs: Synthetic video datasets commonly imitate situations that could occur in the real world. Impossible Videos asks what happens when models encounter instructions or scenes that deliberately violate that world. It separates two questions: whether video generators can create the requested impossible content, and whether video understanding models can interpret it.

The authors introduce IPV-Bench, organized into four domains and fourteen categories. Its scenes challenge physical, biological, geographical, or social laws. A prompt suite tests generation, emphasizing whether models follow unusual instructions and produce the requested creative content. A separate curated video benchmark evaluates how Video-LLMs understand impossible events.

Understanding these scenes requires reasoning about events over time and drawing on world knowledge to interpret their impossibility. The evaluations reveal limitations in current video models and identify directions for further development. The benchmark's contribution is to make impossible content a structured evaluation target, expanding assessment beyond models' ability to reproduce or recognize familiar real-world scenarios.
summary.tldr: IPV-Bench evaluates whether video models can generate and understand scenes that violate physical, biological, geographical, or social laws.

title: Impossible Videos

abstract: Medical Visual Question Answering (MVQA) requires AI models to answer questions related to medical images, offering significant potential to assist medical professionals in evaluating and diagnosing diseases, thereby improving early interventions. However, existing MVQA datasets primarily focus on basic questions regarding visual perception and pattern recognition, without addressing the more complex questions that are critical in clinical diagnosis and decision-making. This paper introduces a new benchmark designed for professional-level medical reasoning, simulating the decision-making process. We achieve this by collecting MRI and clinical data related to Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy, enriched with expert annotations and insights. Building on this data, we generate clinical question-answer pairs and MRI interpretations to enable comprehensive diagnosis, interpretation, and prediction of neurocognitive outcomes. Our evaluation of current large vision-language models (LVLMs) shows limited performance on this benchmark, highlighting both the challenges of the task and the importance of this benchmark for advancing medical AI. Furthermore, we propose a novel “Clinical Graph of Thoughts" model, which integrates domain-specific medical knowledge and clinical reasoning processes with the interpretive abilities of LVLMs. The model demonstrates promising results, achieving around 15% absolute gain on the most important neurocognitive outcome task, while the benchmark still reveals substantial opportunities for further research innovation.

title: Visual and Domain Knowledge for Professional-level Graph-of-Thought Medical Reasoning

abstract: Discrete Diffusion and Flow Matching models have significantly advanced generative modeling for discrete structures, including graphs. However, the dependencies of the noisy distributions across time of these models lead to error accumulation and propagation during the reverse denoising process—a phenomenon known as compounding denoising errors. To address this problem, we propose a novel framework called Simple Iterative Denoising, which simplifies discrete diffusion and circumvents the issue by removing dependencies on previous intermediate states in the noising process. Additionally, we enhance our model by incorporating a Critic, which during generation selectively retains or corrupts elements in an instance based on their likelihood under the data distribution. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing discrete diffusion baselines in graph generation tasks.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion and flow matching generate structures such as graphs through a sequence of denoising steps. The paper identifies dependencies between noisy distributions over time as a source of compounding errors: mistakes can accumulate and propagate as generation proceeds. It proposes a different construction intended to avoid that mechanism.

Simple Iterative Denoising removes dependence on previous intermediate states in the noising process. This changes how the intermediate noisy examples are related while retaining an iterative denoising framework. The authors further add a Critic that evaluates elements during generation according to their likelihood under the data distribution, selectively keeping some elements and corrupting others.

These two changes address complementary parts of generation: the noising construction removes the identified dependency, and the Critic directs which elements receive further revision. Empirical evaluations show substantial improvements over existing discrete diffusion baselines on graph generation tasks. The findings support reconsidering how intermediate states are constructed and how selective revision is controlled when designing generators for discrete structures.
summary.tldr: Simple Iterative Denoising changes noisy-state dependencies and adds selective Critic-guided revision to improve graph generation.

title: Simple and Critical Iterative Denoising: A Recasting of Discrete Diffusion in Graph Generation

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) training is inherently unstable due to factors such as moving targets and high gradient variance. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) introduce additional challenges. For instance, diverse preferences complicate the alignment process, and prediction errors in a trained reward model can become more severe as the LLM generates unseen outputs. These RL challenges create confusion about whether the probability of an action for a given state should be increased or decreased, similar to the noise in labels for classification tasks. In this work, we focus on RL algorithms that share learning difficulties with cross-entropy loss, especially for low-probability predictions. To enhance stability, we adapt reverse cross-entropy (RCE) from supervised learning for noisy data, defining a symmetric RL loss. We demonstrate performance improvements across various tasks and scales. We conduct experiments in discrete action tasks (Atari games) and continuous action space tasks (MuJoCo benchmark and Box2D) using Symmetric A2C (SA2C) and Symmetric PPO (SPPO). Notably, SPPO shows strong performance across different hyperparameters. Furthermore, we validate the symmetric RL loss in the RLHF framework using PPO for natural language processing tasks such as IMDB positive sentiment and TL;DR summarization.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can receive unstable guidance because targets move and gradients have high variance. Human- or AI-feedback training adds further difficulties, including diverse preferences and reward-model errors on unfamiliar outputs. This paper interprets these problems as ambiguity over whether an action’s probability should increase or decrease, drawing a connection to noisy labels in classification.

The loss is further evaluated with PPO-based human-feedback learning for positive-sentiment generation and summarization. This range of evaluations supports the proposed loss as a way to improve learning robustness across several settings.
summary.tldr: A symmetric reinforcement learning loss adapted from noisy-label learning improves reported performance across control tasks and language-model feedback training.

title: Symmetric Reinforcement Learning Loss for Robust Learning on Diverse Tasks and Model Scales

abstract: Deep tabular models have demonstrated remarkable success on i.i.d. data, excelling in a variety of structured data tasks. However, their performance often deteriorates under temporal distribution shifts, where trends and periodic patterns are present in the evolving data distribution over time. In this paper, we explore the underlying reasons for this failure in capturing temporal dependencies. We begin by investigating the training protocol, revealing a key issue in how the data is split for model training and validation. While existing approaches typically use temporal ordering for splitting, we show that even a random split significantly improves model performance. By accounting for reducing training lag and validation bias to achieve better generalization ability, our proposed splitting protocol offers substantial improvements across a variety of methods. Furthermore, we analyses how temporal data affects deep tabular representations, uncovering that these models often fail to capture crucial periodic and trend information. To address this gap, we introduce a plug-and-play temporal embedding based on Fourier series expansion to learn and incorporate temporal patterns, offering an adaptive approach to handle temporal shifts. Our experiments demonstrate that this temporal embedding, combined with the improved splitting strategy, provides a more effective and robust framework for learning from temporal tabular data.

paragraphs: Deep models for tabular data can perform well when training and evaluation data share a distribution, yet struggle as that distribution changes over time. This paper examines two sources of the problem: how data is divided for training and validation, and whether learned representations retain useful trends and periodic patterns.

The authors find that even a random split can substantially improve performance over commonly used temporally ordered splits in their investigation. Their proposed splitting protocol addresses training lag and validation bias to improve generalization across multiple methods. This makes the training protocol itself an important part of understanding performance under temporal shift.

The representation analysis also finds that deep tabular models often fail to capture important temporal structure. To address that gap, the authors introduce a plug-and-play temporal embedding based on Fourier series expansion. It learns and incorporates temporal patterns into existing methods. Experiments show that combining the embedding with the improved splitting strategy produces more effective and robust learning from temporal tabular data.
summary.tldr: Improved data splitting and a Fourier-based temporal embedding help deep tabular models handle changing trends and periodic patterns.

title: Understanding the Limits of Deep Tabular Methods with Temporal Shift

abstract: Time-series forecasting is crucial across various domains, including finance, healthcare, and energy. Transformer models, originally developed for natural language processing, have demonstrated significant potential in addressing challenges associated with time-series data. These models utilize different tokenization strategies, point-wise, patch-wise, and variate-wise, to represent time-series data, each resulting in different scope of attention maps. Despite the emergence of sophisticated architectures, simpler transformers consistently outperform their more complex counterparts in widely used benchmarks. This study examines why point-wise transformers are generally less effective, why intra- and inter-variate attention mechanisms yield similar outcomes, and which architectural components drive the success of simpler models. By analyzing mutual information and evaluating models on synthetic datasets, we demonstrate that intra-variate dependencies are the primary contributors to prediction performance on benchmarks, while inter-variate dependencies have a minor impact. Additionally, techniques such as Z-score normalization and skip connections are also crucial. However, these results are largely influenced by the self-dependent and stationary nature of benchmark datasets. By validating our findings on real-world healthcare data, we provide insights for designing more effective transformers for practical applications.

These models utilize different tokenization strategies, point-wise, patch-wise, and variate-wise, to represent time-series data, each resulting in different scope of attention maps. Despite the emergence of sophisticated architectures, simpler transformers consistently outperform their more complex counterparts in widely used benchmarks. This study examines why point-wise transformers are generally less effective, why intra- and inter-variate attention mechanisms yield similar outcomes, and which architectural components drive the success of simpler models. By analyzing mutual information and evaluating models on synthetic datasets, we demonstrate that intra-variate dependencies are the primary contributors to prediction performance on benchmarks, while inter-variate dependencies have a minor impact. Additionally, techniques such as Z-score normalization and skip connections are also crucial. However, these results are largely influenced by the self-dependent and stationary nature of benchmark datasets. By validating our findings on real-world healthcare data, we provide insights for designing more effective transformers for practical applications.

paragraphs: This paper examines why relatively simple transformers can outperform more elaborate designs on common time-series forecasting benchmarks. It focuses on how models turn measurements into tokens: individual time points, stretches of time, or separate variables. These choices determine which relationships attention can directly examine and help frame questions about where forecasting gains actually come from.

Using mutual-information analysis and synthetic datasets, the researchers find that relationships within a variable contribute most to benchmark prediction performance. Relationships between different variables contribute comparatively little. They also identify normalization using Z-scores and skip connections as crucial components, showing that attention design alone does not explain the success of simpler models.

The interpretation depends heavily on the data. The benchmark series largely depend on their own histories and have stationary behavior, conditions that favor learning within-variable patterns. The paper also validates its findings on real healthcare data. Its practical contribution is to connect architectural choices to dataset properties, rather than treating benchmark success as evidence that one attention strategy will work equally well everywhere.
summary.tldr: Simple forecasting transformers succeed largely through within-variable dependencies and key architectural components, with results strongly shaped by benchmark properties.

title: A Closer Look at Transformers for Time Series Forecasting: Understanding Why They Work and Where They Struggle

abstract: Do contemporary diffusion models preserve the class geometry of hyperspherical data? Standard diffusion models rely on isotropic Gaussian noise in the forward process, inherently favoring Euclidean spaces. However, many real-world problems involve non-Euclidean distributions, such as hyperspherical manifolds, where class-specific patterns are governed by angular geometry within hypercones. When modeled in Euclidean space, these angular subtleties are lost, leading to suboptimal generative performance. To address this limitation, we introduce HyperSphereDiff to align hyperspherical structures with directional noise, preserving class geometry and effectively capturing angular uncertainty. We demonstrate both theoretically and empirically that this approach aligns the generative process with the intrinsic geometry of hyperspherical data, resulting in more accurate and geometry-aware generative models. We evaluate our framework on four object datasets and two face datasets, showing that incorporating angular uncertainty better preserves the underlying hyperspherical manifold.

The contribution is a geometry-aware diffusion framework supported by evidence for the hyperspherical setting studied.
summary.tldr: HyperSphereDiff uses directional noise to model angular uncertainty and better preserve the geometry of hyperspherical data.

title: Harmonizing Geometry and Uncertainty: Diffusion with Hyperspheres

abstract: Language Models (LMs) are prone to ”memorizing” training data, including substantial sensitive user information. To mitigate privacy risks and safeguard the right to be forgotten, machine unlearning has emerged as a promising approach for enabling LMs to efficiently ”forget” specific texts. However, despite the good intentions, is textual unlearning really as effective and reliable as expected? To address the concern, we first propose Unlearning Likelihood Ratio Attack+ (U-LiRA+), a rigorous textual unlearning auditing method, and find that unlearned texts can still be detected with very high confidence after unlearning. Further, we conduct an in-depth investigation on the privacy risks of textual unlearning mechanisms in deployment and present the Textual Unlearning Leakage Attack (TULA), along with its variants in both black- and white-box scenarios. We show that textual unlearning mechanisms could instead reveal more about the unlearned texts, exposing them to significant membership inference and data reconstruction risks. Our findings highlight that existing textual unlearning actually gives a false sense of unlearning, underscoring the need for more robust and secure unlearning mechanisms.

paragraphs: Textual unlearning aims to make language models forget selected training texts, including sensitive information. This paper examines whether existing methods actually provide the expected privacy protection. Its focus is on whether a text remains detectable after unlearning and whether deploying unlearning mechanisms can expose additional information about the targeted material.

The authors introduce U-LiRA+, an auditing method that finds unlearned texts can still be detected with very high confidence. They then develop the Textual Unlearning Leakage Attack, or TULA, with variants for both black-box and white-box access. These attacks investigate privacy risks under different levels of access to the model.

The findings show that textual unlearning mechanisms could reveal more about the texts they are supposed to remove, creating membership inference and reconstruction risks. Membership inference concerns whether a particular text was present, while reconstruction concerns recovering its content. The paper therefore challenges the reliability of the evaluated unlearning mechanisms and motivates approaches whose privacy claims withstand direct auditing.
summary.tldr: Audits and leakage attacks show that existing textual unlearning can leave texts detectable and may expose additional information about them.

title: Textual Unlearning Gives a False Sense of Unlearning

abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluations typically rely on aggregated metrics like accuracy or human preference, averaging across users and prompts. This averaging obscures user- and prompt-specific variations in model performance. To address this, we propose Prompt-to-Leaderboard (P2L), a method that produces leaderboards specific to a prompt or set of prompts. The core idea is to train an LLM taking natural language prompts as input to output a vector of Bradley-Terry coefficients which are then used to predict the human preference vote. The resulting prompt-dependent leaderboards allow for unsupervised task-specific evaluation, optimal routing of queries to models, personalization, and automated evaluation of model strengths and weaknesses. Data from Chatbot Arena suggest that P2L better captures the nuanced landscape of language model performance than the averaged leaderboard. Furthermore, our findings suggest that P2L’s ability to produce prompt-specific evaluations follows a power law scaling similar to that observed in LLMs themselves. In January 2025, the router we trained based on this methodology achieved the #1 spot on the Chatbot Arena leaderboard. Our code is available at this GitHub link: https://github.com/lmarena/p2l.

paragraphs: A single average leaderboard can hide substantial differences in which language model works best for a particular prompt or user. Prompt-to-Leaderboard, or P2L, addresses this by producing rankings conditioned on a prompt or collection of prompts. The evaluation becomes specific to the request being considered rather than relying entirely on aggregate performance.

P2L trains a language model to convert natural-language prompts into Bradley-Terry coefficients, which are used to predict human preference votes. Those prompt-dependent coefficients provide the basis for the rankings. The authors describe applications including task-specific evaluation, routing requests to models, personalization, and automatic analysis of model strengths and weaknesses.

Chatbot Arena data suggest that these rankings capture performance variation better than an averaged leaderboard. The authors also find evidence suggesting power-law scaling in prompt-specific evaluation ability. A router built with the methodology reached the top position on Chatbot Arena in January 2025. Together, the results support using predicted prompt-level preferences to guide both evaluation and model selection.
summary.tldr: P2L predicts prompt-specific human preferences to create tailored model rankings and support routing, personalization, and evaluation.

title: Prompt-to-Leaderboard: Prompt-Adaptive LLM Evaluations

abstract: Many dynamic decision problems, such as robotic control, involve a series of tasks, many of which are unknown at training time. Typical approaches for these problems, such as multi-task and meta reinforcement learning, do not generalize well when the tasks are diverse. On the other hand, approaches that aim to tackle task diversity, such as using task embedding as policy context and task clustering, typically lack performance guarantees and require a large number of training tasks. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach for learning a policy committee that includes at least one near-optimal policy with high probability for tasks encountered during execution. While we show that this problem is in general inapproximable, we present two practical algorithmic solutions. The first yields provable approximation and task sample complexity guarantees when tasks are low-dimensional (the best we can do due to inapproximability), whereas the second is a general and practical gradient-based approach. In addition, we provide a provable sample complexity bound for few-shot learning. Our experiments on MuJoCo and Meta-World show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art multi-task, meta-, and task clustering baselines in training, generalization, and few-shot learning, often by a large margin. Our code is available at https://github.com/CERL-WUSTL/PACMAN.

paragraphs: Decision-making systems may encounter diverse tasks that were unknown during training. This paper proposes learning a committee of policies so that, with high probability, at least one member is near-optimal for a task encountered during execution. This shifts the learning target toward a collection that covers task diversity.

The authors show that the committee-learning problem is generally inapproximable, then develop two practical approaches. One provides approximation and task sample complexity guarantees when tasks are low-dimensional. The other uses gradient-based learning and is intended as a more general practical solution. The paper also establishes a sample complexity bound for learning from only a few examples.

Experiments on MuJoCo and Meta-World report better training, generalization, and few-shot learning performance than state-of-the-art multi-task, meta-learning, and task-clustering baselines, often by a substantial margin. The theoretical and empirical contributions have distinct scopes: low-dimensional structure enables the stated approximation guarantees, while the broader gradient-based method offers a practical route to building committees. Together, they support policy diversity as a means of preparing for varied future tasks.
summary.tldr: Policy committees aim to cover diverse future tasks with a near-optimal member, combining conditional theoretical guarantees with strong empirical personalization results.

title: Learning Policy Committees for Effective Personalization in MDPs with Diverse Tasks

abstract: Addressing reward design complexities in deep reinforcement learning is facilitated by knowledge transfer across different domains. To this end, we define reward translation to describe the cross-domain reward transfer problem. However, current methods struggle with non-pairable and non-time-alignable incompatible MDPs. This paper presents an adaptable reward translation framework neural reward translation featuring semi-alignable MDPs, which allows efficient reward translation under relaxed constraints while handling the intricacies of incompatible MDPs. Given the inherent difficulty of directly mapping semi-alignable MDPs and transferring rewards, we introduce an indirect mapping method through reward machines, created using limited human input or LLM-based automated learning. Graph-matching techniques establish links between reward machines from distinct environments, thus enabling cross-domain reward translation within semi-alignable MDP settings. This broadens the applicability of DRL across multiple domains. Experiments substantiate our approach’s effectiveness in tasks under environments with semi-alignable MDPs.

paragraphs: Designing reinforcement-learning rewards across different domains can be difficult, motivating reuse of reward knowledge from another environment. This paper calls that transfer problem reward translation. Existing approaches struggle when environments cannot be paired directly or aligned in time, making straightforward correspondence between their Markov decision processes unavailable.

Neural reward translation introduces a semi-alignable setting with relaxed requirements for cross-domain transfer. Because directly mapping the environments remains difficult, the method works indirectly through reward machines. These are created with limited human input or automated learning based on a language model. Graph matching then establishes correspondences between the reward machines associated with different environments.

Those correspondences enable reward transfer within the proposed semi-alignable setting. Experiments demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness on tasks whose environments meet that description. The contribution is a way to mediate reward transfer through a separate representation when direct environmental alignment is problematic. Its scope remains semi-alignable Markov decision processes, extending the available transfer setting without claiming that arbitrary incompatible environments can always share rewards.
summary.tldr: Neural reward translation matches reward machines to transfer rewards between environments that permit only partial alignment.

title: Reward Translation via Reward Machine in Semi-Alignable MDPs

abstract: Scaling video generation models is believed to be promising in building world models that adhere to fundamental physical laws. However, whether these models can discover physical laws purely from vision can be questioned. A world model learning the true law should give predictions robust to nuances and correctly extrapolate on unseen scenarios. In this work, we evaluate across three key scenarios: in-distribution, out-of-distribution, and combinatorial generalization. We developed a 2D simulation testbed for object movement and collisions to generate videos deterministically governed by one or more classical mechanics laws. We focus on the scaling behavior of training diffusion-based video generation models to predict object movements based on initial frames. Our scaling experiments show perfect generalization within the distribution, measurable scaling behavior for combinatorial generalization, but failure in out-of-distribution scenarios. Further experiments reveal two key insights about the generalization mechanisms of these models: (1) the models fail to abstract general physical rules and instead exhibit "case-based" generalization behavior, i.e., mimicking the closest training example; (2) when generalizing to new cases, models are observed to prioritize different factors when referencing training data: color $>$ size $>$ velocity $>$ shape. Our study suggests that scaling alone is insufficient for video generation models to uncover fundamental physical laws.

paragraphs: Predicting convincing motion does not by itself establish that a video model has learned physical laws. This paper tests whether diffusion-based video generators can extrapolate physical behavior from visual training data. The authors construct a two-dimensional simulation environment in which object movements and collisions follow one or more classical mechanics laws.

Models receive initial frames and predict subsequent motion. Scaling experiments distinguish examples within the training distribution, unfamiliar combinations, and examples outside the distribution. The authors report perfect generalization within the distribution and measurable scaling behavior for new combinations, but failure on out-of-distribution scenarios. Those differences separate successful prediction in familiar settings from broader physical extrapolation.

Their apparent priorities when choosing reference cases are color, then size, velocity, and shape. The findings suggest that scaling alone is insufficient for uncovering fundamental physical laws in these models, even when it produces strong performance on familiar forms of motion.
summary.tldr: Controlled physics experiments suggest that scaled video generators imitate familiar cases but fail to extrapolate general physical laws.

title: How Far Is Video Generation from World Model: A Physical Law Perspective

abstract: Large language models often struggle with length generalization and solving complex problem instances beyond their training distribution. We present a self-improvement approach where models iteratively generate and learn from their own solutions, progressively tackling harder problems while maintaining a standard transformer architecture. Across diverse tasks including arithmetic, string manipulation, and maze solving, our method enables models to solve problems far beyond their initial training distribution—for instance, generalizing from 10-digit to 100-digit addition without apparent saturation. We observe that filtering for correct self-generated examples leads to exponential improvements in out-of-distribution performance across training rounds. Additionally, starting from pretrained models significantly accelerates this self-improvement process for several tasks. Our results demonstrate how controlled weak-to-strong curricula can systematically expand model capabilities while preserving architectural simplicity.

paragraphs: A transformer trained on easier or shorter problems can struggle when inputs become much longer or more complex. This paper investigates an iterative learning process in which a model generates solutions and then learns from its own outputs. The difficulty of the problems increases progressively while the transformer architecture remains standard.

Filtering for correct generated examples is central to the approach. Across training rounds, the authors observe exponential improvements in performance outside the original training distribution when using this filtering. The curriculum therefore depends on controlling which self-generated examples become training material as the model moves toward harder problems.

Experiments span arithmetic, string manipulation, and maze solving. One reported example extends addition from 10-digit training problems to 100-digit problems without apparent saturation. Starting from pretrained models also speeds up self-improvement on several tasks. These results show that a controlled progression from weaker to stronger capabilities can substantially expand what the evaluated models solve. The advance comes through the iterative training curriculum while preserving the simplicity of the underlying architecture.
summary.tldr: Transformers trained iteratively on filtered self-generated solutions learn to solve substantially longer and harder problems.

title: Self-Improving Transformers Overcome Easy-to-Hard and Length Generalization Challenges

abstract: Sparsifying neural networks often suffers from seemingly inevitable performance degradation, and it remains challenging to restore the original performance despite much recent progress. Motivated by recent studies in robust optimization, we aim to tackle this problem by finding subnetworks that are both sparse and flat at the same time. Specifically, we formulate pruning as a sparsity-constrained optimization problem where flatness is encouraged as an objective. We solve it explicitly via an augmented Lagrange dual approach and extend it further by proposing a generalized projection operation, resulting in novel pruning methods called SAFE and its extension, SAFE$^+$. Extensive evaluations on standard image classification and language modeling tasks reveal that SAFE consistently yields sparse networks with improved generalization performance, which compares competitively to well-established baselines. In addition, SAFE demonstrates resilience to noisy data, making it well-suited for real-world conditions.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces the number of active parameters in a neural network, but the resulting sparse model often loses performance. This paper approaches pruning as a search for subnetworks that are simultaneously sparse and located at flat minima. Flatness makes the optimization landscape around the chosen solution part of the pruning objective.

The authors formulate the task as constrained optimization: sparsity is an explicit constraint, and flatness is encouraged by the objective. They solve this formulation using an augmented Lagrange dual approach. A generalized projection operation extends the method, producing the two proposed pruning procedures, SAFE and SAFE+.

Evaluations cover standard image-classification and language-modeling tasks. SAFE consistently produces sparse networks with improved generalization and performs competitively against established baselines. The authors also report resilience to noisy data. These findings support combining sparsity and flatness within the pruning process as a way to improve the behavior of the resulting subnetworks. The reported gains address the performance challenge of pruning without claiming that every pruned model fully recovers its original performance.
summary.tldr: SAFE jointly targets sparsity and flatness to produce pruned networks with improved generalization and resilience to noisy data.

title: SAFE: Finding Sparse and Flat Minima to Improve Pruning

abstract: Diffusion models excel in high-fidelity image generation but face scalability limits due to transformers’ quadratic attention complexity. Plug-and-play token reduction methods like ToMeSD and ToFu reduce FLOPs by merging redundant tokens in generated images but rely on GPU-inefficient operations (e.g., sorting, scattered writes), introducing overheads that negate theoretical speedups when paired with optimized attention implementations (e.g., FlashAttention). To bridge this gap, we propose Token Merge with Attention (ToMA), an off-the-shelf method that redesigns token reduction for GPU-aligned efficiency, with three key contributions: 1) a reformulation of token merging as a submodular optimization problem to select diverse tokens; 2) merge/unmerge as an attention-like linear transformation via GPU-friendly matrix operations; and 3) exploiting latent locality and sequential redundancy (pattern reuse) to minimize overhead. ToMA reduces SDXL/Flux generation latency by 24%/23% (DINO $\Delta <$ 0.07), outperforming prior methods. This work bridges the gap between theoretical and practical efficiency for transformers in diffusion.

paragraphs: Reducing image tokens can lower the arithmetic cost of attention in diffusion models, but it does not automatically shorten generation time. This paper identifies sorting and scattered writes as sources of overhead in earlier token-merging methods. Those costs can cancel theoretical savings when the model already uses optimized attention implementations such as FlashAttention.

It formulates token selection as a submodular optimization problem to choose diverse tokens, then expresses merging and unmerging as attention-like linear transformations using matrix operations. It also uses latent locality and reuses patterns across sequential computation to reduce additional overhead.

The method is intended for off-the-shelf use. Reported generation latency falls by 24% for SDXL and 23% for Flux, with DINO changes below 0.07, outperforming prior methods. The contribution is the connection between token-reduction design and actual execution costs: the measured benefit comes from making the reduction procedure efficient enough to preserve its savings during image generation.
summary.tldr: ToMA uses GPU-friendly token merging to reduce SDXL and Flux generation latency by 24% and 23%, respectively.

title: ToMA: Token Merge with Attention for Diffusion Models

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown promising progress in understanding and analyzing video content. However, processing long videos remains a significant challenge constrained by LLM’s context size. To address this limitation, we propose LongVU, a spatiotemporal adaptive compression mechanism that reduces the number of video tokens while preserving visual details of long videos. Our idea is based on leveraging cross-modal query and inter-frame dependencies to adaptively reduce temporal and spatial redundancy in videos. Specifically, we leverage DINOv2 features to remove redundant frames that exhibit high similarity. Then we utilize text-guided cross-modal query for selective frame feature reduction. Further, we perform spatial token reduction across frames based on their temporal dependencies. Our adaptive compression strategy effectively processes a large number of frames with little visual information loss within given context length. Our LongVU consistently surpass existing methods across a variety of video understanding benchmarks, especially on hour-long video understanding tasks such as VideoMME and MLVU. Given a light-weight LLM, our LongVU also scales effectively into a smaller size with state-of-the-art video understanding performance.

paragraphs: Long videos can produce more visual tokens than a language model’s context window can accommodate. LongVU addresses this by compressing video representations across both time and space while preserving useful visual detail. Its central idea is to use the text query and relationships between frames to identify information that can be reduced.

The process first uses DINOv2 features to remove frames that are highly similar to others. It then applies a text-guided cross-modal query to selectively reduce frame features. A further stage reduces spatial tokens across frames according to their temporal dependencies. These steps target different sources of redundancy within the same limited context budget.

The reported results show that LongVU processes many frames with little visual information loss and consistently outperforms existing methods across the evaluated video-understanding benchmarks. Gains are especially strong on hour-long video tasks in VideoMME and MLVU. The method also works effectively with a lightweight language model, supporting smaller systems while retaining strong video-understanding performance.
summary.tldr: LongVU compresses redundant video information using text queries and frame relationships to improve long-video understanding within limited context.

title: LongVU: Spatiotemporal Adaptive Compression for Long Video-Language Understanding

abstract: Recent studies indicate that when faced with explicit biases in prompts, models often omit mentioning these biases in their Chain-of-Thought (CoT) output, revealing that verbalized reasoning can give an incorrect picture of how models arrive at conclusions (unfaithfulness). In this work, we show that unfaithful CoT also occurs on naturally worded, non-adversarial prompts without adding artificial biases or editing model outputs. We find that when separately presented with the questions "Is X bigger than Y?" and "Is Y bigger than X?", models sometimes produce superficially coherent arguments to justify systematically answering Yes to both or No to both, despite the contradiction. We present preliminary evidence that this is due to models’ implicit biases towards Yes or No, labeling this Implicit Post-Hoc Rationalization. Our results reveal rates up to 13% for production models, and while frontier models are more faithful, none are entirely so, including thinking models like DeepSeek R1 (0.37%) and Sonnet 3.7 with thinking (0.04%). We also investigate Unfaithful Illogical Shortcuts, where models use subtly illogical reasoning to make speculative answers to hard math problems seem rigorously proven. Our findings indicate that while CoT can be useful for assessing outputs, it is not a complete account of the internal process that produced the model’s answer and should be used with caution in agentic or safety-critical settings.

paragraphs: A plausible written explanation does not necessarily faithfully describe how a language model reached its answer. This paper investigates that problem using naturally phrased prompts, without inserting artificial biases or modifying model outputs. It shows that failures of faithful reasoning can arise in ordinary-looking questions.

One test separately asks whether one item is bigger than another and then reverses their order. Models sometimes give the same yes-or-no response to both questions and supply coherent-looking justifications for the contradiction. The authors present preliminary evidence that an implicit preference for answering yes or no drives this behavior, which they call Implicit Post-Hoc Rationalization.

Reported rates reach 13% for production models. Frontier models perform better, but the tested systems are not entirely free of the behavior; examples include 0.37% for DeepSeek R1 and 0.04% for Sonnet 3.7 with thinking. The paper also examines subtly invalid mathematical arguments that make speculative answers look proven. These findings support treating reasoning traces as useful evidence about outputs, while recognizing that they provide an incomplete account of the process producing an answer.
summary.tldr: Naturally phrased questions can elicit contradictory answers with plausible explanations, showing that reasoning traces are not always faithful.

title: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning In The Wild Is Not Always Faithful

abstract: The increasing situational awareness of language models raises safety concerns: models might be aware when they are evaluated, and adjust their behavior to evade monitoring and resist modification, e.g., pretending to be aligned only in evaluation. This alignment faking behavior is often interpreted as scheming: an intentional effort of strategic deception. In this paper, we examine an alternative interpretation, performative misalignment, which explains the change in behavior as a result of sycophancy towards AI researchers. To examine this hypothesis, we present three empirical findings. First, we show that evaluation awareness persists even when we tell models they are deployed, which contradicts the scheming story which predicts less misalignment when the model perceives evaluation. Second, we use probing and steering to show that our current methods cannot mechanistically distinguish sycophancy and scheming in alignment faking evaluations. Third, we fine-tune models to be more sycophantic and observe increased sensitivity to evaluation cues. To conclude, we emphasize deconfounding sycophancy from scheming for future work on evaluations and mitigations of intent misalignment.

paragraphs: When a language model changes its behavior around evaluation, the change is sometimes interpreted as deliberate strategic deception. This paper examines another explanation: the model may be responding sycophantically to AI researchers and performing the behavior it associates with their expectations. The authors call this alternative performative misalignment.

Three empirical findings support investigating that explanation. Evaluation awareness persists even when models are told they are deployed, challenging the scheming account considered in the paper. Probing and steering also fail to mechanistically separate sycophancy from scheming using the authors’ current methods. Finally, fine-tuning models to become more sycophantic increases their sensitivity to evaluation cues.

Together, these findings identify a confound in interpreting alignment-faking evaluations. Behavior that appears strategically deceptive may also be consistent with responsiveness to perceived researcher expectations. The paper therefore calls for separating these explanations when designing evaluations and mitigations of intent misalignment. Its evidence supports taking sycophancy seriously as an alternative explanation, rather than establishing that every apparent case of scheming has that cause.
summary.tldr: Sycophancy toward researchers can confound interpretations of behavior that appears to demonstrate alignment faking.

title: Sycophancy Towards Researchers Drives Performative Misalignment

abstract: Kronecker adapters have emerged as a promising approach for fine-tuning large-scale models, enabling high-rank updates through tunable component structures. However, existing work largely treats the component structure as a fixed or heuristic design choice, leaving the dimensions and number of Kronecker components underexplored. In this paper, we identify component structure as a key factor governing the capacity of Kronecker adapters. We perform a fine-grained analysis of both the dimensions and number of Kronecker components. In particular, we show that the alignment between Kronecker adapters and full fine-tuning depends on component configurations. Guided by these insights, we propose Component Designed Kronecker Adapters (CDKA). We further provide parameter-budget–aware configuration guidelines and a tailored training stabilization strategy for practical deployment. Experiments across various architectures and modalities demonstrate the effectiveness of CDKA. Code is available at https://github.com/rainstonee/CDKA.

paragraphs: Kronecker adapters provide a way to fine-tune large models through structured updates that can have high rank. Their structure is built from configurable components, but previous work has often chosen those components using fixed rules or heuristics. This paper examines how those choices affect what an adapter can learn.

The analysis separates two design decisions: the dimensions of the components and the number of components used. The authors identify both as important to adapter capacity and show that configuration affects alignment with full fine-tuning. Thus, the structure of the update is a substantive modeling choice, rather than merely an implementation detail.

These findings motivate Component Designed Kronecker Adapters, or CDKA. The method includes configuration guidance that takes the available parameter budget into account, together with a training stabilization strategy tailored to the adapters. Experiments across multiple architectures and modalities demonstrate its effectiveness. The practical contribution is a more systematic basis for designing adapter components under resource constraints, linking configuration decisions to their ability to approximate the behavior of full fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: CDKA systematically designs Kronecker adapter components to improve fine-tuning capacity within a parameter budget.

title: Diving into Kronecker Adapters: Component Design Matters

abstract: We consider imitation learning in the low-data regime, where only a limited number of expert demonstrations are available. In this setting, methods that rely on large-scale pretraining or high-capacity architectures can be difficult to apply, and efficiency with respect to demonstration data becomes critical. We introduce Noise-Guided Transport (NGT), a lightweight off-policy method that casts imitation as an optimal transport problem solved via adversarial training. NGT requires no pretraining or specialized architectures, incorporates uncertainty estimation by design, and is easy to implement and tune. Despite its simplicity, NGT achieves strong performance on challenging continuous control tasks, including high-dimensional Humanoid tasks, under ultra-low data regimes with as few as 20 transitions.

paragraphs: Imitation learning becomes especially challenging when only a small amount of expert behavior is available. In this setting, methods built around extensive pretraining or high-capacity architectures can be difficult to apply. Noise-Guided Transport focuses on extracting useful behavior from limited demonstrations with a lightweight learning method that avoids those requirements.

The method formulates imitation as an optimal transport problem and solves it through adversarial training. It is off-policy, includes uncertainty estimation in its design, and requires neither pretraining nor a specialized architecture. The authors also describe it as easy to implement and tune, emphasizing a combination of data efficiency and a relatively simple learning setup.

Despite that simplicity, experiments show strong performance on challenging continuous-control problems, including high-dimensional Humanoid tasks. The reported ultra-low-data settings include demonstrations containing as few as 20 transitions. These findings indicate that a transport-based adversarial formulation can be effective with extremely sparse expert data in the tested tasks, making it a useful approach to imitation when demonstrations are the central constraint.
summary.tldr: Noise-Guided Transport learns continuous-control behavior from very limited demonstrations using a lightweight adversarial transport formulation.

title: Noise-Guided Transport: Imitation Learning from Random Priors

abstract: We propose a novel framework for measuring privacy from a Bayesian game-theoretic perspective. This framework enables the creation of new, purpose-driven privacy definitions that are rigorously justified, while also allowing for the assessment of existing privacy guarantees through game theory. We show that pure and probabilistic differential privacy are special cases of our framework, and provide new interpretations of the post-processing inequality in these settings. Further, we demonstrate that privacy guarantees can be established for deterministic algorithms, which are overlooked by current privacy standards.

paragraphs: This paper proposes measuring privacy through a Bayesian game-theoretic framework. Its goal is to support privacy definitions tailored to particular purposes while providing rigorous justification for them. The same framework also offers a way to assess established privacy guarantees, connecting the design of new definitions with the interpretation of existing ones.

The authors show that pure and probabilistic differential privacy fit within their framework as special cases. They also derive new interpretations of the post-processing inequality in these settings. These connections matter because they anchor the broader framework in recognized privacy notions while allowing those notions to be understood from a common game-theoretic perspective.

The paper further establishes that privacy guarantees can be given for deterministic algorithms, a category overlooked by current privacy standards according to the abstract. This result expands the kinds of algorithms that the framework can assess. It does not say that every deterministic algorithm is private; the contribution is a framework capable of rigorously establishing such guarantees where its purpose-driven definitions support them.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian game-theoretic framework unifies established privacy notions and supports purpose-driven guarantees, including for deterministic algorithms.

title: Persuasive Privacy

abstract: Sampling from a distribution $p(x) \propto e^{-\mathcal{E}(x)}$ known up to a normalising constant is an important and challenging problem in statistics. Recent years have seen the rise of a new family of amortised sampling algorithms, commonly referred to as diffusion samplers, that enable fast and efficient sampling from an unnormalised density. Such algorithms have been widely studied for continuous-space sampling tasks; however, their application to problems in discrete space remains largely unexplored. Although some progress has been made in this area, discrete diffusion samplers do not take full advantage of ideas commonly used for continuous-space sampling. In this paper, we propose to bridge this gap by introducing off-policy training techniques for discrete diffusion samplers. We show that these techniques improve the performance of discrete samplers on both established and new synthetic benchmarks. Next, we generalise discrete diffusion samplers to the task of bridging between two arbitrary distributions, introducing data-to-energy Schrödinger bridge training for the discrete domain for the first time. Lastly, we showcase the application of the proposed diffusion samplers to data-free posterior sampling in the discrete latent spaces of image generative models.

paragraphs: Many statistical problems specify how plausible each outcome is without supplying the normalization needed to turn those scores into probabilities. Diffusion samplers learn a reusable process for drawing samples from such distributions. This paper develops that approach for discrete spaces, where outcomes take distinct values and techniques developed for continuous sampling have been less fully explored.

The main contribution introduces off-policy training techniques for discrete diffusion samplers, bringing a training idea used in continuous-space sampling into the discrete setting. Experiments on established and newly introduced synthetic benchmarks show improved sampler performance. The focus is on improving how the sampling process is learned, so the learned process can subsequently generate samples efficiently.

The authors also extend the framework to connect two arbitrary distributions through discrete diffusion bridges. They introduce discrete data-to-energy Schrödinger bridge training and demonstrate data-free posterior sampling inside the discrete latent spaces of image generators. Together, these contributions expand discrete diffusion from sampling a single energy-defined target toward learning connections between distributions and supporting inference within generative models.
summary.tldr: Off-policy training improves discrete diffusion samplers, while new bridge formulations extend them to distribution matching and latent-space posterior sampling.

title: Discrete Diffusion Samplers and Bridges: Off-Policy Algorithms and Applications in Latent Spaces

abstract: Classical sample complexity bounds for causal structure learning are minimax in nature, characterizing worst-case difficulty without distinguishing between easy and hard instances. We study instance-specific complexity for Markov equivalence class (MEC) recovery in linear Gaussian structural equation models. We introduce the Fisher dimension, defined as the inverse squared minimum partial correlation that must be detected to recover the MEC. We prove that the Fisher dimension governs sample complexity: it provides both a lower bound and an upper bound (tight up to logarithmic factors) for MEC recovery. A key theoretical finding is that under spectrally well-conditioned models, with bounded noise variances, bounded covariance eigenvalues, and constant-order edge coefficients, the Fisher dimension is uniformly bounded regardless of graph structure. Thus, significant instance-specific variation arises from parametric rather than structural features. Empirical validation shows strong correlation between our predictor and observed sample complexity for structured graph families.

paragraphs: Worst-case sample-complexity bounds say how difficult causal discovery can become, but do not distinguish easy instances from hard ones. This paper studies that distinction for recovering a Markov equivalence class in linear Gaussian structural equation models. The target is a class of observationally equivalent causal structures, rather than necessarily one uniquely identified directed graph.

The proposed Fisher dimension is the inverse square of the smallest partial correlation that must be detected for recovery. A smaller essential signal therefore corresponds to a larger complexity measure. The authors prove upper and lower sample-complexity bounds governed by this quantity, matching up to logarithmic factors.

Under bounded noise variances, bounded covariance eigenvalues, and constant-order edge coefficients in spectrally well-conditioned models, the Fisher dimension remains uniformly bounded regardless of graph structure. Within this setting, substantial variation in instance difficulty comes from numerical parameters rather than structure alone. Experiments on structured graph families find a strong correlation between the proposed measure and the amount of data actually required for recovery.
summary.tldr: The Fisher dimension characterizes instance-specific data requirements for causal equivalence-class recovery through the weakest partial correlation that must be detected.

title: The Fisher Dimension: Instance-Dependent Complexity for Causal Discovery

abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the standard approach for post-training large language models (LLMs), yet it often shows limited generalization. We trace this limitation to its default training objective: negative log likelihood (NLL). While NLL is classically optimal when training from scratch, post-training operates in a different paradigm and could violate its optimality assumptions, where models already encode task-relevant priors and supervision can be long and noisy. In this work, we systematically study various probability-based objectives and characterize when and why different objectives succeed or fail under varying conditions. Through comprehensive experiments and extensive ablation studies across 8 model backbones, 27 benchmarks, and 7 domains, we uncover a critical dimension that governs objective behavior: the model-capability continuum. Near the model-strong end, prior-leaning objectives that downweight low-probability tokens (e.g., $-p$, $-p^{10}$, thresholded variants) consistently outperform NLL; toward the model-weak end, NLL dominates; in between, no single objective prevails. Our theoretical analysis further elucidates how objectives trade places across the continuum, providing a principled foundation for adapting objectives to model capability. The code is available at https://github.com/GaotangLi/Beyond-Log-Likelihood.
