paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning usually trains a language model to increase the likelihood of supplied answers through negative log likelihood, or NLL. This paper questions whether that default remains appropriate when a model already has relevant knowledge and its supervision may be lengthy or noisy. The assumptions supporting NLL when training from scratch may not hold in this setting.

The authors compare probability-based objectives across eight model backbones, 27 benchmarks, and seven domains. Their central finding is a capability continuum. When the model is already strong, objectives that reduce the influence of low-probability tokens consistently outperform NLL. When the model is weak, NLL performs best. Between these ends, no objective consistently wins.

The paper supplements these experiments with theoretical analysis explaining why objectives exchange advantages as capability changes. The practical implication is conditional: the training objective should reflect how much useful task knowledge the model already possesses. The findings support adapting fine-tuning to model capability, rather than treating a successful objective at one point on the continuum as universally preferable.
summary.tldr: The best fine-tuning objective depends on model capability: prior-leaning losses favor stronger models, while negative log likelihood favors weaker ones.

title: Beyond Log Likelihood: Probability-Based Objectives for Supervised Fine-Tuning across the Model Capability Continuum

abstract: Long-context understanding remains challenging for LLMs due to limited context windows. This paper introduces Long Input Fine-Tuning (LIFT), a framework that improves the long-context performance of arbitrary short-context LLMs by dynamically adapting their parameters to each long input. Instead of endlessly extending context windows to fit longer inputs in context, LIFT stores and absorbs the input in parameters. By fine-tuning long inputs into parameters, LIFT enables short-context LLMs to answer questions even when required information is absent from the inference context, avoiding the quadratic input-length complexity of standard long-context models. Rather than simple continued pretraining on new long contexts, LIFT uses carefully designed LLM-generated synthetic tasks to enhance comprehension beyond memorization. To offset fine-tuning overhead, we design a highly optimized pipeline that reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) to under 10 seconds for 8k context. We further analyze LIFT’s strengths and limitations, discuss large-scale deployment feasibility, and highlight future research directions. Implementation is open-sourced at https://github.com/MuLabPKU/LIFT.

paragraphs: LIFT addresses long-input understanding by adapting a language model’s parameters to each input. A short-context model can then answer questions using information absorbed during fine-tuning, even when that information is absent from the context provided at inference. The framework offers a way to handle long inputs through parameter updates.

The training process goes beyond continuing ordinary pretraining on the input text. LIFT uses specially designed synthetic tasks generated by a language model to promote comprehension beyond memorization. This is central to the approach: storing information in parameters must support answering questions about it, rather than merely retaining pieces of the original text.

The authors state that this approach avoids the quadratic input-length complexity of standard long-context models, while introducing fine-tuning overhead of its own. An optimized pipeline reduces time to the first output token to under ten seconds for an 8,000-token context. The paper also examines deployment feasibility and the framework’s strengths and limitations. Its contribution connects per-input learning with an implementation designed to make that adaptation more practical.
summary.tldr: LIFT fine-tunes short-context models on each long input, using synthetic tasks to make its information available through model parameters.

title: LIFT: A Novel Framework for Enhancing Long-Context Understanding of LLMs via Long Input Fine-Tuning

abstract: Recently, cross-modal hashing (CMH) has garnered significant attention due to its low storage costs and high retrieval efficiency. Most existing CMH methods implicitly assume the availability of high-quality annotations, which is often violated in real-world scenarios as label noise inevitably arises from human errors or non-expert annotations. To cope with noisy supervision, current noise-robust CMH methods mainly follow two paradigms, i.e., noise separation and label smoothing. They often discard the predicted noisy instances or smooth discriminative signals to mitigate the impact of noisy labels. However, aggressive separation leads to reduced data utilization, while smoothing weakens the discriminative capability regarding the true distribution of clean instances. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Robust Fuzzy Cross-modal Hashing framework (RFCMH) that introduces fuzzy set theory to endow the labels with admissibility, thereby obtaining reliable discriminative supervision from noisy labels. Specifically, we first leverage possibility and necessity measures to model the noisy labels. Subsequently, we propose Fuzzy Admissibility Refinement (FAR) to dynamically calibrate supervision signals, thereby preventing the model from being misled by false positives. Furthermore, we introduce Dual-Granularity Structural Alignment (DGSA) to enforce both cross-modal alignment and instance-level uniformity, ensuring stable and diverse representations. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that RFCMH achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance. Code is available at https://github.com/XinchengSun/RFCMH.

paragraphs: Cross-modal hashing supports efficient retrieval across different data types using compact representations. Training commonly assumes reliable labels, but annotation errors can undermine the similarity relationships a model learns. Existing responses include discarding suspected noisy examples or smoothing labels, which can respectively waste training data or weaken useful distinctions.

Robust Fuzzy Cross-modal Hashing treats supervision through fuzzy-set admissibility. Possibility and necessity measures represent noisy labels, and Fuzzy Admissibility Refinement dynamically adjusts the resulting supervision. This provides a way to retain discriminative information while reducing the influence of false-positive labels, rather than relying solely on removing examples or broadly softening their targets.

A second component, Dual-Granularity Structural Alignment, combines alignment across modalities with uniformity at the instance level. Together, these objectives aim to produce representations that remain consistent across data types while retaining diversity among examples. Experiments on multiple benchmarks report state-of-the-art retrieval performance. The findings support handling uncertain supervision and representation structure jointly when learning compact cross-modal retrieval codes.
summary.tldr: RFCMH uses fuzzy label admissibility and structural alignment to learn reliable cross-modal retrieval codes from noisy supervision.

title: Learning with Admissibility: Robust Fuzzy Hashing for Cross-Modal Retrieval with Noisy Labels

abstract: Real-time satellite video tracking poses distinct challenges, including accommodating high spatial-temporal resolution, dynamic backgrounds, and constrained onboard computational resources. While Discriminative Correlation Filter (DCF)-based methods offer high-speed inference, they suffer from limited accuracy. In contrast, Vision Transformer (ViT)-based trackers achieve strong performance by unifying representation and aggregation in a single-stream design, yet their heavy computational footprint limits practical deployment in real-time satellite scenarios. In this work, we present FATrack, a novel tracking framework that effectively balances tracking accuracy and computational efficiency. At its core is FA-ViT, a lightweight Vision Transformer backbone that introduces foreground-aware token routing, enabling the model to concentrate computation on target-relevant regions while suppressing redundancy. To mitigate semantic degradation caused by token sparsification, we propose the Adaptive Scatter Module (ASM), which selectively reinforces informative tokens via joint spatial-channel attention and sparse structural propagation, thereby enhancing both semantic fidelity and spatial coherence. By synergistically integrating FA-ViT and ASM, FATrack forms a unified architecture that delivers real-time performance with significantly improved tracking precision. Extensive evaluations on multiple satellite video benchmarks demonstrate that FATrack surpasses existing real-time trackers in accuracy and achieves inference efficiency comparable to DCF-based methods, highlighting its potential for practical deployment in large-scale aerial video tracking systems.

Extensive evaluations on multiple satellite video benchmarks demonstrate that FATrack surpasses existing real-time trackers in accuracy and achieves inference efficiency comparable to DCF-based methods, highlighting its potential for practical deployment in large-scale aerial video tracking systems.

paragraphs: Satellite video tracking must follow targets amid changing backgrounds while processing high-resolution video with limited onboard computation. Fast correlation-filter trackers sacrifice accuracy, while stronger vision-transformer trackers can be too computationally demanding. FATrack aims to combine precise tracking with the speed needed for real-time satellite use.

Its lightweight transformer backbone routes tokens according to their relevance to the foreground target, concentrating computation on useful regions and suppressing redundant processing. Sparsifying tokens can damage the information and spatial relationships needed for tracking. FATrack therefore adds an Adaptive Scatter Module, which reinforces informative tokens using joint spatial-channel attention and sparse structural propagation to preserve semantic content and spatial coherence.

Across multiple satellite video benchmarks, FATrack exceeds existing real-time trackers in accuracy while achieving inference efficiency comparable to correlation-filter methods. The results support pairing selective computation with a mechanism that maintains information quality after sparsification. The paper presents this balance as evidence of potential for practical aerial tracking deployment, with the demonstrated performance grounded in its benchmark evaluations.
summary.tldr: FATrack concentrates transformer computation on target-relevant regions while reinforcing sparse features to deliver accurate real-time satellite tracking.

title: Foreground-Aware Token Routing Vision Transformer for Real-Time Satellite Video Tracking

abstract: Generating realistic 3D Human-Object Interactions (HOI) is a fundamental task for applications ranging from embodied AI to virtual content creation, which requires harmonizing high-level semantic intent with strict low-level physical constraints. Existing methods excel at semantic alignment, however, they struggle to maintain precise object contact. We reveal a key finding termed $\textit{Geometric Forgetting}$: as diffusion model depth increases, semantic feature tend to overshadow object geometry feature, causing the model to lose its perception to object geometry. To address this, we propose MaMi-HOI, a hierarchical framework reconciling Macro-level kinematic fluidity with Micro-level spatial precision. First, to counteract geometric forgetting, we introduce the Geometry-Aware Proximity Adapter (GAPA), which explicitly re-injects dense object details to perform residual snapping corrections for precise contact. Nevertheless, such aggressive local enforcement can disrupt global dynamics, leading to robotic stiffness. In response, we introduce the Kinematic Harmony Adapter (KHA), which proactively aligns whole-body posture with spatial objectives, ensuring the skeleton actively accommodates constraints without compromising naturalness. Extensive experiments validate that MaMi-HOI simultaneously achieves natural motion and precise contact. Crucially, it extends generation capabilities to long-term tasks with complex trajectories, effectively bridging the gap between global navigation and high-fidelity manipulation in 3D scenes.

The authors also demonstrate generation of longer tasks with complex trajectories, extending the approach to interactions that combine movement through a scene with detailed object manipulation. This connects whole-body navigation and local contact within the same generation framework.
summary.tldr: MaMi-HOI coordinates detailed contact corrections with whole-body posture adjustments to generate natural, precise human-object interactions.

title: MaMi-HOI: Harmonizing Global Kinematics and Local Geometry for Human-Object Interaction Generation

abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have recently gained significant attention due to their inherent support for parallel decoding. Building on this paradigm, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) dLLMs with autoregressive (AR) initialization have further demonstrated strong performance competitive with mainstream AR models. However, we identify a fundamental mismatch between MoE architectures and diffusion-based decoding. Specifically, a large number of experts are activated at each denoising step, while only a small subset of tokens is ultimately accepted, resulting in substantial inference overhead and limiting their deployment in latency-sensitive applications. In this work, we propose TEAM, a plug-and-play framework that accelerates MoE dLLMs by enabling more accepted tokens with fewer activated experts. TEAM is motivated by the observation that expert routing decisions exhibit strong temporal consistency across denoising levels as well as spatial consistency across token positions. Leveraging these properties, TEAM employs three complementary expert activation and decoding strategies, conservatively selecting necessary experts for decoded and masked tokens and simultaneously performing aggressive speculative exploration across multiple candidates. Experimental results demonstrate that TEAM achieves up to 2.2$\times$ speedup over vanilla MoE dLLM, with negligible performance degradation. Code is released at https://github.com/PKU-SEC-Lab/TEAM-MoE-dLLM.

The finding indicates that expert activation and token acceptance can be coordinated more efficiently in the evaluated settings. summary.tldr: TEAM exploits routing consistency to reduce expert activation and increase accepted tokens, accelerating MoE diffusion language models by up to 2.2 times.

title: TEAM: Temporal–Spatial Consistency Guided Expert Activation for MoE Diffusion Language Model Acceleration

abstract: Recent advances in large-scale diffusion models have intensified concerns about their potential misuse, particularly in generating realistic yet harmful or socially disruptive content. This challenge has spurred growing interest in effective machine unlearning, the process of selectively removing specific knowledge or concepts from a model without compromising its overall generative capabilities. Among various approaches, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as an effective and efficient method for fine-tuning models toward targeted unlearning. However, LoRA-based methods often exhibit limited adaptability to concept semantics and struggle to balance removing closely related concepts with maintaining generalization across broader meanings. Moreover, these methods face scalability challenges when multiple concepts must be erased simultaneously. To address these limitations, we introduce UnHype, a framework that incorporates hypernetworks into single- and multi-concept LoRA training. The proposed architecture can be directly plugged into Stable Diffusion as well as modern flow-based text-to-image models, where it demonstrates stable training behavior and effective concept control. During inference, the hypernetwork dynamically generates adaptive LoRA weights based on the CLIP embedding, enabling more context-aware, scalable unlearning. We evaluate UnHype across several challenging tasks, including object erasure, celebrity erasure, and explicit content removal, demonstrating its effectiveness and versatility.

UnHype introduces a hypernetwork to make those low-rank modifications adapt to context.

These results support the framework’s versatility across the tested concepts and model families, with dynamic weight generation providing the proposed route to more adaptable and scalable unlearning.
summary.tldr: UnHype generates LoRA weights from CLIP embeddings to support adaptive single- and multi-concept removal in image generators.

title: UnHype: CLIP-Guided Hypernetworks for Dynamic LoRA Unlearning

abstract: Block-wise diffusion language models (DLMs) generate multiple tokens in parallel, offering a promising alternative to autoregressive decoding. However, their inference efficiency remains bottlenecked by memory-bound attention in long-context scenarios. Naïve sparse attention is ineffective for DLMs due to the KV inflation problem: different queries select different prefix positions, causing the union of accessed KV pages to remain large. To address this challenge, we observe that block-wise diffusion exhibits locality of representation changes across denoising steps: only a small fraction of tokens (active tokens) undergo significant hidden-state updates, while most tokens (stable tokens) remain nearly unchanged. Based on this insight, we propose LoSA (Locality-aware Sparse Attention), which reuses cached prefix-attention results for stable tokens and applies sparse attention only to active tokens with large representation changes. This design reduces the number of queries contributing to the union of KV indices, substantially shrinking the KV pages that must be loaded. Across multiple block-wise DLMs and reasoning benchmarks, LoSA preserves near-dense accuracy while significantly improving efficiency, achieving up to 4.14$\times$ speedup over dense attention on RTX A6000 GPUs. LoSA also delivers up to 5% average improvement over baselines across all datasets and configurations, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method.

Simply making each query sparse does not necessarily solve this problem. Different queries may select different prefix positions, so their combined requests still load a large collection of key-value memory pages.

LoSA uses an observation about successive denoising steps: only a small fraction of tokens undergo large changes in their hidden representations. It reuses cached prefix-attention results for stable tokens and computes sparse attention for active tokens with substantial changes. The reported speedup reaches 4.14 times over dense attention on RTX A6000 GPUs. These findings show how temporal stability during denoising can make sparsity more effective at the memory-system level. The method reduces repeated attention work while directly addressing the combined memory footprint of active queries.
summary.tldr: LoSA reuses attention results for stable tokens and sparsifies changing tokens, reaching up to 4.14-times speedup with near-dense accuracy.

title: LoSA: Locality Aware Sparse Attention in Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Zero-shot 3D anomaly detection is essential for industrial quality inspection, where labeled anomaly samples are scarce. Meanwhile, existing methods lack an effective mechanism to fuse complementary 2D color images with 3D geometric structures, limiting their ability to detect both surface and structural defects in a unified framework. To address these issues, we propose CoGeoAD, a unified CLIP-based framework that fuses color and geometric features by constructing pixel-aligned paired multi-view images. The framework introduces a Data-Driven Multi-View Attention (MVA) mechanism to adaptively aggregate 3D features and a Multi-Stage Color-Geometric Fusion (MS-CGF) module to hierarchically integrate multi-level features from both modalities. Extensive experiments on the MVTec3D-AD and Eyecandies benchmarks demonstrate that CoGeoAD achieves state-of-the-art performance, effectively capturing both structural and textural anomalies in complex industrial scenarios.

paragraphs: Industrial inspection needs to recognize defects even when labeled examples of those defects are scarce. Color images and three-dimensional measurements provide complementary evidence: appearance helps reveal surface irregularities, while geometry captures structural problems. CoGeoAD addresses the difficulty of combining these signals within one zero-shot anomaly detection framework.

The CLIP-based approach constructs paired images from multiple viewpoints, with corresponding pixels aligned between color and geometric information. That alignment gives the system a common spatial reference for combining the two modalities. A learned multi-view attention mechanism adaptively aggregates geometric features, while a separate fusion module integrates color and geometry at multiple feature levels.

These components address two different decisions: how to combine information across viewpoints, and how to combine appearance with structure. Experiments on MVTec3D-AD and Eyecandies report state-of-the-art performance and effective detection of both structural and textural anomalies. The findings support the usefulness of explicitly aligning and hierarchically combining complementary inspection signals in the evaluated industrial scenarios.
summary.tldr: CoGeoAD aligns and combines color and geometric views to improve zero-shot detection of both surface and structural defects.

title: CoGeoAD: Hierarchical Color-Geometric Fusion with Multi-View Attention for Zero-Shot 3D Anomaly Detection

abstract: Existing multimodal large language models for long-video understanding predominantly rely on uniform sampling and single-turn inference, limiting their ability to identify sparse yet critical evidence amid extensive redundancy. We introduce Video-o3, a novel framework that supports iterative discovery of salient visual clues, fine-grained inspection of key segments, and adaptive termination once sufficient evidence is acquired. Technically, we address two core challenges in interleaved tool invocation. First, to mitigate attention dispersion induced by the heterogeneity of reasoning and tool-calling, we propose Task-Decoupled Attention Masking, which isolates per-step concentration while preserving shared global context. Second, to control context length growth in multi-turn interactions, we introduce a Verifiable Trajectory-Guided Reward that balances exploration coverage with reasoning efficiency. To support training at scale, we further develop a data synthesis pipeline and construct Seeker-173K, comprising 173K high-quality tool-interaction trajectories for effective supervised and reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments show that Video-o3 substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 72.1% accuracy on MLVU and 46.5% on Video-Holmes. These results demonstrate Video-o3’s strong multi-hop evidence-seeking and reasoning capabilities, and validate the effectiveness of native tool invocation in long-video scenarios.

summary.tldr: Video-o3 iteratively searches and inspects long-video evidence using native tool calls, improving evaluated multi-hop reasoning performance.

title: Video-o3: Native Interleaved Clue Seeking for Long Video Multi-Hop Reasoning

abstract: Flow Matching models have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of generative tasks. However, their reliance on ODE-based iterative sampling incurs substantial computational overhead, which limits their applicability in real-time scenes. While distillation is a promising solution, existing approaches largely borrow from diffusion-based score matching, often failing to exploit the intrinsic geometric structure of flows and suffering from training instability, high variance, and degraded generation quality. In this paper, we propose Mean Flow Distillation (MFD), a novel distillation framework tailored for flow matching models. We theoretically demonstrate that MFD acts as a temporal low-pass filter, effectively suppressing the high-frequency optimization noise inherent in variational score distillation (VSD) while ensuring global trajectory consistency. We further prove the Mean Flow Matching Theorem, establishing that matching expected average velocities is sufficient for strict distribution alignment. Empirically, on challenging high-dimensional manifolds including 4D occupancy forecasting and text-to-image generation, MFD achieves state-of-the-art performance, enabling high-fidelity single-step generation.

paragraphs: Flow matching models generate samples through iterative numerical integration, which can make them expensive for real-time use. Distillation aims to compress that process into fewer steps. This paper argues that methods borrowed from diffusion-based score matching can overlook flow geometry and suffer from unstable training, noisy optimization signals, and reduced generation quality.

Mean Flow Distillation builds the distillation objective around average flow behavior. The theoretical analysis describes it as a temporal low-pass filter: it suppresses rapidly varying optimization noise associated with variational score distillation while maintaining consistency across the full trajectory. The Mean Flow Matching Theorem further establishes that matching expected average velocities is sufficient for strict distribution alignment.

That theorem provides a sufficient route to alignment, without claiming that average-velocity matching is the only possible route. Empirical evaluations cover 4D occupancy forecasting and text-to-image generation on high-dimensional manifolds. The authors report state-of-the-art performance and high-fidelity generation in a single step, supporting flow-specific distillation as a way to combine faster sampling with more stable optimization.
summary.tldr: Mean Flow Distillation uses average flow velocities to stabilize distillation and enable high-fidelity single-step generation.

title: Mean Flow Distillation: Robust and Stable Distillation for Flow Matching Models

abstract: Large language models offer a tempting solution to address the peer review crisis. This position paper argues that today’s AI systems should not be used to produce paper reviews. We ground this position in an empirical comparison of human- versus AI-generated ICLR 2026 reviews and an evaluation of the effect of automated paper rewriting on different AI reviewers. We identify two critical issues: 1) AI reviewers exhibit a hivemind effect of excessive agreement within and across papers that reduces perspective diversity. 2) AI review scores are trivially gameable through paper laundering: prompting an LLM to rewrite a paper could significantly increase the scores from AI reviewers, demonstrating that LLM reviewers are easy to game through stylistic changes rather than scientific results. However, non-gameability and review diversity are necessary but not sufficient conditions for automation. We argue that addressing the peer review crisis requires a science of peer review automation – not general-purpose LLMs deployed without rigorous evaluation.

paragraphs: This position paper argues against using today’s AI systems to produce scientific paper reviews. The authors support their position with an empirical comparison of human and AI reviews for ICLR 2026, alongside tests of how automated paper rewriting affects different AI reviewers. Their concern is whether automated reviewing preserves independent perspectives and evaluates scientific substance reliably.

They report two problems. First, AI reviewers agree excessively within and across papers, reducing diversity of perspective. Second, prompting a language model to rewrite a paper can substantially raise scores from AI reviewers through stylistic changes. The authors call this paper laundering: the evaluation can be influenced without corresponding changes to the scientific results.

These findings motivate a broader demand for rigorous research on peer-review automation before deployment. The authors explicitly state that diversity and resistance to manipulation are necessary but insufficient conditions for automation. Fixing those two observed problems would therefore not, by itself, establish that automated reviewing is appropriate. Their proposed direction is a science of review automation that evaluates whether systems meet the requirements of the task.
summary.tldr: Observed excessive agreement and easily manipulated scores motivate rigorous evaluation before AI systems are used to write peer reviews.

abstract: The supremacy of n-gram models in statistical language modelling has recently been challenged by parametric models that use distributed representations to counteract the difficulties caused by data sparsity. We propose three new probabilistic language models that define the distribution of the next word in a sequence given several preceding words by using distributed representations of those words. We show how real-valued distributed representations for words can be learned at the same time as learning a large set of stochastic binary hidden features that are used to predict the distributed representation of the next word from previous distributed representations. Adding connections from the previous states of the binary hidden features improves performance as does adding direct connections between the real-valued distributed representations. One of our models significantly outperforms the very best ngram models.

We show how real-valued distributed representations for words can be learned at the same time as learning a large set of stochastic binary hidden features that are used to predict the distributed representation of the next word from previous distributed representations. Adding connections from the previous states of the binary hidden features improves performance as does adding direct connections between the real-valued distributed representations. paragraphs: The paper proposes three probabilistic language models that predict the next word from several preceding words. Their motivation is data sparsity, a challenge for language modeling that distributed word representations can help address. The models use real-valued representations of words as part of the mechanism for predicting the next-word distribution.

These representations are learned jointly with a large set of stochastic binary hidden features. The hidden features are used to predict the next word's distributed representation from those of previous words. Learning both components together links the word representation to the predictive structure of the language model.

The authors find that connecting the binary hidden features to their previous states improves performance. Direct connections between real-valued word representations also help. One of the three models significantly outperforms the strongest n-gram models in the reported comparison. The findings support both the distributed-representation approach and particular connection patterns within these graphical models, rather than attributing the same result to all three variants.
summary.tldr: Three language models jointly learn word representations and stochastic hidden features, with one significantly outperforming the best n-gram models in the reported comparison.

title: Three new graphical models for statistical language modelling

abstract: Statistical and computational concerns have motivated parameter estimators based on various forms of likelihood, e.g., joint, conditional, and pseudolikelihood. In this paper, we present a unified framework for studying these estimators, which allows us to compare their relative (statistical) efficiencies. Our asymptotic analysis suggests that modeling more of the data tends to reduce variance, but at the cost of being more sensitive to model misspecification. We present experiments validating our analysis.

In this paper, we present a unified framework for studying these estimators, which allows us to compare their relative (statistical) efficiencies. paragraphs: Parameter estimation can be based on different likelihood objectives, including joint likelihood, conditional likelihood, and pseudolikelihood. Statistical and computational considerations motivate these alternatives, but comparing their statistical behavior requires a common basis. This paper develops a unified framework for studying their relative statistical efficiencies.

The analysis is asymptotic, examining estimator behavior in a large-sample regime. Its main conclusion suggests a tradeoff: modeling more of the data tends to reduce variance, but also makes the estimator more sensitive to model misspecification. In plain terms, broader modeling can make estimates less variable while increasing their exposure to incorrect modeling assumptions.

The authors present experiments that validate the analysis. The findings do not establish that one likelihood objective is always preferable; the stated tendency depends on the balance between variance reduction and sensitivity to misspecification. The framework matters because it explains these estimators through a shared statistical tradeoff, rather than treating generative, discriminative, and pseudolikelihood estimation as unrelated choices.
summary.tldr: A unified asymptotic analysis suggests that modeling more data reduces variance but increases sensitivity to model misspecification.

title: An asymptotic analysis of generative, discriminative, and pseudolikelihood estimators

abstract: Inspired by co-training, many multi-view semi-supervised kernel methods implement the following idea: find a function in each of multiple Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHSs) such that (a) the chosen functions make similar predictions on unlabeled examples, and (b) the average prediction given by the chosen functions performs well on labeled examples. In this paper, we construct a single RKHS with a data-dependent �co-regularization� norm that reduces these approaches to standard supervised learning. The reproducing kernel for this RKHS can be explicitly derived and plugged into any kernel method, greatly extending the theoretical and algorithmic scope of co-regularization. In particular, with this development, the Rademacher complexity bound for co-regularization given in (Rosenberg & Bartlett, 2007) follows easily from well-known results. Furthermore, more refined bounds given by localized Rademacher complexity can also be easily applied. We propose a co-regularization based algorithmic alternative to manifold regularization (Belkin et al., 2006; Sindhwani et al., 2005a) that leads to major empirical improvements on semi-supervised tasks. Unlike the recently proposed transductive approach of (Yu et al., 2008), our RKHS formulation is truly semi-supervised and naturally extends to unseen test data.

paragraphs: Multi-view semi-supervised learning uses several representations of the same examples. The methods considered here learn a prediction function for each view, encourage agreement on unlabeled examples, and require their average prediction to fit labeled examples. Agreement gives the unlabeled data a role in shaping the learned functions.

The paper combines this arrangement into a single reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS, with a data-dependent norm encoding co-regularization. Its kernel can be derived explicitly and used in any kernel method. Once this construction is made, the learning problem takes the form of standard supervised learning, while the kernel retains the influence of the unlabeled examples and multiple views.

This reformulation also makes existing tools for bounding model complexity directly applicable, including more refined localized bounds. The authors propose an alternative to manifold regularization and report major empirical improvements on semi-supervised tasks. Their formulation naturally predicts on unseen test examples, extending its use beyond assigning labels only to the points already included during training.
summary.tldr: A single data-dependent kernel captures multi-view co-regularization, enabling standard kernel methods, existing theory, and prediction on unseen examples.

title: An RKHS for multi-view learning and manifold co-regularization

abstract: To optimize unknown `fitness' functions, we introduce Natural Search, a novel stochastic search method that constitutes a principled alternative to standard evolutionary methods. It maintains a multinormal distribution on the set of solution candidates. The Natural Gradient is used to update the distribution's parameters in the direction of higher expected fitness, by efficiently calculating the inverse of the exact Fisher information matrix whereas previous methods had to use approximations. Other novel aspects of our method include optimal fitness baselines and importance mixing, a procedure adjusting batches with minimal numbers of fitness evaluations. The algorithm yields competitive results on a number of benchmarks.

The Natural Gradient is used to update the distribution's parameters in the direction of higher expected fitness, by efficiently calculating the inverse of the exact Fisher information matrix whereas previous methods had to use approximations. Other novel aspects of our method include optimal fitness baselines and importance mixing, a procedure adjusting batches with minimal numbers of fitness evaluations. The algorithm yields competitive results on a number of benchmarks.

paragraphs: Natural Search is a stochastic method for optimizing an unknown fitness function. It maintains a multivariate normal distribution over candidate solutions and changes that distribution in the direction of higher expected fitness. The search therefore learns how to generate promising candidates by updating the parameters of its candidate distribution.

The update uses the natural gradient. A central technical contribution is efficiently calculating the inverse of the exact Fisher information matrix, where previous methods relied on approximations. The paper presents this as a principled alternative to standard evolutionary methods, with the geometry represented by the Fisher information entering the distribution update directly.

The method also introduces optimal fitness baselines and importance mixing. Importance mixing adjusts batches while minimizing the number of fitness evaluations needed, making the cost of evaluating candidates an explicit concern. Benchmark results are competitive. Taken together, the contributions combine an exact information-matrix calculation with procedures for managing fitness information and evaluation effort, supporting a distinct approach to distribution-based stochastic search.
summary.tldr: Natural Search updates a Gaussian candidate distribution using the natural gradient and reduces evaluation effort through importance mixing.

title: Stochastic search using the natural gradient

abstract: We consider the problem of learning the optimal action-value function in the discounted-reward Markov decision processes (MDPs). We prove a new PAC bound on the sample-complexity of model-based value iteration algorithm in the presence of the generative model, which indicates that for an MDP with N state-action pairs and the discount factor γ∈[0,1) only O ( N log (N/δ)/ ( (1-γ)^3ε^2 ) ) samples are required to find an ε-optimal estimation of the action-value function with the probability 1-δ. We also prove a matching lower bound of Θ ( N log (N/δ)/ ( (1-γ)^3ε^2 ) ) on the sample complexity of estimating the optimal action-value function by every RL algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first matching result on the sample complexity of estimating the optimal (action-)value function in which the upper bound matches the lower bound of RL in terms of N, ε, δ and 1-γ. Also, both our lower bound and our upper bound significantly improve on the state-of-the-art in terms of 1/(1-γ).

paragraphs: The paper studies how many samples are needed to estimate the optimal action-value function in a discounted Markov decision process. The setting assumes access to a generative model. The target is an estimate within a specified error tolerance with a specified high probability, making sample requirements depend on both accuracy and confidence.

For model-based value iteration, the authors establish an upper bound proportional to N log(N/δ) divided by (1−γ)³ε². Here N is the number of state-action pairs, γ is the discount factor, ε is the error tolerance, and δ is the allowed failure probability. The expression describes how larger problems, tighter accuracy requirements, and longer effective reward horizons increase the required data.

A matching lower bound shows that every reinforcement-learning algorithm faces the same order of sample requirements for this estimation problem. Thus, the upper bound matches the fundamental limit in all four parameters. Both bounds improve the stated prior results in their dependence on the discount factor, with the conclusion applying to the generative-model setting analyzed.
summary.tldr: Matching sample-complexity bounds characterize the data needed to estimate optimal action values in discounted MDPs with a generative model.

title: On the Sample Complexity of Reinforcement Learning with a Generative Model

abstract: Recent work in text analysis commonly describes topics in terms of their most frequent words, but the exclusivity of words to topics is equally important for communicating their content.We introduce Hierarchical Poisson Convolution (HPC), a model which infers regularized estimates of the differential use of words across topics as well as word frequency within topics. HPC uses known hierarchical structure on human labeled topics to make focused comparisons of differential usage within each branch of the tree. We develop a parallelized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler that allows for fast and scalable computation.
originalAbstract: Recent work in text analysis commonly describes topics in terms of their most frequent words, but the exclusivity of words to topics is equally important for communicating their content.We introduce Hierarchical Poisson Convolution (HPC), a model which infers regularized estimates of the differential use of words across topics as well as word frequency within topics. HPC uses known hierarchical structure on human labeled topics to make focused comparisons of differential usage within each branch of the tree. We develop a parallelized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler that allows for fast and scalable computation.

paragraphs: Describing a topic through its most frequent words captures what appears often, but does not fully capture what distinguishes that topic. A word can be common within one topic while also appearing broadly elsewhere. This paper treats exclusivity, or how specifically a word belongs to a topic, as equally important for communicating topical content.

The proposed Hierarchical Poisson Convolution model estimates both word frequency within topics and differences in word use across topics. Its estimates are regularized, placing constraints on how freely they can vary. The model uses a known hierarchy of human-labeled topics to focus comparisons within individual branches, so differences in usage are examined in relation to the supplied topic structure.

This approach makes topic description depend on both prevalence and distinctiveness. Its reliance on a known hierarchy is a concrete part of the method: the structure guides which comparisons receive attention. The authors also develop a parallel Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler, providing the computational machinery they describe as enabling fast and scalable estimation.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Poisson Convolution describes topics using both word frequency and distinctiveness, guided by a known hierarchy of labeled topics.

title: Capturing topical content with frequency and exclusivity

abstract: We study the problem of unsupervised domain adaptation, which aims to adapt classifiers trained on a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. Many existing approaches first learn domain-invariant features and then construct classifiers with them. We propose a novel approach that jointly learn the both. Specifically, the proposed method identifies a feature space where data in the source and the target domains are similarly distributed. More importantly, our method learns a discriminative feature space, optimizing an information-theoretic metric as an proxy to the expected misclassification error on the target domain. We show how this optimization can be effectively carried out with simple gradient-based methods and how hyperparameters can be cross validated without demanding any labeled data from the target domain. Empirical studies on the benchmark tasks of visual object recognition and sentiment analysis validate our modeling assumptions and demonstrate significant improvement of our method over competing ones in classification accuracies.

Specifically, the proposed method identifies a feature space where data in the source and the target domains are similarly distributed. More importantly, our method learns a discriminative feature space, optimizing an information-theoretic metric as an proxy to the expected misclassification error on the target domain. We show how this optimization can be effectively carried out with simple gradient-based methods and how hyperparameters can be cross validated without demanding any labeled data from the target domain. paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation transfers a classifier from a labeled source domain to a target domain without target labels. The paper addresses this by learning the feature representation and classifier jointly. This links the search for shared features directly to the classification task they are meant to support.

The method seeks a feature space where source and target data have similar distributions while remaining discriminative. It optimizes an information-theoretic measure as a proxy for expected target classification error. Distribution alignment and class discrimination are therefore both objectives of the learned representation, with the proxy providing a way to pursue target performance without observing target labels.

The authors describe optimization using simple gradient-based methods and a way to cross-validate hyperparameters without labeled target examples. Experiments on visual object recognition and sentiment analysis support their modeling assumptions and show significant accuracy improvements over competing approaches. These findings provide empirical support for joint learning and the information-theoretic objective in the tested adaptation tasks.
summary.tldr: Joint feature and classifier learning uses an information-theoretic objective to improve adaptation to unlabeled target domains in experiments.

title: Information-Theoretical Learning of Discriminative Clusters for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
